paragraphs.text: 1 Now it came to pass in the thirtieth year, in the fourth month, in the fifth day of the month, as I was among the captives by the river of Chebar, that the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God. 2 In the fifth day of the month, which was the fifth year of king Jehoiachin's captivity, 3 The word of the LORD came expressly unto Ezekiel the priest, the son of Buzi, in the land of the Chaldeans by the river Chebar; and the hand of the LORD was there upon him.
The prophet Ezekiel began his book by fixing the date of the first divine vision that was revealed to him, the place where he dwelt at that time, and the circumstances surrounding him.

He says: "Now it came to pass in the thirtieth year" [1]. Most probably he means that when he reached the age of thirty he became a priest, but without any priestly work. Perhaps he meant the thirtieth year from the time King Josiah began the movement of restoring the Temple and the religious reform; it is also possible that he meant the thirtieth year of the reign of Nabopolassar, the father of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, the founder of the Babylonian Empire. Ezekiel was living on the banks of the Chebar canal at Tel Abib or near it (Ezek 3:15).

Ezekiel had reached the lawful age for taking up the priestly work: entering the sanctuary, offering sacrifices, taking part in the daily liturgies, celebrating the feasts and enjoying the joyful praises... But, sadly, he was deprived of all this because of the captivity, so he sat on the banks of the river Chebar weeping over the state of his country, his people and the temple of the Lord, as though he were repeating the psalm that says:
"By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion.
We hanged our harps upon the willows in the midst thereof. For there they that carried us away captive required of us a song of praise; and they that led us away captive said:
Sing us one of the songs of Zion.
How shall we sing the LORD's song in a strange land?!
If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget..." (Ps 137).

Thus the soul of the priest was embittered, and the Spirit lifted him up to the heavens to bring him into the Jerusalem above and let him enjoy the eternal temple. So he does not see the ark of the covenant, the golden lampstand and the altar of incense... etc., but sees the fiery divine chariot and the fiery divine throne. The heavens were opened [1] that he might see the divine mysteries in a manner suited to the circumstances surrounding him, so that his soul might be filled with consolation, as he sees through them human nature, renewed by the fiery Holy Spirit and given to us in Christ Jesus our Lord through the waters of holy Baptism, having become a fiery chariot that carries God Himself!

The heavens were opened before the captive prophet Ezekiel that he might enter, as it were, to the throne of God Almighty, and realize that human affairs do not proceed at random but by a wonderful divine providence, for God, the Ruler of all, cares for everything that touches the life of man. This is the secret of our consolation in the midst of tribulation.
I see (heaven open); others do not see.

Let no one think that heaven is open in a simple material sense. Rather, we who sit here see the heavens open and closed according to our different degrees of worthiness. Perfect faith opens the heavens and doubt closes them.
St. Jerome: This first vision, which will be repeated, serves the following matters:

First: It consoles the broken soul of Ezekiel, that he might repeat the saying: "In the multitude of my thoughts within me thy comforts delight my soul" (Ps 94:19), "For as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so our consolation also aboundeth by Christ" (2 Cor 1:5). For this reason the Apostle Paul probably saw Paradise while he was being stoned at Lystra, and the Apostle John was caught up to the Lord's day while he was exiled on the island of Patmos.

Second: The vision came to suit the circumstances surrounding the ministry, for God grants His vision and His gifts according to the needs of His generosity. When God met Moses, the first leader of the people, who was to bring them across from the state of harsh bondage into the wilderness, to bring them through Joshua into the land of freedom, He appeared to him in the form of the bush full of thorns, burning with fire and not consumed, to declare the mystery of the divine Incarnation, the suffering and the Resurrection. It is as though there is no beginning for the Church except through the work of salvation by the incarnate Christ, crucified and risen from the dead. The miracles that accompanied the prophet Moses came to confirm the same thing. Here, however, the spirit of the people was broken, especially since the Chaldeans were carrying the procession of the god Bel or Marduk through the streets of the capital in splendor and pomp, while this people were deprived of their temple and the songs of rejoicing had ceased among them; so their brokenness appeared as though it were the brokenness of their God. Therefore God did not reveal Himself in a simple burning bush but through the fiery chariot, full of glory and radiance, as though God wanted to assure His prophet and His people that His glory fills heaven and earth even in the moments in which He hands His people over to discipline by the hands of the Gentiles.

Third: This vision declares God's gift to human nature, which is sanctified by the divine Incarnation. The fiery chariot is the holy Church as a divine throne; it represents the universal Church, and it also represents the soul of the believer who has become a member of the Church of God and a burning fiery chariot that carries God within it, by receiving the Holy Spirit in the sacraments of Baptism and the Holy Myron, and by surrendering its life into His hands that He may work in it continually.

Fourth: Perhaps God wanted to declare to the prophet Ezekiel what the servant of the Lord ought to be. If God is a consuming fire, so His servants also ought to be a flame of fire (Ps 104:4); they are made like the fiery chariot, so that by the fiery Holy Spirit they may be able to work for God. In this St. John Chrysostom says: [Whoever takes a leading role must be more radiant than a shining star, so that his life is without blemish, and all look to him and follow his example].

Fifth: Before the survey of the vision it is said: "and the hand of the LORD was there upon him" [3]. This phrase is very dear to the prophet Ezekiel, for if because of the captivity he was deprived of taking up the priestly work by inheritance, yet the hand of the Lord stretched out over him to bless him and entrust him with the spirit of prophecy... He is called by God directly to see the mysteries of the Kingdom of Heaven, and to understand God's plan for all humanity through the generations until the end of the age. God appointed him for the service of the heavenly sanctuaries!

Sixth: In his first homily on the book of Ezekiel, Origen sees that Ezekiel here represents the Lord Christ at the moment of His Baptism. He truly became the son of man, and He is the true Word. He came to us, the captives, not that we might see the fiery chariot but that He might lead us by His Holy Spirit through the waters of Baptism, by the power of His Cross, to His divine throne. He opens His heavens before us, and we find for ourselves a place in the bosom of His Father, in which we settle and in which we rest forever. By His fiery Spirit He transforms His Church into a fiery chariot, and we all rise with our hearts to the throne of His grace, experiencing the pledge of His glory until we see Him face to face.

To understand these matters we need to enter briefly into some details of the vision, which included six things: the wind, the cloud and the fire; the four living creatures; the wheels; the firmament; the likeness of the throne and Him who sat upon it; and finally the rainbow. These carry mysteries concerning the heavenly life, the holy Church, and also the inner life of the believer, especially the servant of the Lord. Since the prophet in this chapter is trying to describe what cannot be described, he often repeats the word "likeness", as though human language, words and symbols could not help him to express what he saw.

entries.section: 1. The wind, the cloud and the fire:

paragraphs.text: "And I looked, and, behold, a whirlwind came out of the north, a great cloud, and a fire infolding itself, and a brightness was about it, and out of the midst thereof as the colour of amber, out of the midst of the fire." [4].

Where the glory of the Lord is revealed, these three things often appear: the stormy wind, the great cloud and the continuous fire. These came together in power on the day of Pentecost in the upper room of Zion, when the Holy Spirit descended upon the disciples to establish the Church of the New Testament, for "suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting. And there appeared unto them tongues as of fire, and it sat upon each of them, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit" (Acts 2:2-4). The stormy wind that filled all the house appeared as a sign of the Church's being filled with the divine Spirit; the continuous fire appeared through the tongues of fire that kindled the hearts of the believers with a divine fire that is not quenched; and the great cloud is the company of the disciples who were sanctified and became a cloud of witnesses for the Lord (Heb 12:1).

As for the stormy wind, we note that the word "wind ruah" in Hebrew is translated wind, spirit or breath according to the text. The connection between wind and spirit does not stop at the limits of the word, for the wind among the Jews was not merely a natural phenomenon, but often carried the meaning of the divine energy revealed in nature. In the Old Testament the divine presence was often linked with the stormy wind. The Lord answered Job out of the whirlwind (Job 28:1), and the Lord spoke to Moses "in the mountain out of the midst of the fire, of the cloud, and of the thick darkness, with a great voice (stormy)" (Deut 5:22). And when Elijah stood on the mountain, "behold, the LORD passed by, and a great and strong wind rent the mountains, and brake in pieces the rocks before the LORD" (1 Kgs 19:11). For this reason the prophet Nahum says: "The LORD hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet" (Nah 1:3). And the psalmist says: "Our God shall come, and shall not keep silence: a fire shall devour before him, and it shall be very tempestuous round about him" (Ps 50:3).

St. Augustine comments on the psalmist's saying thus: [This without doubt makes a kind of separation. It is that separation which they do not expect, when the nets are torn before they bring them to land (Lk 5:6). In the separation a distinction is made between the righteous and the wicked]. It is as though the stormy wind took an eschatological meaning in the mind of St. Augustine. For as long as we are in this world, like fish in the net, the righteous are not separated from the wicked; but when it is brought to land, that is, to the great day of the Lord, the stormy wind separates these from those.

This separation or distinction that accompanies the coming of the great Lord takes place at present inwardly in the heart. On the feast of Pentecost, when the stormy wind blew, it gave the Church the spirit of discernment, not to condemn the wicked outside it but to judge spiritually within it, so that it separates the malicious one who clings to his malice from the simple and pure souls; and so that every member carries within himself the spirit of discernment that condemns the evil or the weakness into which he falls, walking in the light and fleeing from the darkness. He condemns himself and judges his inner depths, his actions and his conduct before he is judged.

In the book of Ezekiel, however, the prophet felt "a stormy wind coming from the north" [4], as though the Lord were affirming that He blows upon His people with the spirit of separation and discernment, to discipline them for their evil and to bring them, through captivity and suffering, into a pure life. The stormy wind or whirlwind comes from the north, and the north among the Jews signified distress and obscurity. Wherever the scorching north wind blows, plagues come and destruction occurs. While the false prophets were speaking smooth things (Isa 30:10), "saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace" (Jer 8:11), to calm the people's fears and to win the leaders to their side at the expense of the truth, the prophets spoke the truth even if it was wounding. This is what the prophet Ezekiel affirms: that God Himself is coming for discipline as in a northern stormy wind!

The Lord Christ linked the divine Spirit with the wind in a new theological understanding, saying: "The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth: so is every one that is born of the Spirit" (Jn 3:8). He revealed that the work of the Holy Spirit in the new birth through Baptism is a hidden, unseen work, yet its work and its effectiveness are perceived in the life of the believer. He blows like the stormy wind to shake the old foundations of the heart and raise up from it a new sanctuary. And the Spirit continues to blow always within us, not as one who comes from outside but as One who dwells in us, working for the growth of our new man; He works in us and we feel Him, but we do not grasp His mysteries. Thus the divine Spirit worked even in the Old Testament, through the discipline of the people coming from the north, in a hidden way that the people could not see, but it was the work of God in them after their return to Him.

As for the great cloud, from of old the divine presence has been linked with the cloud. When the people went out into the wilderness, the Lord went before them by day in a pillar of cloud to lead them the way (Ex 13:21), and the Apostle Paul saw in this a type of the work of the Holy Spirit in Baptism (1 Cor 6:2), by which He brings us across from bondage to the freedom of the glory of the children of God. In more than one place, when Moses spoke with God, the glory of the Lord appeared in the cloud (Ex 16:10; 19:9). And when Moses pitched a special tent outside the camp in which to meet with God, Scripture says: "the cloudy pillar descended, as Moses entered into the tabernacle, and stood at the door of the tabernacle, and the LORD talked with Moses. And all the people saw the cloudy pillar stand at the door of the tabernacle" (Ex 33:9-10). And when the tent of meeting was dedicated, "a cloud covered the tent of the congregation, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle" (Ex 40:34). And when the Temple was built in place of the tent of meeting, on the day of its dedication "the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud: for the glory of the LORD had filled the house of the LORD" (1 Kgs 8:11). And in the New Testament, when the Lord went up with three of the disciples on Mount Tabor and Moses and Elijah appeared, a bright cloud came and overshadowed them (Mt 17:5). And we read in the book of Revelation about the Lord's last coming: "Behold, he cometh with clouds; and every eye shall see him, and they also which pierced him: and all kindreds of the earth shall wail because of him" (Rev 1:7). To what, then, does the cloud point?

A. The saints Cyril the Great, Augustine and Jerome see that the cloud is a symbol of the humanity of the Lord Christ, through which He appeared to us while the divinity was hidden from our eyes; and His appearing on the last day with the clouds means the hiding of the glory of His divinity from the wicked on the day of judgment, so that they do not enjoy it, while the righteous enjoy the glories of the incarnate God and His radiance is unveiled to them.
B. Pope Dionysius of Alexandria sees that the cloud points to the innumerable company of angels who appear surrounding the Lord on the day of His coming.

C. St. Augustine sees that the cloud points to the company of preachers, saying: "The word of God, who is Christ, will be in the cloud, that is, in those who preach the truth"; indeed he sees every member of the members of the Church as representing a cloud, in whom the Lord Christ comes, saying: "He comes now in His members as in the clouds, or He comes in the Church, which is the great cloud".

D. St. Ambrose sees that the cloud that overshadows the Church is the company of the prophets who present to her the person of the Lord Christ through their prophecies, saying: "Moses and Joshua were two clouds. Note that the saints are clouds", "Who are these that fly as a cloud, and as the doves to their houses?" (Isa 60:8). Isaiah and Ezekiel are as two clouds above me; the first showed me the holiness of the Trinity through the Cherubim and Seraphim. The prophets are all clouds, in which Christ came. He came in the Song of Songs in a clear and beloved cloud, shining with the joy of the Bridegroom (Song 3:11). He came in a swift cloud, incarnate of the Virgin, when the prophet saw Him coming as a cloud from the east (Isa 19:1). Rightly he called Him a swift (light) cloud, for there is in Him nothing of earthly attachments to weigh Him down".

E. Speaking of the bright cloud that appeared at the Transfiguration of the Lord Christ, Origen says: "Shall I dare to say that our Savior is also the bright cloud that overshadows the Gospel, the Law and the Prophets, since they received understanding? Those who saw His light in the Gospel, the Law and the Prophets".

As for the continuous fire, it is said of God Himself that He is a consuming fire (Heb 1:9), and His servants are also a flame of fire (Ps 104:4). So the appearing of the divine chariot in a continuous fire declares the presence of God, the burning Fire, who burns the thorns that choke the soul and at the same time grants it an inner illumination, that it may shine like lightning, so that it has "brightness, and out of the midst thereof as the colour of amber, out of the midst of the fire".

St. Cyril of Jerusalem spoke of the fiery Holy Spirit in the human soul through Baptism, saying: [Why do you wonder?! Take an example from reality, though it is poor and commonplace, yet useful for the simple. If fire passes through a piece of iron, it makes it all fire; so one who was cold becomes burning, and if he was black he becomes shining. If fire, which is matter, penetrates iron in this way and works in it without hindrance, and it too is a body (matter), why do you wonder at the Holy Spirit that He penetrates the inner depths of the soul?!].

And St. John Chrysostom says: [Just as the power of fire, when it prevails over veins of raw gold mixed with the dust of the earth, turns them into pure gold, so, and even more than this, the Holy Spirit works in Baptism in those whom He washes, for He turns them into something purer than gold instead of clay. For when the Holy Spirit descends like fire in our souls, He first burns up the image of the earthy in order to give the image of the heavenly, so that it becomes like a bright, shining coin coming out of the furnaces of the smelter].

St. Augustine comments on the psalmist's words: "A fire goeth before him" (Ps 97:3), saying: [Are you afraid? Let us be changed and we shall not fear! Let the straw fear the fire, but what does the fire do to gold?!]. He also comments on the phrase: "For thou, O God, hast proved us: thou hast tried us, as silver is tried" (Ps 66:10) thus: [Not to burn us with fire like stubble but like silver. By the use of fire You do not turn us into ashes but wash us from defilement].

5 Also out of the midst thereof came the likeness of four living creatures. And this was their appearance; they had the likeness of a man. 6 And every one had four faces, and every one had four wings. 7 And their feet were straight feet; and the sole of their feet was like the sole of a calf's foot: and they sparkled like the colour of burnished brass. 8 And they had the hands of a man under their wings on their four sides; and they four had their faces and their wings. 9 Their wings were joined one to another; they turned not when they went; they went every one straight forward. 10 As for the likeness of their faces, they four had the face of a man, and the face of a lion, on the right side: and they four had the face of an ox on the left side; they four also had the face of an eagle. 11 Thus were their faces: and their wings were stretched upward; two wings of every one were joined one to another, and two covered their bodies. 12 And they went every one straight forward: whither the spirit was to go, they went; and they turned not when they went. 13 As for the likeness of the living creatures, their appearance was like burning coals of fire, and like the appearance of lamps: it went up and down among the living creatures; and the fire was bright, and out of the fire went forth lightning. 14 And the living creatures ran and returned as the appearance of a flash of lightning.

We have already spoken about these heavenly beings and said that they are the two orders of the Cherubim (Kerubim) and the Seraphim, and we pointed to the dignity of this creation, its work, its form and what it signifies, at some length in our interpretation of the fourth chapter of the book of Revelation; but we add here the following:

A. In the book of Revelation St. John saw one face for each living creature, so that he saw in the four only four faces. The prophet Ezekiel, however, says that he saw four faces for each living creature, a face on each side. Perhaps the reason is that the former looked at this creation from one side, while the latter looked at it from all sides, since he saw the chariot in a state of movement in every direction.

These faces, as St. John Chrysostom sees them, point to the intercession of these spiritual beings for the human race (like the face of a man), for the beasts of the wilderness (the likeness of the face of a lion), the animals of the field (the likeness of the face of an ox) and the birds of heaven (the likeness of the face of an eagle), because they are beings nearer to God, to whom be glory, than the rest of the heavenly spiritual beings.

If we take the interpretation of St. Gregory of Nazianzus and Origen, we see in the fiery chariot the soul sanctified with all its powers to carry the divine throne: the lion points to the irascible power, the ox to the appetitive, the man to the rational (the mind), and the eagle to the spiritual. This is the work of the Holy Spirit in the soul: He enkindles our powers with His fire, not to destroy them but to sanctify them and make them complete together, so that we become like a fiery chariot that carries God in it!

If we take the interpretation of St. Victorinus and Irenaeus, we see in these faces a reference to the four Gospels, which bring the soul into salvation, so that it enjoys the Kingdom not as something outside itself but within it, and it becomes itself a sanctuary for the Lord.

If we take the interpretation of St. Jerome, we see that the secret of our bearing God, the consuming Fire, lies in our enjoyment of divine salvation through the Incarnation (the likeness of the face of a man), the crucifixion (the ox), the Resurrection (the lion) and the Ascension (the eagle). By this mystery, the mystery of the incarnate God, crucified, risen from the dead and ascended into the heavens, the soul sets out as a fiery chariot to carry within it, by the Holy Spirit, the divine life.

Finally, if these four beings represent the holy Church that carries the divine life within her, then these four are the episcopate, the presbyterate, the diaconate, and the people. They are the principal pillars that work together for the Lord Christ; any difference in one of the pillars makes the Church lose her balance and harms her message. If a pillar loses its work or its interaction with the other pillars, the whole loses its vitality; for the Church is not centered on a bishop, a priest, a deacon or a lay official (from the people), but is a life that is integrated and interacting together.

B. Each creature appears with four wings, whereas in the book of Revelation each creature has six wings. Perhaps the difference results from the appearance of what the prophet Ezekiel called the firmament over the heads of the living creatures, as though each living creature had lifted two wings above its head in the form of a dome to shield its eyes from the radiance of God's majesty, so that the two raised wings did not appear but the other four. So the soul that enjoys the life of fellowship with God, especially the servant of the Lord, becomes like a cherub with six wings: it covers itself with two wings, flies toward God with two wings, and hides its eyes with the other two wings from the radiance of His majesty! The prophet Ezekiel noticed that the wings of the Cherubim are joined one to another [9]; so if the cherub represents the highest heavenly order, then its holy life, burning with fire, does not accept bearing the divine throne, as a secret, except by its union with the life of others. Perhaps this is what led St. Macarius the Great to say: [That a person's salvation is in the lives of others, for he cannot enjoy salvation isolated from his brother but only as a member with him in the one body of the one Head].

C. Their feet were straight feet, and the sole of their feet was like the sole of a calf's foot, and they sparkled like burnished brass [7]. The straight feet represent the uprightness of the spiritual man, who has two feet like burnished brass, which tread the earth and crush the thorns, and sparkle with the radiance of heavenly things without being soiled by the dust of the world. The true believer walks upon the world without fear, directed toward heaven without being entangled in temporal things.

D. "And they had the hands of a man under their wings on their four sides" [8]. The spiritual man lives flying in the heavenly places as with the wings of the Spirit, and his hands are always ready to work for the Kingdom of God, to serve every human being! He has wings as well as hands! Perhaps the presence of the hands under the wings means that the heavenly beings worship God and serve men; they have the spirit of worship and service together!
E. "Their wings were joined one to another" [9], that is, all worship together in a spirit of love, harmony and unity.

F. Also the prophet looked at these living creatures and saw their faces on every side, as though they had no back, able to move in every direction without turning [9]; as though they had no back, for it is fitting for one who bears the divine throne, having entered into the fullness of glory, not to have a back, but to be all faces and all eyes, ever looking to God without hindrance. Therefore, when the people sinned against God, He rebuked them, saying: "they have turned unto me the back, and not the face" (Jer 2:27). This is the expression that He used more than once on the lips of the prophet Jeremiah (Jer 7:24; 18:17; 32:33), and it is as though the prophet Ezekiel came to complete the words of the prophet Jeremiah in another style: instead of rebuking them for offering the back and not the face, he stirs them to imitate this heavenly creation, so that they have no back at all but their life in the Lord is all faces and meetings with Him!

The prophet describes their movement, saying: "whither the spirit was to go, they went" [12]. For the Holy Spirit is the One who leads the divine procession; He leads the heavenly ones and the earthly ones sanctified in the truth. He repeats the word "went" to confirm the necessity of our commitment to walk according to the plan of the Holy Spirit and under His leadership, without deviation to the right or to the left.

G. The prophet saw the living creatures constantly moving in a harmonious way, like burning coals of fire, like the appearance of lamps of fire, and something like lightning went forth from them [13]. It is a living picture of the work of God in us, who makes us ever moving toward Him; He enkindles us and makes us a burning fire, and enlightens us so that we become like lightning, filled with Him in radiance. We move by the fiery, holy Spirit!
H. The sound of their movement is fearful, like the sound of many waters, like the sound of an army.

This is the work of God in our lives: He makes of the soul a mighty army that Satan and all his forces cannot overcome. For this reason St. Cyril of Jerusalem says to the candidates for Baptism: [Each one of you comes and presents himself before God, in the presence of the innumerable hosts of angels, and the Holy Spirit places a seal upon your souls. By this you enroll yourselves in the army of the great King]. And Father Theodore of Mopsuestia says: [Now you have been chosen for the Kingdom of Heaven, and you can be recognized. If anyone examines you, he will find you a soldier of the King of heaven].

I. In the tenth chapter the prophet Ezekiel called the living creature a cherub. And, remarkably, the cherub is closely linked with our salvation: he appeared in the first of the books of the Bible holding a sword burning with fire, guarding the way to Paradise so that man should not enter to the tree of life, since fallen human nature cannot approach the mystery of life; and he appeared in the last of the books of the Bible with the twenty-four heavenly presbyters sharing in the song of the Lamb, which is the song of our salvation (Rev 5:9), since man has been given the right to enter heaven itself, his nature having been glorified in Christ Jesus, the true Lamb. And between the beginning of the Bible and its end two cherubim also appear on the ark of the covenant in the tent of meeting and the Temple as a sign of the divine presence, and God used to speak with Moses from between them. The presence of two cherubim above the ark of the covenant, which represents the throne of God, points to God who dwells in the midst of His people speaking with them and dealing with them through mercy and love. The presence of two also points to the role of the heavenly ones toward us: praying for us and working as servants for those who are about to inherit salvation (Heb 1:14). And the drawing of the form of the cherub on the curtains of the Tabernacle and the veil (Ex 25-26), nearer to the form of a winged man, declares the drawing near of human nature to the divine presence.

Man came to know the cherub, so that he became not a stranger to humanity; therefore the Gentiles knew him, especially the Chaldeans, although they added to him forms of their own devising, as all the nations did with all the truths of the faith that they received orally by tradition and tinted with their distorted thought.

So when we see the cherub we remember our human nature, which enjoyed salvation through its union with God in Christ Jesus our Lord by His Holy Spirit. His four faces point to the sanctification of our new nature in all its aspects: the intellectual (man), the spiritual (the eagle), work (the ox) and authority (the lion).

J. St. Clement of Alexandria followed Philo the Jew, saying: [The word "cherub" means "knowledge", as though through spiritual knowledge our life becomes a chariot that carries God within it]. This was also accepted by St. Jerome, who saw in the cherub a symbol of the storehouse of knowledge that works in our nature to lift it up and set out with it among the heavenly powers. It works in our nature, ruling over the desires like a lion, soaring in the heavenly things like an eagle, laboring with striving like the ox and with discretion like a man. We draw this knowledge from the four Gospels, for the same saint says: [Matthew, Mark, Luke and John are the Lord's four-fold team, the true Cherubim, or storehouse of knowledge; for their body is full of eyes and shines like lightning..., their feet are straight and lifted up, their back winged, ready to fly in every direction, each of them holding on to the other, interlaced one with another, like wheels in the midst of wheels rolling along the line, moving according to the breathings of the Holy Spirit].

K. "And the living creatures ran and returned as the appearance of a flash of lightning" [14]. Perhaps he thereby points to the service of the heavenly ones who are sent to us but quickly run to return to where the divine throne is, enjoying the vision of God. And the true believer whose heart is kindled with longing for his Savior, from time to time his heart and mind run, and all his senses run, to return like lightning, enjoying contemplation of their Savior. It cries out with the Apostle: "I have a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better" (Phil 1:23).

"15 Now as I beheld the living creatures, behold one wheel upon the earth by the living creatures, with his four faces. 16 The appearance of the wheels and their work was like unto the colour of a beryl: and they four had one likeness: and their appearance and their work was as it were a wheel in the middle of a wheel. 17 When they went, they went upon their four sides: and they turned not when they went. 18 As for their rings, they were so high that they were dreadful; and their rings were full of eyes round about them four. 19 And when the living creatures went, the wheels went by them: and when the living creatures were lifted up from the earth, the wheels were lifted up. 20 Whithersoever the spirit was to go, they went, thither was their spirit to go; and the wheels were lifted up over against them: for the spirit of the living creature was in the wheels. 21 When those went, these went; and when those stood, these stood; and when those were lifted up from the earth, the wheels were lifted up over against them: for the spirit of the living creature was in the wheels." [15-20].

A. What are these wheels upon the earth, which carry within them the spirit of the living creatures, and which move in harmony with them, and at the same time are lifted up, and dreadful, and full of eyes, their appearance like the colour of a beryl, a wheel in the middle of a wheel? St. Jerome answers: [The two wheels are the New and Old Testaments, for the Old moves in the New, and the New moves in the Old]. And he gives proof of this from what is said in the tenth chapter: "As for the wheels, it was cried unto them in my hearing, Gelgel" [(Ezek 10:13) the Septuagint]; for the word Gelgel is different from the word Gilgal, which means rolling (Deut 11:30) or a circle, since the former is made of two words "gal gal" which mean "revelation". It is as though the voice that the prophet Ezekiel heard coming from the wheels was "the revelation of the New Testament and the revelation of the Old Testament". For the two Testaments are joined together for the purpose of declaring the mystery of the salvation of mankind through Christ Jesus, the center of the Gospel. In this St. Ambrose says: [The prophet saw a wheel running in the midst of a wheel. This vision certainly does not refer to a bodily matter but to the grace of the two Testaments. The wheel in the midst of the wheel is life under the Law and life through grace. As long as it is within the Church, grace has contained the Law]. And St. John Chrysostom says: [The two Testaments are bound together and joined one with the other; the Old Testament reveals the mysteries of the New Testament and makes them clear through types and prophecies, and the New Testament reveals the mysteries of the Old Testament that were hidden behind the shadows].

He saw the wheels upon the earth, but their rings were high and dreadful, as though the word of God, presented in the two Testaments, came down to us through our human language so that we might understand it and live it while we are here on earth, and at the same time it is lifted up and dreadful, lifting the soul to the heavenly places and entering into the mysteries full of awe and trembling. As St. John Chrysostom says: [One who has been granted the effectiveness of the word of God cannot remain in this present lowliness, but rather seeks for himself two wings with which he may set out to the high places, discovering the light of the boundless good things].
B. The wheels are linked with the earth, for the fiery chariot is linked with us human beings, so that it may carry us from the dust of this world to the fiery heavenly life.
It is the chariot of God, of whom it is said that His way is in the sanctuary and His way is in the sea (Ps 77:13, 19), the God of heaven and earth together; the whole world glorifies Him.

C. The link of the wheels with the earth confirms that God is the Ruler of history and its Maker; He is the One working in all ages... The wheel of His love and care for the sons of men keeps turning without stopping... even if man does not understand its mysteries and wisdom!

D. As for its appearance, it was like the appearance of a beryl, a kind of very hard precious stone of a light green colour, and it is the tenth stone on the breastplate of the high priest (Ex 28:20), by which he enters the sanctuaries of God. It is as though God grants the soul hardness and strength to face all the wars of Satan; the light green colour points to the fruits it produces in the life of man, for it makes his heart a joyful paradise; and its presence on the breast of the high priest reveals the work of the Word in us, for He makes our names engraved upon the breast of the Lord Christ, the Bishop of our souls, who is in the bosom of His Father, interceding for us by His blood to bring us in to the bosom of His Father. Finally, this stone is one of the stones that adorn the foundations of the walls of the new Jerusalem (Rev 21:20)... as though the word of God were the secret of the adornment of the bride, who enjoys entering the bridal chamber of the Bridegroom forever!

So the word of God is the precious stone of great price which the priest, the monk and the people ought to acquire, as the secret of victory, triumph, union with the Lord Christ and entrance into the heavenly life. Therefore, when Father Ignatius Brianchaninov wrote his book "The Arena of Martyrdom", presenting a method for the monastic life from the Fathers of the Church, he began it by directing the monks' eyes to Holy Scripture and the Gospel commandments, saying: [The early holy monks called the monastic life the life according to the commandments of the Gospel], and St. John Climacus defines the monk thus: The monk is the one who is led by the commandments of God and the word of God at every time, in every place and in every matter. The monks who were subject to St. Pachomius the Great were obliged to learn the Gospel by heart, so that the law of the incarnate God might be like a book always open in the memory, seen constantly by the eyes of the soul, imprinted on the soul so that they might fulfill it easily and without failure. The blessed Elder Seraphim of Sarov says: [We must train ourselves so that the mind is immersed in the law of the Lord, which guides and governs our life].
E. "And their rings were full of eyes round about them four" [18]. The spiritual man carries the spirit of discernment and wisdom, full of eyes...

These rings are high and dreadful [18]; the spiritual man is marked by spiritual loftiness, so that he is counted in the eyes of heaven as high and honored... He is so high that the enemy of good cannot catch him, and dreadful because the Spirit of God who is in him is greater than all satanic powers.

22 And the likeness of the firmament upon the heads of the living creature was as the colour of the terrible crystal, stretched forth over their heads above. 23 And under the firmament were their wings straight, the one toward the other: every one had two, which covered on this side, and every one had two, which covered on that side, their bodies. 24 And when they went, I heard the noise of their wings, like the noise of great waters, as the voice of the Almighty, the voice of speech, as the noise of an host: and when they stood, they let down their wings. 25 And there was a voice from the firmament that was over their heads, when they stood, and had let down their wings.
"And the likeness of the firmament upon the heads of the living creatures was as the colour of the terrible crystal, stretched forth over their heads above" [22].

He saw upon the heads of this living heavenly creation the likeness of the firmament of heaven (the dome) in the form of a canopy. So when the believer presents all his bodily, intellectual, psychological and spiritual powers as holy instruments of righteousness to the Lord, his life is transformed into the likeness of a heavenly canopy that overshadows his inner heart.

In this St. John Saba says: [Behold, heaven is within you if you are pure, and the angels in it you see shining], [The kingdom of the pure of soul is within his heart, and the sun that rises in it is the light of the Holy Trinity, and the air of its breeze is the Holy Spirit the Comforter, and those who dwell with him are the spiritual natures of the pure ones, and their life, their joy and their delight is Christ, the radiance of the Father].

As for the firmament's having the appearance of the terrible crystal stretched forth, this is because the nature of crystal is that it reflects within itself the scene before it, as though it were a mirror; so the scene of the Lord who is carried above the firmament is reflected within the believer. That is, the soul, having become a heaven for the Lord and a sanctuary for Him, has become like the crystal that bears His image and reflects His features in it. This scene reminds us of what St. John saw: "And before the throne there was a sea of glass like unto crystal" (Rev 4:6), and Bishop Victorinus sees that this sea points to Baptism, for everyone who desires to meet Him who sits upon the throne must pass through this sea, so that the grace of God penetrates his soul and it is prepared for the Kingdom. As for its being like crystal, it is because it is fitting that the baptized be steadfast and strong.

As the rays of Him who sits on the throne, the Sun of Righteousness, are reflected on the crystal sea, the colors of the spectrum appear clearly upon the living creatures, that is, the many and varied gifts and endowments of God appear in the life of the believers.

entries.section: 5. The throne and Him who sat upon it:

paragraphs.text: "26 And above the firmament that was over their heads was the likeness of a throne, as the appearance of a sapphire stone: and upon the likeness of the throne was the likeness as the appearance of a man above upon it. 27 And I saw as the colour of amber, as the appearance of fire round about within it, from the appearance of his loins even upward, and from the appearance of his loins even downward, I saw as it were the appearance of fire, and it had brightness round about." [26-27].

When the life of the believer is transformed into a heavenly canopy, the different colors are reflected upon it through the likeness of the crystal, and the throne of God appears upon it, and within it the incarnate Word of God appears as a King enthroned upon the heart. He is like the appearance of a man and at the same time like the colour of amber; from His loins upward kindled with fire, and from His loins downward filled with brightness. Thus the Lord appears to us with the burning fire that consumes all evil in us, and with the radiance that He pours upon our inner depths, so that our inner sight is opened and is filled with glory. He draws near to us for our reconciliation, so He burns in us the works of the old man and fills us with radiance through the new man!

St. Gregory the Theologian saw the mystery of the divine Incarnation revealed through this vision, and said: [This God-bearing chariot is the holy Virgin Mary, whom the Holy Spirit overshadowed, so she became glorified and filled with virtues].

28 As the appearance of the bow that is in the cloud in the day of rain, so was the appearance of the brightness round about. This was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD. And when I saw it, I fell upon my face, and I heard a voice of one that spake.

Where the divine throne appears we see a rainbow around it (Rev 4:3), because the glory of God is not only might and majesty but also boundless love. The rainbow is the sign of love that God gave when He made a covenant with Noah after the Flood (Gen 9), and God remains, as the One who loves mankind, offering us all love through His covenant with us. This bow has many colors that declare God's many kindnesses and gifts to us. And as a bow it points to the bow used in wars, as though God defends us with His bow, but without an arrow because He does not love the shedding of blood; by it we overcome sin and trample upon Satan.

Origen sees that the presence of the four faces together (the lion, the eagle, the ox and the man) is an indication of the return of the holy living creatures to their first tame nature. If in the Messianic age the wolf dwelt with the lamb, the leopard lay down with the kid, and the lion ate straw like the ox (Isa 11:6), then this perfect harmony is realized in the final coming of Christ, where He makes all one in Him, enjoying unity and peace together in Him, where we are found in heaven itself with all the heavenly creation.

Finally, we would like to mention what Father Novation, one of the men of the third century, said about this vision. He saw in the fiery chariot a symbol of God's care and providence, He who condescends for the sake of man. In his opinion the chariot is the world and the stars it contains, with their orderly movements. He said that God governs the world by using the angels, who are symbolized by the living creatures. The wheels are the movement of the seasons and the days, and the feet point to the movement of time. The eyes of the wheels are God's providence, from which nothing is hidden. The fire points to the vital power that refreshes the world, or the heat without which the world would stand still. As for the two loins that restrain the living creature, they are the natural law.
Show me Your heavens!
* I long to see Your heavens!
You revealed Your heavenly chariot to Ezekiel Your prophet, and You opened a door in heaven to John Your disciple, and I long to see Your heavens!
I want to know: where shall I find rest, O Beloved of my soul?!
* In the midst of the bitterness in the land of captivity You revealed Your chariot to Your prophet, so he realized that You are the Maker of history and its Controller!
Reveal Your mysteries to me, and I shall be assured that I am carried on Your arms!

* Ezekiel saw You in the midst of the wind, the cloud and the fire; let Your Holy Spirit breathe upon my soul, that I may inhale a heavenly breeze; that You may lift me up as on the cloud, so that the serpent may not snatch me; and let Your Holy Spirit set my heart ablaze with the fire of Your love!
* Your chariot is exceedingly wonderful, a cherubic chariot, with faces like the face of a man, a lion, an ox and an eagle.
Count me a chariot and a throne on which You sit enthroned within me!
Sanctify all that is in:

the feelings of my heart as a man of God, the strength of my soul as a lion, so that I do not fear, my gifts and offerings as an ox, a burnt sacrifice to You, my thoughts and meditations, that I may fly like the eagle in the heavenlies!
* Grant me, with the cherubim, six wings:
Grant me humility and hope as two wings with which I cover my feet, as it were, from sin!
Grant me insight and love as two wings, that I may behold the splendor of Your glory!
Grant me Your revelations and Your grace as two wings with which I fly to Your embrace!
* Grant me, with the living creatures, eyes within and without!
Grant me heavenly wisdom, that I may live on earth and in the heavenlies!
I see Your heavens, and I long to depart to You!
I see the light of Your face, and I am enlightened by You and become light!
* Grant me eyes on every side, that I may become all face, and have no back at all, so that in every direction I move I do not give You the back but the face.
* How wonderful are these two wheels in Your heavenly chariot, which the Spirit moves without ceasing!
How wonderful are the two Testaments, the Old and the New; by Your Holy Spirit I enjoy their mysteries, and I move always toward heaven!
Their rims are lifted up from the earth to heaven...
That Your word in the two Testaments may lift me up, so that I no longer remain in the dust!
* How beautiful You are, O You who sit on the throne, how wonderful is the rainbow around You!
Show me Yourself... I want to enjoy You!
Grant me steadfast faith in Your precious promises and Your everlasting covenant.

entries.section: 1. Enjoying the experience of the resurrection:

paragraphs.text: 1 And he said unto me, Son of man, stand upon thy feet, and I will speak unto thee.

When the prophet beheld the fiery chariot, he fell upon his face in complete helplessness, as though he had reached death. Therefore the Lord commanded him: "Son of man, stand upon thy feet, and I will speak unto thee" [1]. For one cannot speak with someone who has reached death; rather, it is fitting that he first rise, to enjoy listening to the voice of the Lord. If the mission of God's servants is to bring souls dead in sins into the life of resurrection, then it is all the more fitting for the servants themselves to experience the resurrection within them. This is what happened with Saul of Tarsus, who thought that he was able by himself, by his human zeal, his training in the Law, his personal abilities and his gifts, to serve God; but when he met the Lord Christ he fell to the ground as one dead and realized that he was nothing... Then he heard the divine voice: "Rise, and stand upon thy feet: for I have appeared unto thee for this purpose, to make thee a minister and a witness both of these things which thou hast seen, and of those things in the which I will appear unto thee" (Acts 26:16). So he arose and enjoyed the new life of resurrection; therefore he preached to the Gentiles "Jesus, and the resurrection" (Acts 17:18). This is the message of the disciples and the Apostles, that "with great power gave the apostles witness of the resurrection of the Lord Jesus" (Acts 4:33).

Moreover, the command given to the prophet to rise and stand upon his feet carries an indication of the necessity of working without ceasing, for God does not work in the slack but in those who strive continually. For by constant work we bear a divine mark, as the Lord Himself said: "My Father worketh hitherto, and I work" (Jn 5:17).

The command was given to him to stand upon his feet, fully prepared, to accomplish a holy and weighty mission. He had been deprived of the priestly work because of the captivity, but God calls him to the prophetic work, to present the divine will to a rebellious people. Let him stand in reverent awe before God, listening to His voice with all attention in order to fulfill His will.

entries.section: 2. Working by the Spirit of God:

paragraphs.text: 2 And the spirit entered into me when he spake unto me, and set me upon my feet, that I heard him that spake unto me.

The command to rise was given, but how can fallen clay rise?! It needs the Spirit of God Himself, the Giver of life, who grants us union with Christ Jesus who rose from the dead, so that we may experience the power of His resurrection in us.

The prophet Ezekiel describes his resurrection thus: "And the spirit entered into me when he spake unto me, and set me upon my feet, that I heard him that spake unto me" [2]. It is as though he could not hear the divine voice speaking with him, nor enter with Him into the conversation of love, except by the entry of the Holy Spirit into his life. By this he understands the divine words, experiences the divine work, and is able to preach and proclaim by the power of the Spirit!

The prophet Ezekiel began his ministry with the opening of heaven before him, to see the awesome divine chariot; he fell trembling, and needed the Spirit of God to raise him so that he might walk on his feet. As for the Lord Christ, He began His ministry with the opening of heaven, so that those present might realize that He is the only beloved Son of the Father, and behold the Holy Spirit of God resting upon Him in the form of a dove. He opens heaven in order to grant His believers sonship to God, so that they may find a place in the Father's bosom, and receive the Spirit of adoption. The prophet Ezekiel was terrified because through the heavenly chariot he receives the prophecy concerning the divine chastisements, whereas the Lord Christ rejoiced because by His baptism He proclaims the forgiveness of sins and the enjoyment of the believers in the New Covenant of the merits of His precious blood.

3 And he said unto me, Son of man, I send thee to the children of Israel, to a rebellious nation that hath rebelled against me: they and their fathers have transgressed against me, even unto this very day. 4 For they are impudent children and stiffhearted. I do send thee unto them; and thou shalt say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD. 5 And they, whether they will hear, or whether they will forbear, (for they are a rebellious house,) yet shall know that there hath been a prophet among them.

If the work of the Holy Spirit in the life of believers in general is to bring them into the resurrection of the Lord Christ, so that in Baptism they receive the new life in the image of their Creator, then the same Spirit works in the servants of the Church, that they may go down to where people lie in the death of sin, and lead them to the joyful proclamation of their resurrection with Christ and their enjoyment of the risen life. This is the work of the servant... It is a work above all human capacity, it is the work of God Himself, and the servant is only a steward of the mysteries of God. This is what the Lord affirmed, saying: "Son of man, I send thee to the children of Israel, to a rebellious nation that hath rebelled against me: they and their fathers have transgressed against me, even unto this very day. For they are impudent children and stiffhearted. I do send thee unto them" [3-4].

It is as though God confirms to him the difficulty of the work: the matter requires going down to rebellious people, impudent and stiffhearted from father to grandfather. Who then will lead them to obedience instead of rebellion, to gentleness instead of harshness, and to an open heart instead of its hardness and closedness?! It is the work of God Himself; therefore He affirms more than once, "I do send thee unto them." It is My mission and not yours, that I work in the heart within, create it anew and grant it life!

This is what all who labor faithfully in the Lord's vineyard have realized. The Apostle Paul says: "Let a man so account of us, as of the ministers of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God" (1 Cor 4:1). He realized that he is merely a steward who speaks and works not in his own name but in the name of the one who appointed him. St. John Chrysostom comments on this saying thus: [The steward manages the affairs of his master well without attributing to himself what belongs to his master; on the contrary, he attributes what he has to his lord... Do you want an example of faithful stewards? Hear what Peter says: Why look ye so earnestly on us, as though by our own power or holiness we had made this man to walk? (Acts 3:12). And with Cornelius also he said: "Stand up; I myself also am a man." ... And Paul is no less faithful in his saying: "I laboured more abundantly than they all: yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me" (1 Cor 15:10)... And when the Apostle opposed those unfaithful persons he said: "And what hast thou that thou didst not receive?" (1 Cor 4:7)].

The servant, as a steward, works on behalf of his master and not on behalf of himself. Therefore St. John Chrysostom was always wary of the love of vainglory and praise, lest he be usurping the right of God Himself. In this he says: "Surely the mystery of the priesthood will condemn us if we do not use it well," and he also says: [He who enters the work of preaching with such desires (love of praise), what pains and hardships pursue him! It is easier for the sea to be without waves than for such a person to be without troubles or sorrows]. The saint feared for himself as Patriarch of Constantinople, so he said: [I shed tears when I see myself on a throne above the thrones of others, and when more honor is offered to me than to others].

It is not the work of Christ's ambassadors to offer eloquent human phrases, nor to display their achievements and glorify their personal efforts, but to proclaim the word of the Lord Himself, and to call to repentance in a spirit of meekness and humility. The word of the Lord is strong and able, for "where the word of a king is, there is power" (Eccl 8:4), and God is the King of kings; His word shall not return void, without fruit (Isa 55:11).

The sense of stewardship gives the servant strength, so that he does not fear the work however difficult or seemingly impossible, working leaning on the breast of the One who appointed him, whatever the results may be, as he hears the divine voice: "I do send thee unto them... And they, whether they will hear, or whether they will forbear, (for they are a rebellious house,) yet shall know that there hath been a prophet among them" [5]. This does not mean that God does not know whether they will hear or disobey, but He speaks thus in order to leave them the freedom of obedience or disobedience, so that they will have no excuse that He judged them with disobedience beforehand. As St. John Chrysostom says: [He did not say this out of ignorance, but lest any of the obstinate say that his prophecy bound them to disobedience].

6 And thou, son of man, be not afraid of them, neither be afraid of their words, though briers and thorns be with thee, and thou dost dwell among scorpions: be not afraid of their words, nor be dismayed at their looks, though they be a rebellious house. 7 And thou shalt speak my words unto them, whether they will hear, or whether they will forbear: for they are most rebellious.
"And thou, son of man, be not afraid of them, neither be afraid of their words, for they are briers (brambles)
and thorns (prickles) with thee, and thou dost dwell among scorpions. Be not afraid of their words, nor be afraid of their looks.
Be not dismayed, for they are a rebellious house" [6].

The divine mission is not easy, for the servant works as though in the midst of brambles and surrounded by thorns that spoil God's tillage, and like one who dwells among scorpions he is exposed to hidden stings. Yet he must not fear people, nor be troubled by their words or their faces, but, as God had previously commanded Joshua the son of Nun thus:
"Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest" (Josh 1:9).

Indeed, God warned the prophet Jeremiah against fear, saying to him: "Arise, and speak unto them all that I command thee: be not dismayed at their faces, lest I confound thee before them. For, behold, I have made thee this day a defenced city, and an iron pillar, and brasen walls against the whole land... And they shall fight against thee; but they shall not prevail against thee; for I am with thee, saith the LORD, to deliver thee" (Jer 1:17-19). It is as though God threatens His servant that if he is dismayed, not only will He not protect him, but He Himself will terrify him, for He does not work in the heart that does not lean on Him.

St. John Chrysostom has presented to us a wonderful example of a father filled with tenderness, so that he loved his people more than the light of his eyes; if one of his children fell into sin, he felt within himself as though he were in great danger, like one in a dark prison, or one sentenced to ten thousand lashes, or confined in a deep pit. Therefore he used to cry out to his children, saying: [I can no longer bear more than this! Stretch out your hands toward me and rescue me]. And yet he was frank and courageous, speaking boldly and with power, without fear, saying: [I am ready to bear everything. Whoever persists in his conduct and does not listen to my warning, I will bar from entering the church as with the sound of a trumpet, even if he is a prince or an emperor. How can I sit on this chair if I do not do what befits it?! It is better for me to step down from it, for there is nothing more bitter than a bishop who is of no benefit to his people].

God called the rebellious people brambles, thorns and scorpions, not that the servant should despair of them or despise them, but that he may know the difficulty of the work and prepare for it, and say with righteous Job: "I am a brother to dragons, and a companion to owls" (Job 30:29), remembering the words of the Apostle: "That ye may be blameless and harmless, the sons of God, without rebuke, in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom ye shine as lights in the world" (Phil 2:15).

Some may object, saying: Why did the Lord call them thus? St. Clement of Alexandria answers: [This is a very great proof of His love, for despite His perfect knowledge of the shameful state to which the people had come, so that He drove them out and uprooted them (from Jerusalem), He urges them to repentance].

God speaks with all frankness with His servants, declaring to them the difficulty of their mission, for in every generation they find those who resist the truth; and they must prepare to endure pain and persecution, realizing that God grants them grace to be strong to face the opposing currents, so that the servant may know that the path of service is not strewn with roses, but is the narrow way of the cross, which inevitably ends with the joy of the resurrection. Our God has not deceived us, but He reveals to us plainly the difficulty and distress of the way.

God says: "And thou shalt speak my words unto them, whether they will hear, or whether they will forbear: for they are most rebellious" [7]. It is as though his mission is poured into presenting the word of God as it is; they may hear and repent, or they may refrain from responding to the divine voice... So be it. For the success of the servant lies in his faithfulness in presenting the word of the Lord as it is, that is, being faithful in the divine deposit.
8 But thou, son of man, hear what I say unto thee; Be not thou rebellious like that rebellious house.

Although God chose him for the prophetic work and knows his heart and his striving, yet He warns him, saying: "Be not thou rebellious like that rebellious house" [8]. He feared for him lest, while he preaches obedience to the people, he himself fall with them into rebellion instead of raising them up. It is as though God wanted to affirm to His servant that he should not forget the salvation of his soul and his spiritual life during his service, because many have lost their peace and their salvation during their human zeal and their labor in service. For this reason the Apostle Paul says: "I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway" (1 Cor 9:27). This is what moved St. John Chrysostom, whose heart melted with love for the sake of service, to be watchful not only for the salvation of his brethren but also for the salvation of his own soul, saying: [My words are of more benefit to my own life than to those who hear me], and he also says: [I know the seriousness of this office and the difficulty of its work, and the violent storms that sweep over the soul of the priest, for they are more severe in their turbulence than the storms of the sea].

entries.section: 6. Enjoying the experience of the word of God:

paragraphs.text: 8 open thy mouth, and eat that I give thee. 9 And when I looked, behold, an hand was sent unto me; and, lo, a roll of a book was therein; 10 And he spread it before me; and it was written within and without: and there was written therein lamentations, and mourning, and woe. [8-10].

The subject of his work is "the word of God," which the servant must eat, so that his inner depths are filled with it, and it becomes the subject of his continual thought, and he even hides in it, so that he presents nothing of himself but presents what belongs to God.

Eating the word means its entering into his depths; it turns in his life into blood that flows in his veins. It is as though he is blended with it, and counts it as his life! He eats it and lives by it in order to present it to others by presenting his evangelical life as an epistle read of all men.

St. John Chrysostom was accustomed to present to his people from the table of the Holy Bible almost every day, giving special attention to the Gospel and apostolic word. In one of his homilies he says:
[You have heard the apostolic voice!
It is a heavenly trumpet! It is the harp of the Spirit!
Yes. The reading of the Holy Scriptures is a garden, indeed, it is a paradise also, which offers not only fragrant flowers but also fruits that can nourish the soul...!

We are like men who smelt gold extracted from the apostolic mines, not by throwing it into a furnace, but by depositing it in the minds of your souls, not by kindling an earthly fire but by the inflaming of the Spirit.
So let us gather from it small pieces with diligence and effort... for pearls are not valued according to their size but according to the beauty of their nature].

He received a book written without and within. Perhaps he meant that the word of God is declared outwardly in letters on paper, but the matter needs the work of the Holy Spirit, who reveals in the heart the writing that is within, that is, the deep inner meaning. Perhaps he also meant that this book contains on the outside the sins of the people and their transgressions, while within it carries God's chastisements for their repentance.

entries.section: 6. Enjoying the experience of the word of God:

paragraphs.text: As for the writing, as it came in the Septuagint: "lamentations, and a song, and woe" [10]; the following are some comments of the Fathers on this phrase:
*The whole book is full of woe for the perishing, a song for the saved, and lamentations for those between the two (that is, those on the path of repentance).

Origen * It contains two sorrowful things and one joyful; for whoever weeps much in this time will be saved in the future, because "the heart of the wise is in the house of mourning; but the heart of fools is in the house of mirth" (Eccl 7:4), and as the Lord Himself says: "Blessed are ye that weep now: for ye shall laugh" (Lk 6:21).

St. Ambrose * Written in it are lamentations, a song and woe. The first of these three concerns you if, as a sinner, you repent of your sins; the second concerns the saints who are called to sing, praising God, because praise is not in the mouth of sinners; and the third concerns those who are in despair like you and have given themselves over to uncleanness, fornication, gluttony and base lusts, people who think that death is the end of everything, and that after death there is nothing else, who say: "When the overflowing scourge shall pass through, it shall not come unto us" (Isa 28:15).
The book that the prophet eats is the whole collection of the Holy Scriptures, which makes the penitent lament, the righteous honored, and gives woe to the despairing.
St. Jerome
I long to work in Your vineyard
*You revealed Your heavens to Ezekiel Your prophet, and he longed to serve You; reveal them to me, and I will work earnestly in Your vineyard.

Your heavens are joyful and delightful; working with You is a heavy cross, yet it is exceedingly joyful and delightful. How sweet it is to work with You, for You reveal Yourself to those who work for You and with You.

*You sent Your prophet to a very stubborn people, but Your Spirit raised him that he might raise many. Grant me the Spirit of resurrection, so that I do not fear death. Death has crept into me and into my brethren, but You are the very Resurrection. You sent him to a stubborn people, and feared lest stubbornness seep into him.
Keep me lest in my service I grow weak and fall. Keep me by Your grace and keep Your people.
*What shall I offer to my brethren:

Here I open my mouth for You to stretch out Your hand with the scroll; I eat it and find it sweet, O sweetness of my soul. This outstretched hand is none other than Your incarnation and becoming man; You gave me Your body, O Word, that I may partake of it.
*Your word has sweetness and bitterness:
Make it sweet by Your grace, as I acquire Your divine promises.
Grant me to accept Your chastisements as a temporary bitterness for the correction of my soul and its edification forever.

entries.section: 1. The sweetness of the word of God:

paragraphs.text: 1 Moreover he said unto me, Son of man, eat that thou findest; eat this roll, and go speak unto the house of Israel. 2 So I opened my mouth, and he caused me to eat that roll. 3 And he said unto me, Son of man, cause thy belly to eat, and fill thy bowels with this roll that I give thee. Then did I eat it; and it was in my mouth as honey for sweetness.

The command was given to the prophet Ezekiel to eat the scroll (the word of God), as it was given to St. John the Beloved (Rev 10:9). Jeremiah says: "Thy words were found, and I did eat them; and thy word was unto me the joy and rejoicing of mine heart" (Jer 15:16), and the Lord Christ says: "Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God" (Mt 4:4). The word of God is a delicious food, giving life and inner joy and gladness; we are nourished by it, and so we carry it in our depths. It is sweet, even if it carries bitterness because of God's chastisements, which are for our salvation.

When the prophet Ezekiel received His word from the hands of God as an open scroll, he read what was inside it and what was outside, and found that it contained lamentations and woe together with songs of praise; so he opened his mouth for God to feed him with His own hand, and his depths were satisfied, and he found it in his mouth as honey for sweetness.

How wonderful is the love of God! He deals with us as a nurse or a tender mother, stretching out His hand to feed us, the infants beloved to Him. We throw ourselves upon His breast like a nursing child on the breast of its mother, and we find His commandment pure milk coming from His breasts (the two Testaments), like the honey of bees and the honeycomb. His commandment is suitable for the little ones and for the mature grown.

God's commandment is hard and heavy for the natural man; indeed, some sometimes see it as a fetter on human freedom. But when the hand of God is stretched out to present it to us within us, we find it sweet as honey. What is this outstretched hand (Ezek 1:9) that Ezekiel saw but the Son of God, who is called "the arm of the Lord," and who became visible through the divine Incarnation? He presented to us the divine commandment not through commands and prohibitions, but through practical mutual love between God and man, and between man and his brother, offering Himself as an example and helper, for He says: "This is my commandment, That ye love one another, as I have loved you. Ye are my friends... Henceforth I call you not servants; for the servant knoweth not what his lord doeth: but I have called you friends; for all things that I have heard of my Father I have made known unto you" (Jn 14:12-15). Thus the divine commandment became not an order we are bound to obey, but the opening of our inner insight by love to perceive the will of our Beloved, so that we obey Him as beloved ones whose will meets His divine will voluntarily! By this we can understand His words: "Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me... For my yoke is easy (pleasant), and my burden is light" (Mt 11:29-30), although He had previously said: "Think not that I am come to send peace on earth: I came not to send peace, but a sword... And he that taketh not his cross, and followeth after me, is not worthy of me" (Mt 10:34, 38). By love pain becomes sweet and the cross becomes glory, and the commandment is sweet as honey.

The word of God also carries warnings against the fallen, that they may repent; these put the servant of the word in a difficult position and even expose him to troubles and afflictions, yet at the same time they offer sweetness and joy to the servant, as he realizes God's saving purposes. When the Apostle Paul wrote sternly he grieved the Corinthians, but he went on to explain to them that although they had been grieved, he rejoices in this grief which is unto repentance, so that they too rejoice with him, saying: "For if I make you sorry, who is he then that maketh me glad, but the same which is made sorry by me? And I wrote this same unto you, lest, when I came, I should have sorrow from them of whom I ought to rejoice; having confidence in you all, that my joy is the joy of you all. For out of much affliction and anguish of heart I wrote unto you with many tears; not that ye should be grieved, but that ye might know the love which I have more abundantly unto you" (2 Cor 2:2-4).

4 And he said unto me, Son of man, go, get thee unto the house of Israel, and speak with my words unto them. 5 For thou art not sent to a people of a strange speech and of an hard language, but to the house of Israel; 6 Not to many people of a strange speech and of an hard language, whose words thou canst not understand. Surely, had I sent thee to them, they would have hearkened unto thee. 7 But the house of Israel will not hearken unto thee; for they will not hearken unto me: for all the house of Israel are impudent and hardhearted. 8 Behold, I have made thy face strong against their faces, and thy forehead strong against their foreheads. 9 As an adamant harder than flint have I made thy forehead: fear them not, neither be dismayed at their looks, though they be a rebellious house. 10 Moreover he said unto me, Son of man, all my words that I shall speak unto thee receive in thine heart, and hear with thine ears. 11 And go, get thee to them of the captivity, unto the children of thy people, and speak unto them, and tell them, Thus saith the Lord GOD; whether they will hear, or whether they will forbear. 12 Then the spirit took me up, and I heard behind me a voice of a great rushing, saying, Blessed be the glory of the LORD from his place. 13 I heard also the noise of the wings of the living creatures that touched one another, and the noise of the wheels over against them, and a noise of a great rushing. 14 So the spirit lifted me up, and took me away, and I went in bitterness, in the heat of my spirit; but the hand of the LORD was strong upon me.

God did not send him to foreign nations nor to a people of strange dialect, but sent him to his own people, to the nation that has the law of God. But, sadly, it was a disobedient nation that refused to listen to the law that Moses received on Mount Sinai, and continued to reject the word of God on the tongues of the prophets... until the Word Himself came, and they rejected Him.

God punishes them in an indirect way, saying to Ezekiel: "Surely, had I sent thee to them, they would have hearkened unto thee" [6]. And indeed, when the Word came, the nations of foreign race received Him.

Ezekiel's mission was exceedingly difficult, "for all the house of Israel are impudent and hardhearted" [7]. This is the effect of sin in the life of man: it makes his heart hard as stone and his forehead hard; he does not want to hear the divine voice but resists it violently without shame. But God gives His servants strength, for He says: "Behold, I have made thy face strong against their faces, and thy forehead strong against their foreheads. As an adamant harder than flint have I made thy forehead: fear them not, neither be dismayed at their looks, though they be a rebellious house" [8-9]. Though evil is violent by nature, it cannot stand to the end, for good shatters it, as light scatters darkness and truth falsehood, and the Kingdom of God remains forever while the kingdom of the devil is for a time. Thus, whenever the servant hides in God as his refuge, the enemy of good cannot stand before him.

When Ezekiel received the word of God he heard behind him a voice of a great rushing [12]; these are the heavenly powers working in secret within his heart, thundering to shatter the evil that hardened the hearts of sinners. He heard the noise of the wings of the living creatures that touched one another. It is as though the heavenly creation, which works together in one spirit, also supports us by its prayers on our behalf. As for the noise of the wheels, it is the authority of the Gospel word, which captivates hearts and draws them.

With all these resources, the divine heavenly resources and the support of the heavenly ones besides the power of the word itself, the service is full of toil and pain... The inner bitterness of heart for the sake of shattered souls is enough, for the prophet says: "So the spirit lifted me up, and took me away, and I went in bitterness, in the heat of my spirit; but the hand of the LORD was strong upon me" [14]. It is as though he were saying with the psalmist: "Despondency hath taken hold of me because of the sinners who have departed from thy law" (Ps 118).

Ezekiel had to declare the message among those who had suffered the captivity, and they had either to receive the word of God as a savour of life unto life or a savour of death unto death. Sadly, they did not benefit from the captivity, nor were their hearts softened by the chastisement, nor did they listen to the word of God in the midst of their exile, but increased in hardness and stubbornness against God and His prophets. God made clear to him that they would refuse to listen to him, and would even resist and persecute him... It is their responsibility, not his. As for him, he must enjoy a divine power that makes him hard as adamant to face their hardness [8].

The Spirit of the Lord carried him from before the throne to bring him to the captives to serve them [12-15], that he might realize that his movements are not according to his human will but according to God's plan... that he is carried by the Spirit. He came, and his soul was filled with bitterness, and the hand of the Lord was strong upon him [14]. Perhaps the secret of his soul's bitterness sprang from comparing his standing before the divine throne, sharing the praises of the heavenly ones, with his transfer to the captives, whose peace and joy of heart sin had shattered; he became embittered in his soul, saying with the Apostle Peter: "Lord, it is good for us to be here." He did not want to leave the divine throne. Perhaps he was also embittered because he felt the people's deprivation of what he had seen and experienced by standing before the divine throne!
