15 Then I came to them of the captivity at Telabib, that dwelt by the river of Chebar, and I sat where they sat, and remained there astonished among them seven days. 16 And it came to pass at the end of seven days, that the word of the LORD came unto me, saying, 17 Son of man, I have made thee a watchman unto the house of Israel: therefore hear the word at my mouth, and give them warning from me. 18 When I say unto the wicked, Thou shalt surely die; and thou givest him not warning, nor speakest to warn the wicked from his wicked way, to save his life; the same wicked man shall die in his iniquity; but his blood will I require at thine hand. 19 Yet if thou warn the wicked, and he turn not from his wickedness, nor from his wicked way, he shall die in his iniquity; but thou hast delivered thy soul. 20 Again, When a righteous man doth turn from his righteousness, and commit iniquity, and I lay a stumblingblock before him, he shall die: because thou hast not given him warning, he shall die in his sin, and his righteousness which he hath done shall not be remembered; but his blood will I require at thine hand. 21 Nevertheless if thou warn the righteous man, that the righteous sin not, and he doth not sin, he shall surely live, because he is warned; also thou hast delivered thy soul.

When Ezekiel had eaten the word of God and been satisfied with it, he remained among the captives seven days in bewilderment, not knowing what to do, and the voice of the Lord came to him: "Son of man, I have made thee a watchman" [17]. It is as though two things are necessarily required for appointing the watchman: that he eat the word of God, and that he live seven days among his people. The number 7 points to perfection, or the completeness of the days of the week; it is as though the watchman is not an employee who performs a work for wages, who works for a while and rests, but truly a loving man who throws himself among his people all the days of his life, knowing no rest for himself. When the Apostle Paul wanted to describe the first leader of the people, that is, Moses the prophet, he said of him: "By faith Moses, when he was come to years, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter; choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God, than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season; esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures in Egypt: for he had respect unto the recompence of the reward" (Heb 11:24-26). Thus Moses threw himself into the disgrace of his people, counting that better than living in the comfort of Pharaoh's palace, leaving every temporary pleasure for the sake of the eternal reward. These are the marks of the spiritual watchman. He works among his people as their servant, bearing their reproach, seeking not his own but what is for their comfort.
His being called "watchman" is a sign of the existence of a spiritual war; in his service he washes the feet of others and fights Satan and his hosts.

In ancient times cities were often built on hills, and a tower was built on the city walls, and in the tower was a watchman who could track the movements of any enemy coming toward the city and warn the people; then the gates of the city were closed and the army prepared for war.

As for God's commandment to him, it is: "Hear the word at my mouth, and give them warning from me" [17]. As a watchman he must bear a spirit of discernment through his keeping of the word of the Lord and his fellowship with God, so that he does not warn from himself but by what he hears from the mouth of God, and does not speak in his own name but in the name of God ("from me"). By this he can warn with all strength, without fear, flattery or compromise, lest souls perish and their blood be required of him.

God made clear to His servant the extent of his responsibility for the perishing of every soul he fails to warn out of negligence, a matter that has terrified the servants of God throughout the ages. Therefore when St. Ambrose felt that the Emperor Theodosius had committed an error, he hastened to write to him warning him, saying to him: [Can I keep silent?! For my conscience would be bound, my speech taken from me, and I would be in the worst state I could be in...! If the priest does not speak with the one who sins... the sinner dies in his sin, and the priest himself is subject to punishment because he did not warn against the error]. Again he writes to him thus: [I beg you to listen patiently to what I say. If I am unworthy to be heard by you, I am also unworthy to offer sacrifices on your behalf, you who have trusted in your vows and prayers... It is not for the emperor to refuse freedom of speech, nor for the priest not to say what he thinks].

St. John Chrysostom has presented to us a wonderful example of the watchman's care not for the congregation as a whole but for each soul as if it were the whole congregation, saying: [Each one of you, in my eyes, is equal to the whole city].

Again he says: [Let no one say to me that many have fulfilled the commandment, for I do not seek this, but I want everyone to do so. I cannot catch my breath until I see that fulfilled! For if one man committed fornication among the Corinthians, Paul sighed as though the whole city were lost].

St. Paul felt his responsibility as a watchman, and he says to the presbyters of the Church in Ephesus: "Wherefore I take you to record this day, that I am pure from the blood of all men. For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God... Therefore watch, and remember, that by the space of three years I ceased not to warn every one night and day with tears" (Acts 20:26-27, 31). And as Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles, says: [From whose blood is the Apostle pure...? The blood of souls, of course, and not the blood of bodies]. He also says: [We must fear lest the souls of many perish because of the famine of the word of God resulting from our negligence, and it be required of our souls on the day of judgment].

22 And the hand of the LORD was there upon me; and he said unto me, Arise, go forth into the plain, and I will there talk with thee. 23 Then I arose, and went forth into the plain: and, behold, the glory of the LORD stood there, as the glory which I saw by the river of Chebar: and I fell on my face.

As he acts as a watchman, the Lord commanded him not to hasten to begin the work but to go forth into the plain to speak with him [22], and there He showed him His heavenly glory again, as he had seen by the river Chebar. For the success of the mission does not rest on the abundance of work but on the quality of the servant; he is obliged to be sanctified through his solitude with God, to lift his heart to the divine glories and so present to the people in his life "the power of the heavenly life."

Going forth into the plain to behold the glory of the Lord is necessary for every servant; therefore after the Apostle Paul was called to service he committed himself to stay three years in the wilderness in a long solitude with God to prepare for the apostolic work. St. Augustine speaks of the servants' commitment to spiritual solitude without solitude hindering the work or the work hindering the life of solitude, saying: [Those to whom works of good and the care of souls have been entrusted are obliged to bring to people a witness of the other life (contemplation); therefore they must devote themselves to the study and contemplation of the truth and of eternal life. Nor is it fair that the life of contemplation should be a cause for hindering a man from performing the tasks of the Church].

For the success of our service we need the Lord to be manifested in our hearts, and to enjoy the divine presence, not once only but from time to time, so that we enjoy continual new visions that reveal the glory of God, His power and His resources... and we are assured that He is working in us and through us. He is always present within us, manifesting Himself continually in our depths.

entries.section: 5. A time to keep silence and a time to speak:

paragraphs.text: 24 Then the spirit entered into me, and set me upon my feet, and spake with me, and said unto me, Go, shut thyself within thine house. 25 But thou, O son of man, behold, they shall put bands upon thee, and shall bind thee with them, and thou shalt not go out among them: 26 And I will make thy tongue cleave to the roof of thy mouth, that thou shalt be dumb, and shalt not be to them a reprover: for they are a rebellious house. 27 But when I speak with thee, I will open thy mouth, and thou shalt say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD; He that heareth, let him hear; and he that forbeareth, let him forbear: for they are a rebellious house.

The vision was repeated and the prophet Ezekiel's falling on his face was repeated, and the divine Spirit also entered him to raise him up and he heard this message: "Go, shut thyself within thine house... And I will make thy tongue cleave to the roof of thy mouth, that thou shalt be dumb, and shalt not be to them a reprover: for they are a rebellious house. But when I speak with thee, I will open thy mouth, and thou shalt say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD" [24-27]. Thus the Lord wanted him not to work by human zeal but to be silent and not speak until He permits him to speak, so that he speaks at the time the Lord sees fit and with the words of the Lord and in His name. Although as a watchman he is condemned for his silence in the face of evil, he must learn what the wise man said: "a time to keep silence, and a time to speak" (Eccl 3:7). As St. Ambrose says: [Weigh your speech and measure your words], and also: [The wise man in his speech takes into consideration what he says, to whom he speaks, and the circumstances of place and time... Thus there must be a measure for keeping silence as for speaking]. Father Gregory the Great says: [The shepherd must be discreet in his silence and profitable in his speech].
Feed me with Your commandment, O desire of my heart!
*Feed me with Your commandment, O desire of my heart!
Stretch out Your hand and give me Your commandment as heavenly bread.
I am a child, even an infant; I will not accept food from anyone but You!
You are more tender to me than my parents, O Savior of my soul!

*Your commandment is hard, O Savior of my soul, Your cross is heavy, and Your way is a narrow affliction, but from Your hands Your commandment becomes bread and honey of the bees, Your cross becomes glory, and Your way a new heaven!
*You sent Your prophet carrying Your word to Your stubborn people; grant me to carry Your commandment to every soul, however stubborn!
With the receiving of Your word a great rushing took place in heaven.
Let heaven thunder and shake every hardness in my heart and in their hearts.
Let the shaken earthly nature be removed from them, and let them enjoy an eternal heavenly life.
*Your prophet presented Your word to a stubborn people, and his soul became embittered.
Was he perhaps bitter in soul because he did not want to leave the beholding of Your chariot?!
Was he perhaps bitter in soul because he came into contact with the stubbornness of humanity?!
Grant me, in the midst of my soul's bitterness, to see Your heavens; grant me, in the midst of my sorrow, to touch the repentance of many.
My heart rejoices in Your divine work in them and through them, O divine Word.
Your prophet remained among the captives seven days; grant me to spend all the days of my exile working in Your vineyard.
I am not a hired servant counting the time, but a son who longs to work in my Father's vineyard.
*Teach me, O divine Word:
When shall I be alone with You to know Your mysteries?!
And when shall I work in the vineyard to serve Your people?!
Grant me in my solitude not to forget Your people, and in my service not to cease contemplating Your mysteries.
*Guide me, O true Word, for I do not know when to be silent and when to speak, how to be silent and how to speak?!
Here I am in Your hands; be my leader who works in me.

1 Thou also, son of man, take thee a tile, and lay it before thee, and pourtray upon it the city, even Jerusalem: 2 And lay siege against it, and build a fort against it, and cast a mount against it; set the camp also against it, and set battering rams against it round about. 3 Moreover take thou unto thee an iron pan, and set it for a wall of iron between thee and the city: and set thy face against it, and it shall be besieged, and thou shalt lay siege against it. This shall be a sign to the house of Israel.

The Lord commanded him to draw on a tile (a brick of clay) a city besieged by armies, and to set against it a fort, a mount and battering rams (war machines for demolishing walls), declaring that the siege of Jerusalem was coming by divine permission for chastisement, since the holy Temple had for many long years been defiled by the setting up of images of idols and pagan gods inside the holy places.

When Zion felt that the Lord had forsaken her and her Lord had forgotten her, He assured her: "Behold, I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands" (Isa 49:16). I have engraved you in My Son Jesus Christ, since you are His holy body and He is the Head; I see you in Him holy and justified, lifted up through Him and in Him into My embrace, enjoying fellowship in My glories. Here, however, since Zion insists on sin and clings to temporal things and does not want to rise above earthly things, God asked Ezekiel to draw her on a tile of clay, instead of being drawn on the palm of the Lord; He gives her the desire of her heart. Therefore He often repeats such a phrase: "I will recompense thy ways upon thee" (Ezek 7:4). She desired the earth, so He made her engraved on clay!! After the names of the tribes of Israel were engraved on precious stones placed on the breast of the high priest, that he might enter with them into the Holy of Holies in the shadow of the heavenlies, behold the city of Jerusalem is engraved on the clay with which she wanted to be weighed down!

In the Song of Songs God prides Himself on His children, comparing them to the horses working together in one spirit in His divine chariot for salvation (Song 1:9); He sees them as comely as Tirzah, terrible as an army with banners (Song 6:4)... But since they insist on withdrawing from Him and clinging to abominations, He raises against them from the nations a fort, a mount and battering rams to shatter every strength in them! He even commands the setting up of a wall of iron around the city [3], not to protect it but so that no one may escape the chastisements that come upon it!

The wonder is that God, in the midst of this bitterness, asks the prophet more than once to set his face against the city (Ezek 3:7) and to have his arm uncovered when he prophesies against it [7]. The affirmation, twice, of setting his face against the besieged city is a sign of God's care for His people, from the Jews as from the Gentiles; the Church, of all races, is the object of His care, His providence and His concern even in the bitterest moments of chastisement. He permits His children afflictions with all their bitterness, and with them salvation. Therefore St. John Chrysostom calls suffering "the school of philosophy," and says: [When we sin, God raises our enemies against us to chastise us; therefore it is fitting for us not to fight them, but to call ourselves to account and instruct ourselves. Let us receive sufferings as we receive medicines from the physician for our salvation, and as we receive chastisement from a father so that we may be glorified. Therefore the wise Ben Sira says: My son, if thou come to serve the Lord, prepare thyself for temptation and endure].

As for the uncovered arm, it points to the divine Incarnation, for the Fathers see in "the arm of the Lord" a reference to the Son, and in "the finger of the Lord" a reference to the Holy Spirit. It is as though Jerusalem remains under siege in the grip of sin and under its dominion until the arm of the Lord is uncovered, as St. John says: "For the life was manifested, and we have seen it, and bear witness, and shew unto you that eternal life, which was with the Father, and was manifested unto us" (1 Jn 1:5). He who is invisible became, by the Incarnation, uncovered, for He "dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth" (Jn 1:14). Our heart, the inner Jerusalem, was besieged and our temple defiled and we were in a state of death, until the Father bared His arm, that is, sent His only Son to free us and bring us back to salvation. This is what the prophet Isaiah saw by the spirit of prophecy when he proclaimed good tidings to Jerusalem, captive to sin, which had slept the sleep of death and been buried in the dust and utterly shattered, saying:
"Awake, awake; put on thy strength, O Zion;
put on thy beautiful garments, O Jerusalem, the holy city.
Shake thyself from the dust; arise, and sit down, O Jerusalem: loose thyself from the bands of thy neck, O captive daughter of Zion.

How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!...

Break forth into joy, sing together, ye waste places of Jerusalem: for the LORD hath comforted his people, he hath redeemed Jerusalem. The LORD hath made bare his holy arm in the eyes of all the nations; and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God" (Isa 52).

It is clear that the secret of Zion's awakening, her putting on her strength, her shaking herself from the dust, her freedom from the bands of slavery around her neck, and her enjoyment of peace, is the baring of the arm of the Lord in the eyes of the nations, that is, the Incarnation of the Lord to gather into His body congregations enjoying salvation.

Moreover, the baring of the arm points to readiness to strike, and as I believe He does not mean striking His people but striking the sin that shattered this people, for the Lord Christ came not to condemn man but to save him... He condemned the sin into which we had fallen, in His body!

God's heart toward His people has not changed, but His holiness requires the shattering of sin and the punishment of the wicked who persist in their evil, that perhaps they may return to Him in repentance.

4 Lie thou also upon thy left side, and lay the iniquity of the house of Israel upon it: according to the number of the days that thou shalt lie upon it thou shalt bear their iniquity. 5 For I have laid upon thee the years of their iniquity, according to the number of the days, three hundred and ninety days: so shalt thou bear the iniquity of the house of Israel. 6 And when thou hast accomplished them, lie again on thy right side, and thou shalt bear the iniquity of the house of Judah forty days: I have appointed thee each day for a year. 7 Therefore thou shalt set thy face toward the siege of Jerusalem, and thine arm shall be uncovered, and thou shalt prophesy against it. 8 And, behold, I will lay bands upon thee, and thou shalt not turn thee from one side to another, till thou hast ended the days of thy siege.

Having declared the siege of Jerusalem and her captivity, with a hint of His concern for her and of the baring of the arm of His holiness for her salvation, the Lord began to make clear the effect of sin in the life of man: it shatters him completely, casts him into a state of continual sleep without vitality or work, man lying on one side like one stricken with palsy (paralysis).

He asked him to lie on his left side 390 days (and according to the Septuagint 190 days), then to return and lie on his right side for forty days; the first lying points to the iniquity of the house of Israel and the second to the house of Judah. The first work points to man's falling under the authority of the left-hand stroke, that is, the visible sins such as fornication, murder, theft, lying and so on, while the right-hand stroke is the hidden sins to which believers and those who serve the Lord are exposed, such as the sins of self-righteousness and love of honor and praise, things that have not the appearance of sin before people but corrupt the lives of believers and servants. Lying on the left side lasts a longer time than lying on the right side, because the people of Judah, although they were later in their evil than the northern kingdom of Israel, completed their evil in a short time. Thus by the right-hand strokes believers fall with dangerous speed, and their evil is completed in a short time, which made St. John Chrysostom declare: [I marvel at a bishop (a head) who is saved!], just as the desert Fathers used to warn their sons the monks against the right-hand strokes more than the left-hand ones, because the latter are clear and repentance for them is easy, while the former are often hidden, creeping into the heart and shattering its repentance!

Why was the left side ascribed to Israel and the right to Judah? Because when a man looks toward the rising of the sun the north is on his left and the south on his right; so Israel, the northern kingdom, is represented by his left side, and Judah, the southern kingdom, is represented by his right side.
As for the numbers, I do not wish to enter into many details, since various interpretations have been found for them, so I am content here to highlight the following points:

a. Some see that by adding the two numbers together (390+40) the result is 430 days, a symbol of the years of bondage which the Jewish nation lived in Egypt under slavery. It is as though these numbers are only a symbol of the effect of sin in the life of believers, as it brings them into bitter bondage.

b. Some see that the number 390 points to the years Israel lived from the apostasy of Jeroboam until the destruction of Jerusalem, while the number 40 points to the years in which Judah declined before the captivity.

c. Some interpret the number 390 thus: the siege of Jerusalem lasted 18 months (Jer 52:4-6); if five months are removed from it, in which the besiegers withdrew when the army of Pharaoh approached (Jer 37:5-8), the remainder is 13 months, that is, 390 days.

d. The two numbers 390 and 40 symbolize the sin that has included every man and included all temporal life, shattering all humanity with its palsy, and shattering each one all the days of his time. The number 390 is the product of multiplying 39 by 10, because the number of the tribes of the kingdom of Israel is (10), and the wages of evil are 39 stripes, as though all the tribes had deserved the scourging. As for the number 40, it points to the whole temporal life; therefore the Lord Christ fasted forty days, and so did Moses and Elijah, a sign of the necessity of our asceticism all the days of our exile. So the first number means that sin includes the life of all people, and the second that it includes all the days of our time.

Some see that what is stated here about his lying 390 days on his left side and 40 days on his right side contradicts what is stated in (Ezek 8:1), where we find the prophet sitting among the elders of his people during the mentioned period, besides the contradiction of this command of God to him with human ability, for it is inconceivable that Ezekiel was able to carry it out.

The reply to this: the preceding text includes an ancient Eastern custom, namely the custom of men "reclining" while sitting on the ground, resting on a cushion placed under the right or left hand, according to the person's wish.

The mentioned text does not require the prophet's immobility during the carrying out of the Lord's command, but requires of him the necessity of committing to recline on his left side during the 390 days and on the right side during the 40 days whenever he wished to sit only, and it also required the necessity of uncovering the whole arm on which he reclines [7]. This command does not contradict the prophet's practicing everything he wants of various movements and works during the mentioned period, and we find no difficulty for the prophet or for anyone else in practicing this command. Nor do we find any contradiction with the text in (Ezek 8:1) concerning the sitting of the prophet Ezekiel among the elders of his people. The first text does not forbid the prophet to sit with others, and at the same time affirms that he was sitting in his house, that is, reclining, and without doubt he was committed to the position that the divine revelation specified for him, so there is no disagreement between the two texts.

entries.section: 3. Eating by weight and with care:

paragraphs.text: 9 Take thou also unto thee wheat, and barley, and beans, and lentiles, and millet, and fitches, and put them in one vessel, and make thee bread thereof, according to the number of the days that thou shalt lie upon thy side, three hundred and ninety days shalt thou eat thereof. 10 And thy meat which thou shalt eat shall be by weight, twenty shekels a day: from time to time shalt thou eat it. 11 Thou shalt drink also water by measure, the sixth part of an hin: from time to time shalt thou drink. 12 And thou shalt eat it as barley cakes, and thou shalt bake it with dung that cometh out of man, in their sight. 13 And the LORD said, Even thus shall the children of Israel eat their defiled bread among the Gentiles, whither I will drive them. 14 Then said I, Ah Lord GOD! behold, my soul hath not been polluted: for from my youth up even till now have I not eaten of that which dieth of itself, or is torn in pieces; neither came there abominable flesh into my mouth. 15 Then he said unto me, Lo, I have given thee cow's dung for man's dung, and thou shalt prepare thy bread therewith. 16 Moreover he said unto me, Son of man, behold, I will break the staff of bread in Jerusalem: and they shall eat bread by weight, and with care; and they shall drink water by measure, and with astonishment: 17 That they may want bread and water, and be astonied one with another, and consume away for their iniquity.

Eating by weight and with care, and drinking by measure and with astonishment, is a sign of the famine that comes upon the people for chastisement. It is a symbol of the work of sin in the life of man, as it afflicts his soul with a state of hunger with care and thirst with astonishment... all this besides the palsy (paralysis) that has struck it.

He fixed for him ten shekels (about 8 ounces) of bread each day, and a sixth of a hin (about half a pint or 16/1 of a gallon) of water. The bread was of the poorest kinds, such as is given to horses and swine, a mixture of wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet (sorghum) and vetch (a wild seed like wheat), which he ate while lying on one side. He also asked him to bake it using human excrement instead of firewood, a sign of the defilement and uncleanness the people had reached (Deut 23:13-14), but when he pleaded with Him to excuse him from this, He allowed him to bake it on animal dung. This custom is still found in some villages of Upper Egypt, where dried dung (the galla) is used as fuel instead of firewood. In any case this action symbolizes the hardship to which the people come!
In Your love You engraved me on Your palms
* In Your love You engraved me on Your palm, O my God; You counted me beloved Jerusalem and holy Zion.
But by my sins and the uncleannesses of my heart I became engraved on a tile of clay.
I became despised, wallowing in the mire.
Through my negligence the enemy surrounded me and shattered my walls, O You who desire to set up Your fiery Spirit as a wall for my life!
* You stretched out, O Father, Your divine arm, when You sent me Your Son incarnate, to wash me from the dust, and give me Your fiery Spirit, and carry me to Your embrace!

* My sin has removed my vitality from me; I became sick with palsy, at one time reclining on my left side, struck by evils, and at another reclining on the right, struck by self-righteousness. * My sin deprived me of satisfaction, and turned my inner paradise into a desolate wasteland.
Who will rescue me from this famine but You, O satisfaction of my soul?!

entries.section: 1. The shaving of the prophet’s hair:

paragraphs.text: 1 “And thou, son of man, take thee a sharp knife, take thee a barber’s razor, and cause it to pass upon thine head and upon thy beard: then take thee balances to weigh, and divide the hair. 2 Thou shalt burn with fire a third part in the midst of the city, when the days of the siege are fulfilled: and thou shalt take a third part, and smite about it with a knife: and a third part thou shalt scatter in the wind; and I will draw out a sword after them. 3 Thou shalt also take thereof a few in number, and bind them in thy skirts. 4 Then take of them again, and cast them into the midst of the fire, and burn them in the fire; for thereof shall a fire come forth into all the house of Israel.”
“And thou, son of man, take thee a sharp knife, take thee a barber’s razor, and cause it to pass upon thine head and upon thy beard: then take thee balances to weigh, and divide the hair.

Thou shalt burn with fire a third part in the midst of the city, when the days of the siege are fulfilled: and thou shalt take a third part, and smite about it with a knife: and a third part thou shalt scatter in the wind” [1-2].

God commanded Moses to speak thus to the priests, the sons of Aaron: “They shall not make baldness upon their head, neither shall they shave off the corner of their beard, nor make any cuttings in their flesh. They shall be holy unto their God, and not profane the name of their God: for the offerings of the LORD made by fire, and the bread of their God, they do offer: therefore they shall be holy” (Lev 21:5-6). The divine commandment was clear and explicit that no razor should touch the head or beard of a priest, for he is holy to the Lord. For the hair left on a woman’s head is her adornment, but for a man it is a sign that he is not occupied with temporal matters, having consecrated every breath of his life to the priestly service. Therefore the command given to the prophet Ezekiel is a declaration of the defilement of the priests at that time, and of the Lord’s rejection of their sacrifices, their offerings and their prayers.

When the Lord wished in former times to save the people, the angel of the Lord appeared to the wife of Manoah, who was barren, and said to her: “For, lo, thou shalt conceive, and bear a son; and no razor shall come on his head: for the child shall be a Nazarite unto God from the womb: and he shall begin to deliver Israel out of the hand of the Philistines” (Judg 13:5). When this man’s hair was shaved off, the strength of the Lord departed from him and he became weak (Judg 16:17); indeed the Lord Himself departed from him (Judg 16:20), and he lost his eyes and was bound with fetters of brass, and became like an ox grinding in the prison house (Judg 16:21), and he was a mockery and a laughingstock to the pagans! But now it is God Himself who commands the shaving of the head and the beard, as a sign of His departure from the priests of His people, of their loss of spiritual sight, of their entering into captivity and of their becoming a laughingstock of the nations and the object of their derision.

The complete shaving of the hair signifies God’s refusal to enter into any relationship with them through the priests or the prophets; He accepts no offering and hears no prayer until He has disciplined them for their wickedness. It also signifies His rejection of His people because of their insistence on sin. If the Lord is the Head, then our life consists in abiding in Him. So the removal of the hair is the end of the people’s abiding in the source of their life. In this St. Jerome says: [The prophet Isaiah speaks of a sharp razor that shaves the head of sinners and the hair of their feet (Isa 7:20); he shaves his head as a type of Jerusalem, which had become a harlot (Ezek 5:1-5), a sign that everything in her had become insensible and life had been taken away from her.]

The complete shaving of the hair signifies intense grief, especially in the case of a death, and this was defilement in the eyes of the Lord. Therefore He warned His people, saying: “Ye are the children of the LORD your God: ye shall not cut yourselves, nor make any baldness between your eyes for the dead. For thou art holy unto the LORD thy God, and the LORD hath chosen thee to be a peculiar people unto himself” (Deut 14:1-2). But now Jerusalem had become as one reckoned among the dead. And since His people rejected Him, He commanded them, in the person of Ezekiel, to defile themselves by shaving the hair of their heads.

The shaving of the hair is also a sign of shame, humiliation and slavery. A man becomes without dignity, with no authority even over his own hair, whether to leave it or to shave it. For this reason the heads of slaves were shaved completely, and also those of kings when they were taken captive. This is what sin does to a man: it strips him of all authority and brings him down from the state of king and power to the shame of slavery, falling into captivity and humiliation. The servants of David were ashamed to meet their king because Hanun, king of the children of Ammon, suspected them and shaved off their beards, so they stayed at Jericho until their beards were grown, and then returned... Likewise a man cannot meet the Lord, his heavenly King, while he is in the shame and disgrace of sin; rather he waits until he declares his repentance, receives forgiveness and recovers his dignity, and so becomes able to meet God and all His heavenly and earthly hosts.

The shaving of the hair with a sharp knife signifies a bloody war, in which God allowed the hard-hearted Chaldeans to invade Judah, according to what His divine providence required. He allowed this because Judah had rebelled against God: a third would perish in the siege of Jerusalem, a third would be killed mercilessly by the sword at the hands of the soldiers of Nebuchadnezzar, and the remaining third would be scattered over the face of the earth among the peoples.

As for the weighing of the hair, it is a sign that what befalls the people of hunger, thirst, falling by the sword and scattering among the peoples does not take place randomly or by mere chance, but by divine ordering, and the Lord’s balances are just, faithful and exact.

“The LORD weigheth the hearts” (Prov 21:2) and the spirits (Prov 16:2); He before whose eyes are the ways of man, and “he pondereth all his goings” (Prov 5:21); who weighs the winds and weighs the waters by measure (Job 28:25), and comprehends the dust of the earth in a measure, and weighs the mountains in scales and the hills in a balance (Isa 40:12). His balances are true and just; He cannot bear deceit or partiality. This is the nature of God, which He desires to pour out into the lives of His children; therefore He often repeats the commandments: “Thou shalt not have in thy bag divers weights, a great and a small. Thou shalt not have in thine house divers measures, a great and a small. But thou shalt have a perfect and just weight, a perfect and just measure shalt thou have” (Deut 25:13-15); “Divers weights are an abomination unto the LORD; and a false balance is not good” (Prov 20:23); “A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight” (Prov 11:1). God weighs our lives and, sadly, finds them “in the balances they go up” (Ps 62:9), or as the wise Daniel said to King Belshazzar: “Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting” (Dan 5:6). And now, what does the Lord do toward us, who have been found so? He bears the secret of our lack; He bears our iniquity upon Himself and comes forward to the balance, and behold, He is priced as a slave, He who is the Judge who judges the whole world. In bitterness He says: “So they weighed for my price thirty pieces of silver” (Zech 11:12). The Lord is valued as a slave, while the slave stands in his self-righteousness to say: “Let me be weighed in an even balance, that God may know mine integrity” (Job 31:6). The Perfect One was weighed, bearing our lack, and came under shame, while man in the pride of his heart wishes to be justified in the balances before God.

In any case, Ezekiel’s hair was weighed as a symbol of the people fallen under the weight of sin, and found deserving of hunger, thirst, the sword and scattering... These are the fruits of uncleanness and evil.

Although the people were found wanting in the balance, God does not forget the very few among them, those who, because of their faithfulness to Him and their obedience to His words, He keeps in the skirt of His garment, under His care. This remnant perhaps refers to the remnant that was left in Jerusalem under the leadership of Gedaliah. And perhaps it refers to the remnant that remains faithful to the Lord in the days of the false prophet or the Antichrist. They are the hidden company of the Lord, kept and concealed in Him; He knows them by name and puts a hedge around them so that none of them is lost, and the wicked enemy does not snatch them away. But sadly, the Lord commanded that a few of this small number be burned, because after entering under His care they rejected Him. Of these the Apostle said that they began in the Spirit but are being made perfect by the flesh (Gal 3:3). Therefore the Lord instructs us to endure to the end (Mt 10:12), and warns us of the last days, when it is feared that even the elect may be deceived (Mt 24:24).

5 “Thus saith the Lord GOD; This is Jerusalem: I have set it in the midst of the nations and countries that are round about her. 6 And she hath changed my judgments into wickedness more than the nations, and my statutes more than the countries that are round about her: for they have refused my judgments and my statutes, they have not walked in them. 7 Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; Because ye multiplied more than the nations that are round about you, and have not walked in my statutes, neither have kept my judgments, neither have done according to the judgments of the nations that are round about you,” God, like a father disciplining his children, reveals to them the secret of their punishment. He is not a tyrannical master nor an avenger; rather, even in the severity of His discipline He desires our return and repentance... Therefore He shows us our weaknesses so that we may abandon them.

Two things grieve the heart of God: the broken commandment and the defiled temple. Concerning the commandment He says: “For they have refused my judgments and my statutes, they have not walked in them” [6]. And it is strange that when the believer falls into disobedience he becomes more wicked than the unbeliever, for the Lord says: “She hath changed my judgments into wickedness more than the nations” [6]. As for the defiling of the temple, He says: “Surely, because thou hast defiled my sanctuary with all thy detestable things, and with all thine abominations, therefore will I also diminish thee; neither shall mine eye spare, neither will I have any pity” [11].

The keeping of the commandment and worship (the temple) are two things that go together and are joined in the life of the believer. By obeying the commandment we gain boldness to stand before God, and standing before Him in worship supports our life in obedience to the commandment. Whoever thinks that he keeps the commandment apart from the spirit of worship deceives himself, and so does whoever thinks that he pleases the Lord by worship without walking in obedience to the commandment.

8 “Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I, even I, am against thee, and will execute judgments in the midst of thee in the sight of the nations.” When He sent to the people of Judah the prophet Jeremiah to rebuke them for their sins, He said to him: “Go and cry in the ears of Jerusalem” (Jer 2:1), as though He wished to whisper in their ears so that they might repent without anyone knowing what they had done; but when they did not listen, He asked him to stand in the gate of the house of the Lord and proclaim the word of rebuke (Jer 7:1), and when they still did not listen, He was compelled to make His chastisements of His people public before all the nations. They sinned openly without shame, and He tried to correct them without wounding their feelings, but in the face of their growing arrogance He says: “I will execute judgments in the midst of thee in the sight of the nations” [8], “Moreover I will make thee waste, and a reproach among the nations that are round about thee, in the sight of all that pass by. So it shall be a reproach and a taunt, an instruction and an astonishment unto the nations that are round about thee” [14-15].

Jerusalem became a lesson to the nations around her, and a visible lesson to the whole world. For the holy God does not accept sin, nor does He make peace with it, even if His people commit it in the holy city!

God, as the Lover of mankind, covers our sins and weaknesses once and many times, but when He finds our healing in exposing us, He announces His severe chastisements upon us. This is also what the Church does with her children and servants: she heals with love and covers, but if the matter calls for public discipline she does not refrain, for the sake of the salvation of her children. In the apostolic age the Apostle judged publicly the one who fell into sin with his father’s wife, saying: “It is reported commonly that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as is not so much as named among the Gentiles, that one should have his father’s wife... For I verily, as absent in body, but present in spirit, have judged already, as though I were present, concerning him that hath so done this deed, In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when ye are gathered together, and my spirit, with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, To deliver such an one unto Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus... Purge out therefore the old leaven, that ye may be a new lump, as ye are unleavened” (1 Cor 5:1-7).

9 “And I will do in thee that which I have not done, and whereunto I will not do any more the like, because of all thine abominations. 10 Therefore the fathers shall eat the sons in the midst of thee, and the sons shall eat their fathers; and I will execute judgments in thee, and the whole remnant of thee will I scatter into all the winds. 11 Wherefore, as I live, saith the Lord GOD; Surely, because thou hast defiled my sanctuary with all thy detestable things, and with all thine abominations, therefore will I also diminish thee; neither shall mine eye spare, neither will I have any pity. 12 A third part of thee shall die with the pestilence, and with famine shall they be consumed in the midst of thee: and a third part shall fall by the sword round about thee; and I will scatter a third part into all the winds, and I will draw out a sword after them.”

They vied with one another in evil and surpassed the nations; therefore God also disciplines them with unique chastisements: “And I will do in thee that which I have not done, and whereunto I will not do any more the like, because of all thine abominations. Therefore the fathers shall eat the sons in the midst of thee, and the sons shall eat their fathers; and I will execute judgments in thee, and the whole remnant of thee will I scatter into all the winds” [9-10].

This is the bitterest punishment under which believers can fall: that one of them eats the other, indeed that the father eats his son and the son his father! For when the grace of God abandons them, corruption creeps into them from within, and through divisions and schisms one member eats another, even if he is bound to him by ties of flesh or of spirit, and finally nothing is left of them except ashes that the Lord scatters into every wind!

I say that the fruit of sin is that the community eats one another instead of supporting one another; indeed division creeps into the man himself, so that he rises up against himself, loses his peace, his balance and his vitality, and the man, because of sin, becomes like ashes of no value, scattered by the winds in every direction!

13 “Thus shall mine anger be accomplished, and I will cause my fury to rest upon them, and I will be comforted: and they shall know that I the LORD have spoken it in my zeal, when I have accomplished my fury in them. 14 Moreover I will make thee waste, and a reproach among the nations that are round about thee, in the sight of all that pass by. 15 So it shall be a reproach and a taunt, an instruction and an astonishment unto the nations that are round about thee, when I shall execute judgments in thee in anger and in fury and in furious rebukes. I the LORD have spoken it.”
The Lord assured Judah that this unique public chastisement does not come from the prophet, who is not speaking against them, but from God Himself: “I the LORD have spoken it” [15].

Although the Chaldeans fight against you and take your people captive, in truth they are an instrument in the hand of God, who raises the nations against His people to discipline them. Therefore He affirms: “Behold, I, even I, am against thee” [9], repeating the phrase “I the LORD have spoken it” and the like about 14 times in this book.

For this reason, when Absalom rose up against his father David and the latter fled, Shimei the son of Gera came out against him, cursing and casting stones at David, and all the servants of the king, and the people and the mighty men around him; then Abishai said to the king: “Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? let me go over, I pray thee, and take off his head” (2 Sam 16:9). But David, in wisdom and humility, said: “Let him curse, because the LORD hath said unto him, Curse David. Who shall then say, Wherefore hast thou done so?... It may be that the LORD will look on mine affliction, and that the LORD will requite me good for his cursing this day.” St. John Chrysostom sees in the plots of others against us an opportunity for repentance, for he says: [If we sin, God raises our enemies against us to discipline us. Therefore it is fitting for us not to fight them, but to examine ourselves and instruct ourselves. Let us accept sufferings as we accept medicines from the physician for our salvation, and as we accept discipline from a father, so that we may be glorified.]

16 “When I shall send upon them the evil arrows of famine, which shall be for their destruction, and which I will send to destroy you: and I will increase the famine upon you, and will break your staff of bread: 17 So will I send upon you famine and evil beasts, and they shall bereave thee; and pestilence and blood shall pass through thee; and I will bring the sword upon thee. I the LORD have spoken it.”

In His longsuffering and love, God began with secret speaking to His people, then with open speaking, and finally was compelled to open chastisement; and here too He disciplines in stages, that perhaps they may repent and He may remove the pain from them. He allows them to hunger, then increases His pressure upon them until they are in need of bread. And when they do not return, He stirs up the wild beasts against them to devour their children, then He allows pestilence and the shedding of blood... He seeks not vengeance but repentance, by every way.
Establish me in You, O tender Disciplinarian!
* Establish me in You, O tender Disciplinarian!

You allowed Your prophet Ezekiel to shave off all the hair of his head, to declare Your intense grief over the corruption of Your people as though they were dead, and to threaten Your people that You would remove them from You as hair from the head, and to reject their priesthood, which had become defiled, and to assure them that they live as captive slaves with shaven heads!
* Discipline me... but do not hand me over to another than You!
For You are the tender Disciplinarian!
* You disciplined me in secret and I was not restrained; behold, You expose me among my people, indeed even among the nations...
Let it be... but do not deprive me of Your salvation!
For You are the tender Disciplinarian!

entries.section: 1. A prophecy against the mountains of Israel:

paragraphs.text: 1 And the word of the LORD came unto me, saying, 2 “Son of man, set thy face toward the mountains of Israel, and prophesy unto them, 3 And say, Ye mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord GOD; Thus saith the Lord GOD to the mountains, and to the hills, to the valleys, and to the lowlands; Behold, I, even I, will bring a sword upon you, and I will destroy your high places. 4 And your altars shall be desolate, and your sun images shall be broken: and I will cast down your slain men before your idols. 5 And I will lay the dead carcases of the children of Israel before their idols; and I will scatter your bones round about your altars. 6 In all your dwellingplaces the cities shall be laid waste, and the high places shall be desolate; that your altars may be laid waste and made desolate, and your idols may be broken and cease, and your sun images may be cut down, and your works may be abolished. 7 And the slain shall fall in the midst of you, and ye shall know that I am the LORD.

The Jews took from the pagans their worship of idols on the mountains, hills, rivers and valleys. Therefore the Lord asked the prophet Ezekiel to direct his gaze toward the mountains of Israel, which had been defiled by pagan worship, and to prophesy against them. He looks like a judge who looks toward the accused in order to pass sentence on him face to face, to shake his foundations and destroy them.

Mountains have a symbolic meaning in the Holy Bible. For “the earth” often signifies in the Holy Bible the soul that has descended to earthly thought, so that the earthly body with its lusts has taken it captive and bound it to material things, whereas “the mountains” often signify in the Holy Bible souls lifted above earthly things to dwell with Him in the heavenly places, a holy, heavenly Church. For this reason God often ascribes the mountain to Himself and calls it “his holy mountain” (Ps 2:6), (Ps 99:9; Isa 65:11, 25; Joel 2:1; Obad 16), and the Holy Bible also calls it “Jerusalem, thy holy mountain” (Dan 9:16; Isa 66:20), “Zion my holy mountain” (Joel 3:17).

The two angels asked Lot to flee to the mountain lest he perish (Gen 9:17), as though asking him to rise above temporal things lest they ensnare him in their whirlpool. And the psalmist longed to dwell in the holy hill of the Lord (Ps 15:1), that is, for his heart to be lifted up on high, where it meets God who dwells in the heights and who answers him (Ps 30:4).

The soul that becomes a holy mountain becomes like Mount Horeb, where the Lord comes to it, not to give it His Law engraved on stones as to Moses, but to engrave His commandment on its heart by the Holy Spirit. The Lord sits in it as He sat on the mount to teach the multitudes with His words, drawing them to Himself with authority (Mt 5). It becomes like the mount of temptation, on which the Lord Himself ascends to lead the spiritual battle against Satan, shattering his authority, so that the soul gains the ability to overcome and the angels come to minister to it. It becomes like Mount Tabor, where the soul enjoys fellowship with the men of the Old Testament (Moses and Elijah) and the men of the New Testament (Peter, James and John) in the presence of the Lord Christ Himself, who overshadows it with His bright cloud and reveals His radiance to it within. It becomes like the Mount of Olives, where the Lord sits in it weeping over His fallen children who killed the prophets and stoned His messengers, so that it becomes a center of work and spiritual service; or rather it becomes like Mount Golgotha, enjoying the Cross of the Lord Christ planted within it, sharing with its Bridegroom His sufferings and crucifixion so as to enjoy the power of His resurrection. In short, the mountains mentioned in the Holy Bible hold memories that move the soul to enjoy, in one form or another, the life of union with God in Christ Jesus.

St. Jerome sees that these holy mountains are the prophets and the apostles, for he says: [We interpret the mountains in two ways: in the Old Testament they are the prophets, and in the New Testament the apostles. Of these mountains the Holy Bible says: “I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help” (Ps 120:1). On these mountains the city of God is established, for “a city that is set on an hill cannot be hid” (Mt 5:12). And we also, who were in darkness and the shadow of death, have been shone upon by the Lord from His eternal mountains, that is, through His prophets and apostles.]

And just as the Lord God raises His children as holy mountains in which He dwells, so the enemy of good raises from his servants defiled and stumbling mountains. If the holy mountain means the soul’s rising to the heavenly places by the Holy Spirit, then the evil mountain means the pride of the soul and its disobedience to the divine commandment. So instead of the soul being a mountain to which the Lord goes to pray (Mk 6:46), “the hill which God desireth to dwell in for ever” (Ps 68:16), it becomes defiled, a place where swine feed (Lk 8:32). And instead of the soul being that mountain to which the Church goes up with her Bridegroom as on Mount Tabor, it becomes a cause of wandering (Heb 11:38). Therefore the Lord declares His wrath against the evil mountains and shakes their foundations, or as the psalmist says: “the mountains are carried into the midst of the seas” (Ps 46:2), “What ails you, O mountains, that you skipped like rams?” (Ps 114:2). The Lord threatens these mountains, saying: “Behold, I am against thee, O destroying mountain, saith the LORD, which destroyest all the earth: and I will stretch out mine hand upon thee, and roll thee down from the rocks, and will make thee a burnt mountain. And they shall not take of thee a stone for a corner, nor a stone for foundations; but thou shalt be desolate for ever, saith the LORD” (Jer 51:25-26); as He also says: “I hated Esau, and laid his mountains and his heritage waste for the wolves of the wilderness” (Mal 1:3), “Lift ye up a banner upon the bare mountain, exalt the voice unto them” (Isa 13:2).

The people turned aside to pagan worship, so the Lord threatened them through the prophet with evil coming upon every place used for evil, whether mountain or hill, valley or river. The sword extends to the doers of evil, so that they are killed and their works are blotted out, their cities become waste and desolate, their high places are destroyed, their altars laid waste and their sun images broken (perhaps the canopies used for protection from the sun during worship, though the English translations say “the images that are worshiped”), and their bones are scattered around their altars as a sign of their defilement (2 Kgs 23:16). Thus the worshipers, the object of their worship and the place of worship itself are all shattered.

This is the prophecy that was directed against the mountains of Israel, and it is a bitter threat in order to move them to repentance. It is a prophecy standing in every generation against the arrogant soul: God destroys its high places, that is, He shatters the pride and haughtiness of its heart; He lays waste its altars, that is, He shatters its emotions which it has misused; He breaks its sun images, that is, He exposes it in the middle of the day and no longer covers for it (or perhaps by the sun images he meant the idols belonging to the worship of the sun). He casts down its slain before its idols, that is, He humbles it before those with whom it commits sin; its bones are scattered around its altar, that is, He declares its death spiritually, psychologically and bodily and the defilement of its life, so that all loathe it; He makes its dwelling a desolation, that is, He leaves its heart desolate, without satisfaction; and He blots out its works, a sign of the removal of all vitality and energy for work within it. This discipline is in fact the natural fruit of sin in the life of man: it kills him, kills his inner energies and shatters every possibility in him!

Here we notice that the Promised Land, flowing with milk and honey, which bore witness to God’s good pleasure in His believers, turns into a mass grave. Instead of bearing fruit, it becomes a place of death.

On another side, God threatens to kill them beside the altar of the demons, to prove to them its inability to help... Perhaps He wished to show them His justice: since they defiled His temple with idols, He allows the idols to be defiled by killing them in the pagan temples and turning these into graves that carry corruption.

entries.section: 2. His acceptance of the repentant remnant:

paragraphs.text: 8 “Yet will I leave a remnant, that ye may have some that shall escape the sword among the nations, when ye shall be scattered through the countries. 9 And they that escape of you shall remember me among the nations whither they shall be carried captives, when I have broken their whorish heart, which hath departed from me, and their eyes, which go a whoring after their idols: and they shall lothe themselves for the evils which they have committed in all their abominations. 10 And they shall know that I am the LORD, and that I have not said in vain that I would do this evil unto them.

entries.section: 2. His acceptance of the repentant remnant:

paragraphs.text: Each time He threatens the community or the whole people, He does not forget to stress His care for the repentant remnant who return to Him, despite their small number, those who are saved from the punishment not by accepting the discipline (the captivity) but by their repentance from their sins: “When I have broken their whorish heart, which hath departed from me, and their eyes, which go a whoring after their idols: and they shall lothe themselves for the evils which they have committed in all their abominations” [9]. They sinned like their brothers and fell into fornication, idolatry and every abomination, but they accepted the Lord’s discipline with wisdom, so that their hearts were broken by repentance and they regretted, unable to bear themselves because of what they had done. Therefore the Lord returns to them to save them, “and they shall know that I am the LORD” [10]... that is, He grants them His divine knowledge.

Truly, there is no way to our salvation except repentance, which blots out all our faults by the merits of the precious Blood through the Holy Spirit. Therefore St. Mark the Ascetic says: [God does not judge us because we have sinned, but He judges us because we have not repented.]

11 “Thus saith the Lord GOD; Smite with thine hand, and stamp with thy foot, and say, Alas for all the evil abominations of the house of Israel! for they shall fall by the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence. 12 He that is far off shall die of the pestilence; and he that is near shall fall by the sword; and he that remaineth and is besieged shall die by the famine: thus will I accomplish my fury upon them. 13 Then shall ye know that I am the LORD, when their slain men shall be among their idols round about their altars, upon every high hill, in all the tops of the mountains, and under every green tree, and under every thick oak, the place where they did offer sweet savour to all their idols. 14 So will I stretch out my hand upon them, and make the land desolate and waste, from the wilderness to Diblah, in all their habitations: and they shall know that I am the LORD.”

The Lord commanded him to clap his hand and stamp the ground with his feet like a stubborn child who has no strength or power, groaning over all their abominations, especially since the fruit of evil had begun to come upon them, killing by the sword, hunger and pestilence. It is as though the divine wrath had come upon them, so that people rose up against them, and the earth declared its anger, and all nature with it. The discipline will be more severe in the places used for pagan worship: the high hills, the tops of the mountains and under the shade of the trees, especially the oak... where they used to offer “sweet savour to all their idols” [13], which became for them the savour of death!

He declared that devastation creeps over the land from the wilderness to Diblah. Some see it as a town in the place of modern Dibl, north of Galilee, but the prevailing opinion is that it is Riblah, a city in the land of Hamath (2 Kgs 23:33; 25:20-21), as though by saying “from the wilderness to Diblah” he meant from the farthest south to the farthest north. Perhaps he also wished to declare the bitterness of what would happen to them in the person of their king: when Zedekiah was arrested after fleeing from Jerusalem, he was brought to Nebuchadnezzar, who was at Riblah, and he put out his eyes and bound him in chains to send him to Babylon (2 Kgs 25:6 etc.; Jer 39:5-7; 25:9-11).
The holy mountain!
* Wonderful are Your works, O Lord!
You have made me a mountain holy to You, I who am dust and sand!

Count me as Mount Horeb on which You declare Your Law, and as Mount Tabor on which You are transfigured in Your radiance, and as Mount Golgotha on which You offer the surpassing sacrifice of Your love!
* On the mountains Israel set up his idols like the nations, and defiled the high places with his abominations!
In Your love You discipline, bringing a sword and destroying the high places, and the cities turn into desolation!
But You do not forget the holy remnant, for You are the merciful God!
Remove from my mountains all abominations; burn with the fire of Your Holy Spirit all the thorns of sin!
Sanctify me, and count me Your holy mountain!

entries.section: 1. The end is at the doors:

paragraphs.text: 1 Moreover the word of the LORD came unto me, saying, 2 “Also, thou son of man, thus saith the Lord GOD unto the land of Israel; An end, the end is come upon the four corners of the land. 3 Now is the end come upon thee, and I will send mine anger upon thee, and will judge thee according to thy ways, and will recompense upon thee all thine abominations. 4 And mine eye shall not spare thee, neither will I have pity: but I will recompense thy ways upon thee, and thine abominations shall be in the midst of thee: and ye shall know that I am the LORD. 5 Thus saith the Lord GOD; An evil, an only evil, behold, is come. 6 An end is come, the end is come: it watcheth for thee; behold, it is come. 7 The turn is come unto thee, O thou that dwellest in the land: the time is come, the day of trouble is near, and not the sounding again of the mountains. 8 Now will I shortly pour out my fury upon thee, and accomplish mine anger upon thee: and I will judge thee according to thy ways, and will recompense thee for all thine abominations. 9 And mine eye shall not spare, neither will I have pity: I will recompense thee according to thy ways and thine abominations that are in the midst of thee; and ye shall know that I am the LORD that smiteth. 10 Behold the day, behold, it is come: the circle hath turned about; the rod hath blossomed, pride hath budded. 11 Violence is risen up into a rod of wickedness: none of them shall remain, nor of their multitude, nor of their wealth: neither shall there be wailing for them.

St. Peter the Apostle recorded for us the thinking of the scoffers who walk after their own lusts, those who say: “Where is the promise of his coming? for since the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of the creation” (2 Pet 3:4). And the Apostle Paul rebukes them: “Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance? But after thy hardness and impenitent heart treasurest up unto thyself wrath against the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God” (Rom 2:4-5).

Here the Lord affirms that the time of punishment has drawn near, which the Jewish people thought would never happen. Therefore the phrases are repeated in this chapter: “An end, the end is come, now is the end come upon thee (against thee), an evil is come, the time is come, the day is come” [2, 5, 6, 12]. And he spoke of the end from three sides:
a. The end is extremely painful [1-6].

entries.section: 1. The end is at the doors:

paragraphs.text: b. The end is at the doors [7-10].
c. The end is inevitable, with no escape [10-15].

The end came when their consciences became utterly hardened and there was no longer in their lives the least sign of repentance. Therefore God judges them according to their evil ways and abominations, because they did not listen to His prophets, nor did they repent of their idolatry.

The end is extremely painful, not because God wants the bitterness of their souls, for He still loves them, but because this is the nature of sin itself, its nature being turmoil and distress, for He says: “the day of trouble is near, and not the sounding again of the mountains” [7]. The songs of praise ended, joy was taken from them, and anxiety and distress came with the coming of sin into their lives. This is what He affirms by saying: “I will recompense thy ways upon thee, and thine abominations shall be in the midst of thee” [4]. It is as though the Lord affirms that what befalls her is the very nature of the corruption of sin and the abominations which man has chosen for himself, for it carries its punishment within itself.

This is what St. Augustine affirms as he comments on the words of the psalmist: [“As wax melteth, so let the wicked perish”] (Ps 68:2): [They perish by a kind of fire of their lusts. Here (in the world) there is a kind of hidden punishment of sinners of which the psalm speaks... For evil lust is like burning and fire. Does fire burn a garment while the lust of fornication does not burn the soul?! For the Scripture says of deliberate fornication: “Can a man take fire in his bosom, and his clothes not be burned?” (Prov 6:27)... And the Apostle says: “Wherefore God also gave them up to uncleanness through the lusts of their own hearts” (Rom 1:24). See the fire that makes him melt like wax!]

“The turn is come unto thee, O thou that dwellest in the land” [7]. Since the heart of the wicked dwells on the earth and becomes dust, his turn comes with the turning of the wheel of divine judgment, and there is none who can turn it from its course... The day of wrath comes. But whoever lifts his heart by repentance to heaven does not fall under wrath but enjoys the divine mercy.

entries.section: 1. The end is at the doors:

paragraphs.text: When the wicked who persist in their evil fall under wrath, they do not see the Lord the Shepherd but “the LORD that smiteth,” for He says: “and ye shall know that I am the LORD that smiteth” [9].
When the Lord declares the nearness of the painful end, which is the natural fruit of uncleannesses, He makes clear what the uncleannesses are so that believers may turn back from them.

entries.section: 1. The end is at the doors:

paragraphs.text: a. Pride: “the rod hath blossomed, pride hath budded” [10]. For the people’s fall into pagan worship or fornication was caused by pride. This is the beginning of the pains of the soul, which shattered the devil and brought him down from the highest heavenly ranks to the abyss, and which drove Adam and Eve out of Paradise. Therefore God humbles the proud, not because He desires to humble them, but in order to cut off from them what belongs to Satan, so that they may, in the spirit of humility, repent, submitting to the divine commandment.

entries.section: 1. The end is at the doors:

paragraphs.text: b. Violence: “Violence is risen up into a rod of wickedness” [11]. If pride touches chiefly man’s relationship with God, violence touches man’s relationship with his brother, and though the two are linked together, both are indicators of hardness of heart as an evil nature that corrupts man’s inner life and consequently his dealings with God and man.

Pride drives man to humiliation with none to be gentle with him, and violence drives him to the loss of what he has with none to have mercy on him: “none of them shall remain, nor of their multitude, nor of their wealth: neither shall there be wailing for them” [11].

12 “The time is come, the day draweth near: let not the buyer rejoice, nor the seller mourn: for wrath is upon all the multitude thereof. 13 For the seller shall not return to that which is sold, although they were yet alive: for the vision is touching the whole multitude thereof, which shall not return; neither shall any strengthen himself in the iniquity of his life. 14 They have blown the trumpet, even to make all ready; but none goeth to the battle: for my wrath is upon all the multitude thereof. 15 The sword is without, and the pestilence and the famine within: he that is in the field shall die with the sword; and he that is in the city, famine and pestilence shall devour him. 16 But they that escape of them shall escape, and shall be on the mountains like doves of the valleys, all of them mourning, every one for his iniquity. 17 All hands shall be feeble, and all knees shall be weak as water. 18 They shall also gird themselves with sackcloth, and horror shall cover them; and shame shall be upon all faces, and baldness upon all their heads. 19 They shall cast their silver in the streets, and their gold shall be an unclean thing: their silver and their gold shall not be able to deliver them in the day of the wrath of the LORD: they shall not satisfy their souls, neither fill their bowels: because it is the stumblingblock of their iniquity.

If our temporal life distracts us from spiritual preparation to meet the Lord, God sometimes allows us distress in all aspects of our temporal life, perhaps so that we may return and think about God’s threats and chastisements. Therefore He speaks to them here of a state of ruin and complete destruction of the city socially and economically: the buyer does not rejoice because he has nothing to buy with, nor the seller because he will not return to his trade; the trumpets are blown for war, but there is no man who rises to fight... a state of total loss! The sword pursues them from without, and pestilence and famine from within, and those who flee are not like strong lions but in the weakness of the doves that fly with constant moaning; they mourn as they see the city utterly ruined. They lose all bodily, psychological and spiritual energy: “All hands shall be feeble, and all knees shall be weak as water.” They enter a state of intense grief like one mourning a dead man, for “they shall also gird themselves with sackcloth... and baldness upon all their heads” [18].

Horror takes hold of them, and their silver and their gold which they had stored up cannot deliver them in the day of the divine wrath. They have lost all their hope, all their strength and all their holiness!

Their wealth, which distracted them from attention to the divine commandments and heavenly threats, cannot save them but becomes the cause of their destruction, since they use it in the worship of idols: “They shall cast their silver in the streets, and their gold shall be an unclean thing” [19]. What is silver but the word of God, purified seven times? Instead of keeping it in their hearts and preserving it in their inner storehouses, they cast it into the streets and neglect it. As for gold, which signifies the heavenly things, instead of lifting their lives to fellowship with God so as to experience the heavenly life within them, they stumble over heavenly things and grow in uncleanness!

entries.section: 3. The end of formal religious life:

paragraphs.text: 20 “As for the beauty of his ornament, he set it in majesty: but they made the images of their abominations and of their detestable things therein: therefore have I made it unto them an unclean thing. 21 And I will give it into the hands of the strangers for a prey, and to the wicked of the earth for a spoil; and they shall pollute it. 22 My face will I turn also from them, and they shall pollute my secret place: for the robbers shall enter into it, and defile it. 23 Make a chain: for the land is full of bloody crimes, and the city is full of violence. 24 Wherefore I will bring the worst of the heathen, and they shall possess their houses: I will also make the pomp of the strong to cease; and their holy places shall be defiled. 25 Destruction cometh; and they shall seek peace, and there shall be none. 26 Mischief shall come upon mischief, and rumour shall be upon rumour; then shall they seek a vision of the prophet; but the law shall perish from the priest, and counsel from the ancients.

If the former left God because of love of the world, and therefore God allowed the ruin of the city and all that is in it, others were occupied away from God through the formalities of worship, and therefore God allowed the ruin of the visible temple, perhaps that they might care for the inner temple in the heart.
God delivered their cities and their land to be plundered by foreign hands, and behold, He delivers His temple also to strangers.

entries.section: 3. The end of formal religious life:

paragraphs.text: His people defiled His altar with the worship of idols, so the Lord delivered His temple to the foreign soldiers who besieged it, to plunder it, and to the wicked of the earth to spoil it. He turned His face from His house since His children had turned it into a den of robbers, leaving the wicked to do what is not fitting: “My face will I turn also from them, and they shall pollute my secret place: for the robbers shall enter into it, and defile it” [22].

entries.section: 3. The end of formal religious life:

paragraphs.text: The defilement of the altar does not stop at their accepting pagan worship, but extends to their breaking the divine commandment and walking in injustice. Therefore God counts their worship a defilement of His temple, since it comes from a heart stained with blood and full of injustice. They defiled His temple, so He lets strangers defile their holy places, perhaps meaning the temple itself or their houses as sanctuaries. He says: “Make a chain: for the land is full of bloody crimes, and the city is full of violence. Wherefore I will bring the worst of the heathen, and they shall possess their houses: I will also make the pomp of the strong to cease; and their holy places shall be defiled” [23-24]. He allows the preparing of the chain, that is, the fetters for their captivity, for they had bound themselves with the chains of their sins; therefore they are delivered into the hands of the enemies, bound with visible chains of metal. Perhaps He also prepared the chain of His divine justice to punish them!

Besides their worship of idols and their breaking of the commandment, they resort to deceiving themselves with false prophecies. Instead of repentance they ask the prophets and priests for a false and deceptive peace. Therefore false prophets appeared who prophesy not according to God’s command but according to what pleases the desires of the people, and the law perished from the priest and counsel from the ancients... These say “Peace, peace; when there is no peace” (Jer 8:11).

Let every believer beware, and every family, and also every church, for if something forbidden enters, ruin comes and all fall under the wrath of God! And it is said, “There is an accursed thing in the midst of thee, O Israel” (Josh 7:13).

entries.section: 4. The end of the temporal kingship:

paragraphs.text: 27 “The king shall mourn, and the prince shall be clothed with desolation, and the hands of the people of the land shall be troubled: I will do unto them after their way, and according to their deserts will I judge them; and they shall know that I am the LORD.”

“The king shall mourn, and the prince shall be clothed with desolation, and the hands of the people of the land shall be troubled” [27]. Thus man sometimes relies on temporal authority, thinking that the Lord’s chastisements will not touch him; therefore the Lord breaks this temporal authority, and the king mourns... Here he refers to Jehoiachin (Ezek 27:12) and the former kings (Ezek 43:7, 9), as well as to the kings who will rule in the future (Ezek 37:22, 24), but he does not mean King Zedekiah (Ezek 12:12; 21:25). As for the prince (Prince), he means the head of the new community, or the ruling class at that time. As for the people of the land, before the captivity this referred to non-Hebrews (Ezra 4:4; Neh 10:31), but here he means the Jewish people.
How long will you wait, O my soul?!
* Your voice, O my God, has never ceased!
It warns me: the end is at the doors!
You are the Architect of the whole world; You know its secrets; You assure me: heaven and earth shall pass away, and I in my folly grow slack and am humiliated!
* How long will you wait, O my soul?!
Will you flee to the mountains?! Behold, they are shaken!
Will you rely on your friends?!
Behold, all hands are feeble, and all knees become like water!
Will you trust in your gold and your silver?
They cannot save you!
Will you depend on the formalities and the letter of worship!
Your God asks for the heart and the depths!
Will you lean on authority?!
Behold, everything passes away!
How long will you wait, O my soul?!

1 And it came to pass in the sixth year, in the sixth month, in the fifth day of the month, as I sat in mine house, and the elders of Judah sat before me, that the hand of the Lord GOD fell there upon me. 2 Then I beheld, and lo a likeness as the appearance of fire: from the appearance of his loins even downward, fire; and from his loins even upward, as the appearance of brightness, like shining brass. 3 And he put forth the form of an hand, and took me by a lock of mine head; and the spirit lifted me up between the earth and the heaven, and brought me in the visions of God to Jerusalem, to the door of the inner gate that looketh toward the north; where was the seat of the image of jealousy, which provoketh to jealousy. 4 And, behold, the glory of the God of Israel was there, according to the vision that I saw in the plain.

Fourteen months after his call (Ezek 1:12), the Spirit carried him in a vision to discover for himself the state the temple had reached. He was sitting in his house on the banks of the river Chebar, and the elders of Judah gathered to him and sat with him, perhaps in the period after his lying on his left side 390 days, prophesying of the sins of Israel, and before he began to lie on his right side forty days to prophesy of the iniquity of Judah. He says: “the hand of the Lord GOD fell there upon me. Then I beheld, and lo a likeness as the appearance of fire: from the appearance of his loins even downward, fire; and from his loins even upward, as the appearance of brightness, like shining brass” [1-2]. There was revealed to him the sight of “the incarnate Word of God,” who is “the likeness as the appearance of a man”; he saw Him as fire from His loins downward, and full of radiance from His loins upward. And as the Lord was carrying the prophet to the temple to reveal to him the uncleannesses the worshipers had reached, at all their levels, He feared that the prophet might collapse or despair; therefore He gave him this vision so that Ezekiel’s soul might be reassured that the incarnate Word of God must work, for He is the consuming fire who burns up all uncleanness and evil, and He is full of glory and radiance, entering with His people into His eternal glories.
