As for the other great eagle, he is Pharaoh of Egypt; he is great-winged, a symbol of the strength of his army, and he has thick feathers, a symbol of the large number of his soldiers, but he is not of divers colors, because he does not rule over many nations as Babylon does; it is toward him that the vine bent her roots and turned her branches that he might water it as its plants grew. This vine points to King Zedekiah, who inclined, with the majority of the people, to take refuge in Pharaoh of Egypt against Nebuchadnezzar, so the king betrayed the covenant and broke the oath when he thought of revolting against the king of Babylon. Here Ezekiel warned the king of two errors: first, the breaking of the oath even if it was with a pagan king, and second, leaning on the arm of man (Pharaoh of Egypt) instead of repenting and returning to God with all the heart. He declared that Zedekiah's fate would be like that of his predecessors, Jehoahaz, who was taken captive to Egypt in 607 B.C. (Ezek 19:4), and Jehoiachin, who was taken captive to Babylon (Ezek 19:9).

entries.section: 1. The riddle of the vine and the two eagles:

paragraphs.text: When King Zedekiah rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar by sending his messengers to Egypt that they might give him horses and much people [15], God asks him: "Shall he prosper?" [9] and the answer came at once: "Shall he not pull up the roots thereof, and cut off the fruit thereof, that it wither? it shall wither in all the leaves of her spring, even without great power or many people to pluck it up by the roots thereof. Yea, behold, being planted, shall it prosper? shall it not utterly wither, when the east wind toucheth it? it shall wither in the furrows where it grew" [9-10]. Thus He affirms more than once that the vine will wither in its roots and its fruit, in its leaves as in the furrows where it grew, that is, it will dry up completely on every level!

Origen asks why both Nebuchadnezzar and Pharaoh are called "an eagle," which is among the abominable birds (Lev 11:13), while at the same time the righteous and the good are likened to eagles. In Proverbs it is said: "Labour not to be rich: cease from thine own wisdom. Shall thine eyes fly toward it, and it is not? for it maketh itself wings; as an eagle it flieth toward heaven" (Prov 23:4-5); (the righteous man cares not for his own wisdom but makes for himself the two wings of an eagle, which are faith and works, or the love of God and the love of men, with which he flies to heaven to rest by the grace of God in the divine bosom); as it is also said: "But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint" (Isa 40:31).

Origen says: [If the eagle is abominable and accursed, it is not fitting for us to take wings like the wings of an eagle when we are good, and if the riches of the rich increase, they ought not to make for themselves wings like eagles] Why, then, was the eagle used as a likeness for the good?
He answers this question, saying:
[There are in the Holy Bible names of some animals that can be considered good and evil at the same time...

For example, the lion has two sides: a good side: "Judah is a lion's whelp: from the prey, my son, thou art gone up... he stooped down, he couched as a lion, and as a lioness; who shall rouse him up?" (Gen 49:9). And an evil side: "Because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour: whom resist stedfast in the faith" (1 Pet 5:8-9). In addition to this, the crafty deceiver, wishing to make us stand and fall: "He lieth in wait secretly as a lion in his den: he lieth in wait to catch the poor" (Ps 10:9).
Thus, as we have seen, the lion can be considered from two sides, one good and the other evil, and so also the eagle...
The good man is not an eagle, but is like the eagle, because he rivals the eagle.

Likewise the bronze serpent (Num 21:8) was a type of the Savior, because it was not a real serpent but like one. It points to the Savior: "And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up" (Jn 3:14)... And in another place the good man is commanded to be wise as serpents (Mt 10:16), not that he himself should become a serpent, and that, of course, in order to avoid acquiring the deceit of the real serpent...

The eagle and the lion are among the pure creatures, for we find for the cherubim "the face of a man, and the face of a lion, on the right side: and they four had the face of an ox on the left side; they four also had the face of an eagle" (Ezek 1:10)... They are pure, for there is nothing unclean in the presence of God.

And you, O believer, have become pure, and what God has made pure you must not make unclean. Thus it was said to the Apostle Peter concerning everything: "What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common" (Ar 10:15).

Thus the purity of the lion and the eagle that appeared with the cherubim was also declared. In addition to this, the prophecy of the coming of Christ is fulfilled by recognizing the pure lion and the pure eagle... "The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid; and the lion shall eat straw like the ox" (Isa 11:6), and that is when this is realized by faith in Christ, where the different natures are united among themselves, so the lion is not abominable but forgets its ferocity. And all the animals that are said to be abominable in the law of God receive again the nature of their former state at the beginning of creation. This transformation has already begun and will be accomplished at the Second Coming...
Do not be very astonished, then, if both Pharaoh and Nebuchadnezzar were likened to the eagle...].

11 Moreover the word of the LORD came unto me, saying, 12 "Say now to the rebellious house, Know ye not what these things mean? tell them, Behold, the king of Babylon is come to Jerusalem, and hath taken the king thereof, and the princes thereof, and led them with him to Babylon; 13 And hath taken of the king's seed, and made a covenant with him, and hath taken an oath of him: he hath also taken the mighty of the land: 14 That the kingdom might be base, that it might not lift itself up, but that by keeping of his covenant it might stand. 15 But he rebelled against him in sending his ambassadors into Egypt, that they might give him horses and much people. Shall he prosper? shall he escape that doeth such things? or shall he break the covenant, and be delivered? 16 As I live, saith the Lord GOD, surely in the place where the king dwelleth that made him king, whose oath he despised, and whose covenant he brake, even with him in the midst of Babylon he shall die. 17 Neither shall Pharaoh with his mighty army and great company make for him in the war, by casting up mounts, and building forts, to cut off many persons: 18 Seeing he despised the oath by breaking the covenant, when, lo, he had given his hand, and hath done all these things, he shall not escape. 19 Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; As I live, surely mine oath that he hath despised, and my covenant that he hath broken, even it will I recompense upon his own head. 20 And I will spread my net upon him, and he shall be taken in my snare, and I will bring him to Babylon, and will plead with him there for his trespass that he hath trespassed against me. 21 And all his fugitives with all his bands shall fall by the sword, and they that remain shall be scattered toward all winds: and ye shall know that I the LORD have spoken it."

The Lord did not leave the riddles obscure but gave to the rebellious house [12] their interpretation, so that they might have no excuse in their rush to rely on Pharaoh of Egypt and his armies, and He focused in the interpretation on the gravity of breaking and violating the covenant and swearing falsely, even if it was with a pagan king, which compelled the Lord Himself to intervene to chasten them with defeat. He affirmed that the ruin does not come about by human power, but God Himself rose up against them to chasten them. He affirms:
"Shall he prosper?!
shall he escape that doeth such things? or shall he break the covenant, and be delivered?!
As I live, saith the Lord GOD, surely in the place where the king dwelleth that made him king, whose oath he despised, and whose covenant he brake, even with him in the midst of Babylon he shall die.
Neither shall Pharaoh with his mighty army and great company make for him in the war, by casting up mounts, and building forts, to cut off many persons.
Seeing he despised the oath by breaking the covenant, when, lo, he had given his hand, and hath done all these things, he shall not escape.

Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; As I live, surely mine oath that he hath despised, and my covenant that he hath broken, even it will I recompense upon his own head. And I will spread my net upon him, and he shall be taken in my snare, and I will bring him to Babylon, and will plead with him there for his trespass that he hath trespassed against me. And all his fugitives with all his bands shall fall by the sword, and they that remain shall be scattered toward all winds: and ye shall know that I the LORD have spoken it" [15-21].

Thus God considered the oath to be His own oath, and the breaking of it a personal insult to Him, so Pharaoh with all his armies cannot rescue him from the hand of the Lord nor from the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, and the One who catches him in His net is the Lord, who carries him to Babylon to die there for his betrayal of the covenant. He will fall, he and his counselors and his army, by the sword, and the rest of the people will be taken captive and scattered toward every wind!

Therefore the Lord Christ warned us against swearing entirely, saying: "Ye have heard that it hath been said by them of old time, Thou shalt not forswear thyself, but shalt perform unto the Lord thine oaths: But I say unto you, Swear not at all; neither by heaven; for it is God's throne: Nor by the earth; for it is his footstool: neither by Jerusalem; for it is the city of the great King. Neither shalt thou swear by thy head, because thou canst not make one hair white or black. But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil" (Mt 5:33-37).
St. John Chrysostom warned much against the use of oaths; among his words:

[Today I am ready to show not the ruin of one house or two or three because of an oath, but the ruin of an entire city and a people beloved of God, who always enjoyed much divine care, and a race that escaped many dangers, Jerusalem itself, the city of God, which had the holy temple and all the divine service, in which were found the prophets and the grace of the Spirit and the ark and the two tablets of the covenant and the golden vessel, and which the angels often visited... it perished only because of an oath].

[It is not the oath that makes a man trustworthy, but the testimony of his life, the uprightness of his words and his good repute. Many open their throats with oaths and yet cannot persuade anyone to trust them, and others merely express their acceptance of a thing and are more worthy of belief than those who swear much].
[Truly the troubles of swearing are exceedingly great...

Since we know this, let us avoid swearing, and let our mouth practice at all times saying "believe me," and this will become a source of every godly conduct. For when the tongue is trained to use this expression alone, it becomes modest and ashamed to utter evil and wicked words].
[When we refrain from swearing entirely, we close the entrance completely before (Satan), but if we utter one oath we give him an opportunity to cause us endless harm].
St. John Chrysostom demands of us not only not to swear but also not to require others to swear, for he says:
[I ask you, are you in doubt concerning financial matters, so that you kill the soul of (your brother by asking him to swear)...?!
If you believe that he is truthful, do not oblige him to swear, and if you know that he is lying, do not force him to commit perjury].

entries.section: 3. The promise of a new kingdom:

paragraphs.text: 22 "Thus saith the Lord GOD; I will also take of the highest branch of the high cedar, and will set it; I will crop off from the top of his young twigs a branch, and will plant it upon an high mountain and eminent: 23 In the mountain of the height of Israel will I plant it: and it shall bring forth boughs, and bear fruit, and be a goodly cedar: and under it shall dwell all fowl of every wing; in the shadow of the branches thereof shall they dwell. 24 And all the trees of the field shall know that I the LORD have brought down the high tree, have exalted the low tree, have dried up the green tree, and have made the dry tree to flourish: I the LORD have spoken and have done it."

If entering into a treaty with the king of Babylon helped Judah for a time, so that she became like a willow tree and like a spreading vine of low stature [5-6], and if taking refuge in Pharaoh of Egypt destroyed her completely, then there is no salvation for man by a human arm. God Himself must intervene and plant His vine with His own hands, planting it in Himself, the lofty, towering mountain, so that the enemy cannot approach it. "Thus saith the Lord GOD; I will also take of the highest branch of the high cedar, and will set it; I will crop off from the top of his young twigs a branch, and will plant it upon an high mountain and eminent" [22]. He takes from the branch of the house of David (the cedar), where the Lord Christ, the Son of David, becomes incarnate, and plants the Church in Him! He is the head of the new branches, He is the branch planted not by a human arm nor from a human seed, but He is the Word of God, born before all ages, who became incarnate in the high mountain of Israel, and appears as a fruitful branch, and becomes a great cedar under which dwell the believers of every color and every tribe and tongue and nation. They fly to Him by the Holy Spirit and settle in the shadow of His branches [23]!

Thus in the midst of the dark prophecies and the severe chastenings the Lord dawns upon them with the hope of salvation by a divine arm through the Messiah, the true King, of the seed of David, who gathers into His Body members from all peoples!

God, who permitted them the two eagles, the king of Babylon and Pharaoh of Egypt, to chasten them, carries them as on the wings of an eagle, not to bring them into the Promised Land, but to carry humanity from all nations to the Father's bosom, in the heavenly Jerusalem, where eagles cannot snatch away!
Carry me as on eagles' wings!
* Of old You carried Your people from the bondage of Pharaoh as on eagles' wings, and brought them to Yourself, and led them into the Promised Land!
But when they forsook You they became prey to the eagles!
Nebuchadnezzar carried them off like an eagle devouring them, they took refuge in Pharaoh of Egypt, and behold, he was like an eagle snatching them away!
Now You have come to our world, to humanity that believes in You, carrying them as on eagles' wings to the bosom of Your Father!
* My God... how much I need You!
Behold, my sins have stirred up the eagles against me!
I fled from Your hands and became cheap prey!
Come, O wonderful in Your love, carry me in Yourself, and hide me, and cover me!
Give me the wings of a dove that I may fly to heaven!
Grant me Your Holy Spirit working in her!
May You carry me to the bosom of Your Father, O Holy One!
How I long for You, O Rock of my soul!

1 The word of the LORD came unto me again, saying, 2 "What mean ye, that ye use this proverb concerning the land of Israel, saying, The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge? 3 As I live, saith the Lord GOD, ye shall not have occasion any more to use this proverb in Israel. 4 Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sinneth, it shall die. 5 But if a man be just, and do that which is lawful and right, 6 And hath not eaten upon the mountains, neither hath lifted up his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel, neither hath defiled his neighbour's wife, neither hath come near to a menstruous woman, 7 And hath not oppressed any, but hath restored to the debtor his pledge, hath spoiled none by violence, hath given his bread to the hungry, and hath covered the naked with a garment; 8 He that hath not given forth upon usury, neither hath taken any increase, that hath withdrawn his hand from iniquity, hath executed true judgment between man and man, 9 Hath walked in my statutes, and hath kept my judgments, to deal truly; he is just, he shall surely live, saith the Lord GOD.

In this chapter the Lord dealt with the proverb that was common among the Jewish people: "The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge" [2]. They felt that the divine wrath that came upon them was only the fruit of the evil of their fathers, who had brought idol worship into the divine sanctuaries. But the Lord wanted to affirm that He will not recompense a man for the sins of his parents, and that the discipline He permits is because of what people do in their own time.

We dealt with this subject earlier, in the commentary on the Book of Exodus, where the Lord says, "For I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me" (Ex 20:5). We saw that God does not mean by this that He makes one generation bear the sins of the former generations; rather, in His love He is longsuffering toward one generation and a second, that perhaps they may repent. If they do not repent, He makes the third generation, and the fourth as well, bear the discipline, because they did not repent through their fathers, since He calls them "them that hate me." But if they repent through their fathers, they are not counted as sons of the wicked; rather God Himself becomes their Father, and they enjoy His grace.
* The soul that does not dwell in God is the source of its own evils, so it sins, and the soul that sins is the one that dies.

St. Ambrose: There is no partiality with God; the soul of the father is as the soul of the son, or as He says: "Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sinneth, it shall die" [4]... Here we ask:
First: Does a man inherit nothing of the weaknesses of his father?
Second: Does the soul die?

entries.section: First: Does a man inherit nothing of the weaknesses of his father?

paragraphs.text: The Holy Bible does not ignore the effect of parents on a person's life. A person who is born in a holy home and brought up between godly parents finds a possibility that helps the growth of his spiritual life and the setting out of his soul to live with God. On the contrary, if he has a wicked father and a wicked mother, then even if they do not encourage their son to sin and evil, at the very least they stand as a stumbling block before his spiritual growth. Nevertheless, many children loved evil in spite of the godliness of their parents, such as the two sons of Eli the priest, and there are also children who loved righteousness in spite of the evil of their fathers. The environment in which a person lives may be good or evil, but it does not compel him to goodness or evil. Indeed, a man himself may begin his life with evil and then return and complete his way with God, and he may begin in the Spirit and then fall back into evil and live in sin. For this reason this chapter has presented to us four examples: one who was wicked though his father was righteous, one who was righteous though his father was wicked, and one who was righteous and then turned aside, or the opposite. This happened in the kings of Judah. Hezekiah the good king was a consecrated servant, who "did that which was right in the sight of the LORD, according to all that David his father had done" (2 Chr 29:2); he opened his reign by repairing and cleansing the Temple, removed the high places and cast out the images... But his father Ahaz had his heart attached to the love of idols from the beginning of his reign, made his son pass through the fire and sacrificed on the high places (2 Kgs 16:3-4); indeed he shut up the doors of the porch of the Temple, put out the lamps, and burned no incense nor offered burnt offerings to the living God (2 Chr 29:7). As for Manasseh the son of Hezekiah, he led his people astray from the truth, and made them sacrifice to all the host of heaven, and they did worse than the nations whom the LORD had destroyed before the children of Israel (2 Kgs 21:2-9), although in the last of his days he amended much of what he had corrupted (2 Chr 33:1-20).

St. Jerome distinguishes between the saying of the Psalmist: "What man is he that liveth, and shall not see death?" (Ps 89:48), and what is said by Ezekiel the prophet: "The soul that sinneth, it shall die" [4], saying: [There is a difference between seeing death and tasting it, for he who sees, sees indeed but does not taste it, while he who tastes it of necessity sees it]. By this he means that all mankind sees death, the death of the body, but he whose soul is sanctified in the Lord sees the death of his body yet does not taste death, since he bears the power of Christ's resurrection working in him.

* As there is a death of the body, there is a death of the soul... The death of the soul is in any case not like the death of the body; it is utterly dreadful. The death of the body is the separation of the soul from the body, the one from the other, so that man is released from pending cares and toils, and the other (the soul) is transferred to a clear dwelling. Then, when the body is dissolved and decomposes, it is gathered together again in incorruption and receives its soul back again. This is the death of the body, but the death of the soul is fearful and terrifying. In it, when dissolution takes place, the soul does not come to an end as the body does, but is joined to the body again and is not annihilated; it is cast with it into the fire that is not quenched.
St. John Chrysostom: * This death (of the soul) has as its opponent and enemy Him who said: "I am the life" (Jn 14:6).
Origen: * According to the Holy Scriptures we learn that there are three kinds of death:

A death when we die to sin and live to God. Blessed is this death by which we flee from sin and are consecrated to God, for it separates us from what is mortal and sanctifies us to Him who is immortal.
The other death is the departure from this life, as the father Abraham and the father David died and were buried with their fathers, when the soul is freed from the bonds of the body.

The third death is that of which it was said, "Let the dead bury their dead" (Mt 8:22). By this death not only the body dies but the soul also, for "the soul that sinneth, it shall die" (Ezek 18:4); it dies to the Lord, not through the weakness of nature but through the weakness of committing transgression. This death is not a leaving of this life but a falling into error.
Therefore spiritual death is one thing, natural death another, and the third is death as punishment.

St. Ambrose: St. Clement of Alexandria sees that the words found in this chapter [4-9] "contain a description of the conduct of Christians, in which God nobly urges us to the blessed life, which is the reward of a life of goodness, eternal life." This description includes the positive and negative aspects in the life of the believer:

A. It befits the Christian to walk in righteousness, to do that which is lawful and right [5], not to eat upon the mountains that were defiled by the sacrifices of the idolaters, nor to lift up his eyes to their idols. Thus he is sanctified entirely: he is sanctified in his heart by righteousness, truth and justice, and sanctified in his eating by refraining from taking part in pagan feasts, and sanctified even in the glances of his eyes, so that he does not lift up his eyes to their idols. He is sanctified by the positive work, which is doing righteousness and loving truth and justice, and negatively by refraining from everything that is evil...

B. The Christian does not defile his neighbour's wife, nor does he come near his own wife when she is menstruous; he loves holiness in his inner life and in his body as in others; he does not covet his brother's wife...

C. He does not practice injustice against anyone, not only by giving others their lawful rights, but he gives the poor man his right in sharing his needs, and gives the naked man his right in sharing his clothes with him, and offers the needy debtor the right of love and mercy, so that he demands no usury from him, and he offers others the right of supporting the wronged against the wrongdoer, so that he does not stand by passively but "hath executed true judgment between man and man" [8].
D. The secret of his righteous life is his entering into the divine commandment, as the Lord says: "Hath walked in my statutes, and hath kept my judgments, to deal truly; he is just" [9].

entries.section: 2. A wicked son of a righteous father:

paragraphs.text: 10 "If he beget a son that is a robber, a shedder of blood, and that doeth the like to any one of these things, 11 And that doeth not any of those duties, but even hath eaten upon the mountains, and defiled his neighbour's wife, 12 Hath oppressed the poor and needy, hath spoiled by violence, hath not restored the pledge, and hath lifted up his eyes to the idols, hath committed abomination, 13 Hath given forth upon usury, and hath taken increase: shall he then live? he shall not live: he hath done all these abominations; he shall surely die; his blood shall be upon him.

entries.section: 2. A wicked son of a righteous father:

paragraphs.text: The first example the Lord gave concerning personal responsibility is the wicked son of the righteous father. He "shall not live: he hath done all these abominations; he shall surely die; his blood shall be upon him" [13]. His father's righteousness does not rescue him from the fruit of his abominations, but he shall surely die.

St. Jerome wrote to the deacon Sabinianus, urging him to repent, as follows: [Perhaps you are deluded in yourself that the bishop who ordained you is a holy man, and you think that his merits atone for your transgressions. I have already told you that the father is not punished for his son, nor the son for his father. The soul that sinneth, it shall die].

entries.section: 3. A righteous son of a wicked father:

paragraphs.text: 14 "Now, lo, if he beget a son, that seeth all his father's sins which he hath done, and considereth, and doeth not such like, 15 That hath not eaten upon the mountains, neither hath lifted up his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel, hath not defiled his neighbour's wife, 16 Neither hath oppressed any, hath not withholden the pledge, neither hath spoiled by violence, but hath given his bread to the hungry, and hath covered the naked with a garment, 17 That hath taken off his hand from the poor, that hath not received usury nor increase, hath executed my judgments, hath walked in my statutes; he shall not die for the iniquity of his father, he shall surely live. 18 As for his father, because he cruelly oppressed, spoiled his brother by violence, and did that which is not good among his people, lo, even he shall die in his iniquity. 19 Yet say ye, Why? doth not the son bear the iniquity of the father? When the son hath done that which is lawful and right, and hath kept all my statutes, and hath done them, he shall surely live. 20 The soul that sinneth, it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son: the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him.

The people in the days of King Zedekiah thought that they were more righteous than the people in the days of King Manasseh, so they felt that they were bearing the iniquity of their fathers. But the Lord affirms here: "If he beget a son, that seeth all his father's sins which he hath done, and considereth, and doeth not such like... he shall not die for the iniquity of his father, he shall surely live. As for his father, because he cruelly oppressed, spoiled his brother by violence, and did that which is not good among his people, lo, even he shall die in his iniquity" [14-19].
When a man commits iniquity he loses his life, as St. Gregory of Nyssa says: [Sin is nothing but estrangement from God, who alone is the true life].

But perhaps some will ask: How does the righteous son not bear the iniquity of his father when it has been said: "Let the iniquity of his fathers be remembered with the LORD; and let not the sin of his mother be blotted out" (Ps 109:14)?

St. Augustine answers: [Is it to be understood that even the iniquity of his fathers comes upon a man? Those who are converted in Christ do not have the iniquity of their fathers come upon them, since they are no longer sons of the wicked, because they did not imitate their conduct. Therefore it is added to the words: "visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children... of them that hate me" (Ex 20:5), that is, those who hate me as their fathers hated me].

entries.section: 4. A man's turning from his evil:

paragraphs.text: 21 "But if the wicked will turn from all his sins that he hath committed, and keep all my statutes, and do that which is lawful and right, he shall surely live, he shall not die. 22 All his transgressions that he hath committed, they shall not be mentioned unto him: in his righteousness that he hath done he shall live. 23 Have I any pleasure at all that the wicked should die? saith the Lord GOD: and not that he should return from his ways, and live? 24 But when the righteous turneth away from his righteousness, and committeth iniquity, and doeth according to all the abominations that the wicked man doeth, shall he live? All his righteousness that he hath done shall not be mentioned: in his trespass that he hath trespassed, and in his sin that he hath sinned, in them shall he die. 25 Yet ye say, The way of the Lord is not equal. Hear now, O house of Israel; Is not my way equal? are not your ways unequal? 26 When a righteous man turneth away from his righteousness, and committeth iniquity, and dieth in them; for his iniquity that he hath done shall he die. 27 Again, when the wicked man turneth away from his wickedness that he hath committed, and doeth that which is lawful and right, he shall save his soul alive. 28 Because he considereth, and turneth away from all his transgressions that he hath committed, he shall surely live, he shall not die. 29 Yet saith the house of Israel, The way of the Lord is not equal. O house of Israel, are not my ways equal? are not your ways unequal? 30 Therefore I will judge you, O house of Israel, every one according to his ways, saith the Lord GOD. Repent, and turn yourselves from all your transgressions; so iniquity shall not be your ruin. 31 Cast away from you all your transgressions, whereby ye have transgressed; and make you a new heart and a new spirit: for why will ye die, O house of Israel? 32 For I have no pleasure in the death of him that dieth, saith the Lord GOD: wherefore turn yourselves, and live ye.

We have said that the Lord wanted by His speech here to move His people toward repentance, that they should not be troubled because of the sins of their fathers, and also that they should not be troubled by their own previous or present personal sins if they offer true repentance, for He says: "If the wicked will turn from all his sins that he hath committed, and keep all my statutes, and do that which is lawful and right, he shall surely live, he shall not die" [21]. Some consider this statement the center of the whole book, the most precious statement found in it; it is a powerful call to repentance! "Have I any pleasure at all that the wicked should die? saith the Lord GOD: and not that he should return from his ways, and live?" [23]. He opens the door of hope wide, so that not one soul may perish in a spirit of deadly despair.

The Fathers of the Church found in this chapter a fertile field into which every fallen, despairing person may enter to eat of the fruit of repentance and be filled with hope, while it also gives clear warnings to the souls that stand, lest by their negligence they lose all their past labor. The following are some comments of the Fathers:
* By encouragement He lightens the weight of sins and lessens the passions, inspiring hope of salvation.

St. Clement of Alexandria: * For those who are in danger of despair He provided the refuge of forgiveness, and for those who are in danger of (presumptuous) hope, who delay by putting off, He made the day of death uncertain.
St. Augustine: * If they hear this voice and believe it, they will be healed of despair and rise from the bottomless pit of depths into which they have fallen.
St. Augustine: * We do not despair of any man as long as God's longsuffering leads the wicked to repentance, so we do not drive him out of this life.

St. Augustine: * Do not despair of salvation. Remember what is written in the Holy Scripture, that he who falls arises and he who strays returns (Jer 8:4), and the wounded is healed, and he who fell prey to the beasts escapes, and he who confesses his sins is not despised... It is a time for endurance and longsuffering, a time for healing and correction. Have you stumbled? Arise! Have you sinned? Cease from sin!
St. Augustine: * Repentance is a "life" better than death...
Hasten to it, O sinner, and embrace it as a drowning man embraces some planks, so that it may snatch you from drowning amid the waves of sins and carry you to the divine harbor, full of tenderness.
Tertullian: * Since what the Lord says is true, when I repent He forgets all my past sins and all my iniquities; why do you frighten me?
God promises me forgiveness; would you cast me into despair?

entries.section: 4. A man's turning from his evil:

paragraphs.text: Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles: At the very time when He opens the doors of hope with all power before sinners that they may repent, He warns those who stand lest they fall, saying: "But when the righteous turneth away from his righteousness, and committeth iniquity, and doeth according to all the abominations that the wicked man doeth, shall he live? All his righteousness that he hath done shall not be mentioned: in his trespass that he hath trespassed, and in his sin that he hath sinned, in them shall he die" [24]. And as St. Anba Anthony says: [Let us persevere in our training every day, knowing that if we neglect it for one single day the Lord will not forgive us for the sake of the past, but will bring His wrath upon our negligence... for Judas ruined his past striving because of one night].

And St. Basil the Great says: [When a change occurs, the labor of the righteous becomes vain, just as the sinner is not blamed, by the first turning away from what is good to what is worse, and the second inclining from what is evil to what is better].

But is not this statement harsh and severe? St. John Chrysostom answers: [Even in this matter God showed the greatness of the tenderness of His love, presenting to us these terrifying things in order to raise us up and awaken in us a desire for the Kingdom]. And St. Clement of Alexandria says: [The punishments of God are for salvation, and discipline leads us to repentance, for God longs for repentance more than for the death of the sinner].

entries.section: 4. A man's turning from his evil:

paragraphs.text: "For I have no pleasure in the death of him that dieth, saith the Lord GOD: wherefore turn yourselves, and live ye" [32].
God speaks these words to you if you are wretched: "For I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked."
Even if you want your own death, I do not want it.
You did not create yourself, but by despair you perish.
In any case, God created you when you did not exist; afterward He sought you when you went astray, and found you through the blood of His Son and saved you.
He Himself calls you: Return from the abyss of despair. Come, for I do not desire the death of the sinner but that he return and live...
Do not lose confidence through despair about your sins, and at the same time do not trust in length of life. Therefore repent... Why do you not repent today?

Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles: Origen sees in this divine speech concerning the possibility of sinners' returning to God and the warning of those who stand against falling, a confirmation of the error of those who say that there are different natures created thus, showing that the sinner can become good and the opposite.
You did not create me to die!
* You created me to live in the world as a king, in my royal palace!
You did not create me to die, but to live by You and with You!
* You are wonderful, O Lord, in Your love for me, for even if I seek death, You desire my life!
I do not know what is for my edification and my glory!
But You know all that is for my life, O my Creator!
* You do not will my death but my life; You do not hold me accountable for the errors of my fathers, nor wound my feelings for sins I have left behind. You are wonderful in Your care for me!
* You are the Savior of souls from corruption; You alone are able to renew my nature, O my Savior!

entries.section: 1. The lioness and her two whelps:

paragraphs.text: 1 "Moreover take thou up a lamentation for the princes of Israel, 2 And say, What is thy mother? A lioness: she lay down among lions, she nourished her whelps among young lions. 3 And she brought up one of her whelps: it became a young lion, and it learned to catch the prey; it devoured men. 4 The nations also heard of him; he was taken in their pit, and they brought him with chains unto the land of Egypt. 5 Now when she saw that she had waited, and her hope was lost, then she took another of her whelps, and made him a young lion. 6 And he went up and down among the lions, he became a young lion, and learned to catch the prey, and devoured men. 7 And he knew their desolate palaces, and he laid waste their cities; and the land was desolate, and the fulness thereof, by the noise of his roaring. 8 Then the nations set against him on every side from the provinces, and spread their net over him: he was taken in their pit. 9 And they put him in ward in chains, and brought him to the king of Babylon: they brought him into holds, that his voice should no more be heard upon the mountains of Israel.

Here he offers a lamentation for the kings of Judah, especially the two kings: Jehoahaz, who met his sorrowful fate by being carried captive to Egypt in 608 B.C. after a reign that lasted 3 months, and King Jehoiachin, who was taken captive to Babylon in 597 B.C. after a reign that likewise lasted about 3 months.
In this lamentation we notice:

entries.section: 1. The lioness and her two whelps:

paragraphs.text: A. That he does not say "a lamentation for the princes of Judah" or "the kings of Judah" but for "the princes of Israel"... for what befalls one of the two kingdoms befalls the whole people. God looks upon believing mankind as one people: if one member suffers, the rest of the members suffer with it, "and if one member be honoured, all the members rejoice with it" (1 Cor 12:27). These two kings did not wrong themselves alone by their sinful conduct, nor the kingdom of Judah alone, but all Israel, who represented the people of God at that time. Thus when one member in us grows weak, the whole body grows weak with it, and when one of the members repents, all heaven rejoices over him! Our worship is a personal relationship with God, but it is not individual, that is, not isolated from the holy congregation, whether the militant or the triumphant, or even the members who will come in the future. It is one Church interacting together in love and the spirit of unity. B. "And say, What is thy mother? A lioness: she lay down among lions, she nourished her whelps among young lions" [2]. She is a queen who lies down in strength among kings, and she is likened to a lioness and not a lion because she is a queen who bears kings and brings them up: "And she brought up one of her whelps: it became a young lion, and it learned to catch the prey; it devoured men. The nations also heard of him; he was taken in their pit, and they brought him with chains unto the land of Egypt" [3-4]. This is Jehoahaz, who was brought up in a royal family, became king and learned war, but instead of fighting to protect his people he fought his own children to devour them. He worked for himself and not for the kingdom that had raised him and made him king. He proved to be weak and stripped of moral principles; Pharaoh Necho carried him captive down to Egypt, and he never returned to his land.
In any case, he is a young lion who protected neither his people nor even himself, but preyed upon his flock...

How hard it is for the shepherd to turn into a wolf, and instead of protecting his sheep to slaughter them that he himself may be filled! He should have offered his life as a sacrifice of love for his people, not slaughtered his people for the sake of his own honor or private interests. In this St. Aphrahat says: [Imitate our sweet Shepherd (Jesus), whose life was not dearer to Him than His sheep. Train the young, love the lambs, and carry them in your bosoms, so that when you stand before the Chief Shepherd you may present the flock complete, and He will give you what He promised you: "that where I am, there ye may be also"].

And St. Augustine says: [Let us not love ourselves but love Him, and in tending His sheep let us seek what is His and not what is ours... For he who cannot live by himself surely dies if he loves himself. And in this he is not a lover of himself, for by loving himself he loses his life...
May the shepherds of the flock not be lovers of themselves, lest they tend the flock as though it were their own property and not as the flock of Christ, seeking material gain as "lovers of money."
Or they domineer over the people as profiteers, or seek glory from the honor offered them as the proud, or fall into heresies as blasphemers, and despise the holy fathers as disobedient to parents.
And they repay with evil the good done to those whom they wish to reform, lest they perish, as the unthankful.

And they kill their own souls and the souls of others as those who are without mercy, and try to distort the characters of the saints as false witnesses, and give free rein to base desires as the unclean, and are always complaining... as the unmerciful.

And they know nothing of the service of love, as those who have no compassion; they trouble mankind with their foolish disputes as the obstinate; they do not understand what they say or what they insist upon, as the blind; and they prefer fleshly delights to joy, as lovers of self more than lovers of God.

These and other similar vices, whether they all appear together in one person, or one of them dominates one person and another dominates another, appear in one form or another from the starting point of being lovers of themselves. This is the vice against which those who tend the flock of Christ must be on guard, lest they seek what is their own and not what is Jesus Christ's, and use for the fulfillment of their lusts those for whom Christ shed His blood].

Jehoahaz preyed upon his sheep instead of defending them and laying down his life for them, so he himself became the prey of the nations; he fell into their snares and was led captive to Egypt. He who tends himself at the expense of his brethren and at the expense of the salvation of his own soul loses even his bodily pleasure and his earthly honor.

The matter was repeated with another king, "Jehoiachin," who was no better than the former, but devoured his people and laid waste their cities by his evil conduct, so the land became desolate because of him, and he was carried captive to Babylon.

10 "Thy mother is like a vine, like thee, planted by the waters: she was fruitful and full of branches by reason of many waters. 11 And she had strong rods for the sceptres of them that bare rule, and her stature was exalted among the thick branches, and she appeared in her height with the multitude of her branches. 12 But she was plucked up in fury, she was cast down to the ground, and the east wind dried up her fruit: her strong rods were broken and withered; the fire consumed them. 13 And now she is planted in the wilderness, in a dry and thirsty ground. 14 And fire is gone out of a rod of her branches, which hath devoured her fruit, so that she hath no strong rod to be a sceptre to rule. This is a lamentation, and shall be for a lamentation."

After offering a lamentation for these two kings, he begins to offer a lamentation for the people of God, who were like a vine planted by the waters of divine grace, so that she was "fruitful and full of branches by reason of many waters" [11]. The nations could not stand against her, but her stem rose high and her branches multiplied... But when she left her God and turned back to idolatry, she was plucked up from her land and carried to Babylon, so she withered by the winds of discipline and lost her fruit through her multiplied sins... Her branches became fuel and she entered into a state of extreme weakness, with none to support her! This is the lamentation over every man who leaves the way of the Lord and runs after the desires of his heart and the pleasures of his body: he is deprived of enjoying the waters of the Holy Spirit, who gives life and bears fruit, and he is removed from the position of sonship to God to become, by his wicked heart and evil life, a stranger and a captive in the land of the enemy (the devil); his branches are broken to become fuel consumed by the flames, and his soul dries up completely like a barren land!
Restore my kingship to me!
* The kings of Israel turned from shepherds into wolves!
They preyed upon the flock and practiced the love of power!
They sought what was their own and not what belonged to their people!
So they perished, and lost all riches and pleasure and honor!
* I complain to You about myself!
I forgot my kingship and turned to preying; I did not seek love, what belongs to others, but what is for myself!
Restore to me the nature of kingship, O King of kings!
Teach me love, and I shall become a queen!

1 And it came to pass in the seventh year, in the fifth month, the tenth day of the month, that certain of the elders of Israel came to enquire of the LORD, and sat before me. 2 And the word of the LORD came unto me, saying, 3 "Son of man, speak unto the elders of Israel, and say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Are ye come to enquire of me? As I live, saith the Lord GOD, I will not be enquired of by you. 4 Wilt thou judge them, son of man, wilt thou judge them? cause them to know the abominations of their fathers, In the previous year a group of elders came to ask the prophet in the land of captivity about what would happen to the kingdom of Judah and to the captive people at that time, but he directed the speech toward repentance, for the Lord said: "As I live, saith the Lord GOD, I will not be enquired of by you" [3]. If you have come to ask me, first remove from yourselves the nature of rebellion that your fathers lived and you live, and then I shall answer your requests.

We often cry out to the Lord in time of distress, and He wishes to deliver and longs to save, but He wants the distress to achieve its goal, which is our repentance from the heart and our returning to Him with all the heart! If God delays in answering, it is not out of neglect of us but a sign of His care, for He waits for the sincerity of our repentance that we may profit from the trial. Our rebellious nature needs the fire of affliction that we may turn back to our God and seek Him sincerely.

5 And say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD; In the day when I chose Israel, and lifted up mine hand unto the seed of the house of Jacob, and made myself known unto them in the land of Egypt, when I lifted up mine hand unto them, saying, I am the LORD your God; 6 In the day that I lifted up mine hand unto them, to bring them forth of the land of Egypt into a land that I had espied for them, flowing with milk and honey, which is the glory of all lands: 7 Then said I unto them, Cast ye away every man the abominations of his eyes, and defile not yourselves with the idols of Egypt: I am the LORD your God. 8 But they rebelled against me, and would not hearken unto me: they did not every man cast away the abominations of their eyes, neither did they forsake the idols of Egypt: then I said, I will pour out my fury upon them, to accomplish my anger against them in the midst of the land of Egypt. 9 But I wrought for my name's sake, that it should not be polluted before the heathen, among whom they were, in whose sight I made myself known unto them, in bringing them forth out of the land of Egypt.

The nature of rebellion is not something new in their life, but it has accompanied them since the beginning of their appearance as a people or nation in the land of Egypt. Jacob and his sons entered Egypt as a family and came out as a people under the leadership of the first leader, Moses the prophet. In Egypt, where this nation and people grew, the idols of Egypt were nurtured within their heart. The Lord uncovered the secret of their bondage in Egypt: it was not the hardness of Pharaoh's heart but the perversion of the people's heart: "Then said I unto them, Cast ye away every man the abominations of his eyes, and defile not yourselves with the idols of Egypt: I am the LORD your God. But they rebelled against me" [7-8]. At the time when God was spying out for them the land flowing with honey and milk, "the glory of all lands" [6], they refused to cast away the abominations of their eyes and to forsake the idols, and yet He did not pour out His wrath on them in the land of Egypt but brought them out with power for the sake of His holy name [9], that He might be glorified in them among the nations.

Thus God cares for man from his creation, and He even devised our salvation and our crossing over from the bondage of sin and our being brought into His bosom, the paradise of truth that overflows for the soul with honey and milk, while man is born with the microbe of disobedience running in his blood. Rebellion is a nature we inherited from the disobedience of our first parents; therefore our reform needs a complete change of our nature.

10 Wherefore I caused them to go forth out of the land of Egypt, and brought them into the wilderness. 11 And I gave them my statutes, and shewed them my judgments, which if a man do, he shall even live in them. 12 Moreover also I gave them my sabbaths, to be a sign between me and them, that they might know that I am the LORD that sanctify them. 13 "But the house of Israel rebelled against me in the wilderness: they walked not in my statutes, and they despised my judgments, which if a man do, he shall even live in them; and my sabbaths they greatly polluted: then I said, I would pour out my fury upon them in the wilderness, to consume them. 14 But I wrought for my name's sake, that it should not be polluted before the heathen, in whose sight I brought them out. 15 Yet also I lifted up my hand unto them in the wilderness, that I would not bring them into the land which I had given them, flowing with milk and honey, which is the glory of all lands; 16 Because they despised my judgments, and walked not in my statutes, but polluted my sabbaths: for their heart went after their idols. 17 Nevertheless mine eye spared them from destroying them, neither did I make an end of them in the wilderness.

How many were God's gifts in the wilderness! He gave them fresh food every day for nothing, so that they needed neither to plow the land and clear it, nor to sow and reap, nor to gather the harvest and prepare the food. And He gave them a rock that gushed forth sweet water and followed them wherever they went, a thing that costs man much, especially in the desert! They lacked neither new clothes nor shoes, nor medicines to heal the sick... He cared for them in every great and small thing, and yet in His reproach to them He mentioned nothing of this but concentrated on two things that He considered the best He had given them: the divine commandment and His sabbaths, for He says: "And I gave them my statutes, and shewed them my judgments, which if a man do, he shall even live in them. Moreover also I gave them my sabbaths, to be a sign between me and them, that they might know that I am the LORD that sanctify them" [11-12]. He gave them the commandment as His own statutes and judgments, and the sabbaths as His own sabbaths. By the commandment man lives, and by the sabbaths he is sanctified. This, in God's view, was the summit of what He did for them in the wilderness.

As for the commandment, it is a sign of God's love for man and His care, for He did not accept to make him like the irrational creatures, walking as the nature given to him by God dictates, but gave him free will, and granted him the commandment as a sign of this freedom: he may accept life with God and he may refuse it. As Tertullian says: [He enabled him, as a human being, to boast that he alone was worthy to receive commandments from God, as a being capable of reason and knowledge, who restrains himself quietly with the bonds of reasoning freedom, subject to God, to whom He subjected all things].

The commandment is also the sphere in which man surrenders his will to the Lord by obedience, so that he receives the divine will working in him. For in accepting the commandment he accepts the word of God, who works in him. Therefore the Lord says: "If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed; and ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free" (Jn 8:31, 33), "the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life" (Jn 6:63). And St. Mark the Ascetic says: [God is hidden in His commandments, so whoever seeks Him finds Him in them].

As for the sabbaths, which God gave us for our sanctification, they point to the Lord Christ Himself, who came on the seventh day as the mystery of our true rest. For the word "sabbath" means in Hebrew "rest," and we have no rest except in Christ Jesus. He is the mystery of the Sabbath: in Him the Father rested in us, since He found Him, as our representative, the object of His pleasure, and in Him we rested in the Father, since we find in Him the Father's bosom receiving us. The Lord Christ is the mystery of our sabbath and the mystery of our sanctification!
St. Augustine divides the history of the world's salvation into the days of the week as follows:

The first day: from Adam to the Flood; the second day: from the Flood to Abraham; the third day: from Abraham to David; the fourth day: from David to the captivity; the fifth day: from the captivity to the Incarnation of Christ; the sixth day: from the Incarnation to the great day of the Lord; the seventh day: the great day of the Lord, in which mankind finds its rest in Christ Jesus our Lord. By this the Lord brings us into a life without end, in which our souls rest with our bodies. "There we shall rest and see, see and love, love and praise. This is what shall be in the end that has no end, for what other end have we for ourselves than to attain the Kingdom that has no end?"!
St. Clement of Alexandria says: [We keep the spiritual Sabbath until the coming of the Savior, since we have rested from sin].

The Lord gave them His commandment as a sign of His esteem for man above every other earthly creature, but man despised it and did not walk in it. And He gave him His sabbaths for his sanctification, but man greatly polluted the sabbaths of the Lord [13]. And yet the Lord says: "Nevertheless mine eye spared them from destroying them, neither did I make an end of them in the wilderness" [17]. This is God's longsuffering toward us and His love for us!

entries.section: 4. The rebellion of the new generation in the wilderness:

paragraphs.text: 18 But I said unto their children in the wilderness, Walk ye not in the statutes of your fathers, neither observe their judgments, nor defile yourselves with their idols: 19 I am the LORD your God; walk in my statutes, and keep my judgments, and do them; 20 And hallow my sabbaths; and they shall be a sign between me and you, that ye may know that I am the LORD your God. 21 Notwithstanding the children rebelled against me: they walked not in my statutes, neither kept my judgments to do them, which if a man do, he shall even live in them; they polluted my sabbaths: then I said, I would pour out my fury upon them, to accomplish my anger against them in the wilderness. 22 Nevertheless I withdrew mine hand, and wrought for my name's sake, that it should not be polluted in the sight of the heathen, in whose sight I brought them forth. 23 I lifted up mine hand unto them also in the wilderness, that I would scatter them among the heathen, and disperse them through the countries; 24 Because they had not executed my judgments, but had despised my statutes, and had polluted my sabbaths, and their eyes were after their fathers' idols. 25 Wherefore I gave them also statutes that were not good, and judgments whereby they should not live; 26 And I polluted them in their own gifts, in that they caused to pass through the fire all that openeth the womb, that I might make them desolate, to the end that they might know that I am the LORD.

God again affirmed to the new generation that was born in the wilderness that they should not walk in the spirit of their fathers, who came out of Egypt carrying its idols in their heart, but should walk in His statutes, keep His judgments and do them, and hallow His sabbaths as the sign of the covenant between Him and them. Yet the children were no less rebellious than their fathers. They were drawn to the idols of their fathers and not to the Lord their God. And in spite of all this, for His name's sake He did not wish to pour out His wrath on them in the wilderness, lest He be despised in the sight of the nations.
Perhaps some will object to the divine saying:

entries.section: 4. The rebellion of the new generation in the wilderness:

paragraphs.text: "Wherefore I gave them also statutes that were not good, and judgments whereby they should not live; and I polluted them in their own gifts, in that they caused to pass through the fire all that openeth the womb, that I might make them desolate, to the end that they might know that I am the LORD" [25-26].

When sinners insist on disobedience, He gives them His commandments and judgments for their salvation [11], but He does not compel them to keep them... If they continue in their insistence, He gives them over to a reprobate mind, to do those things which are not convenient (Rom 1:28).
The word "gave" here means "permitted them" to accept the statutes and judgments of pagan worship, so that they practiced passing through the fire... and perished.

27 "Therefore, son of man, speak unto the house of Israel, and say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Yet in this your fathers have blasphemed me, in that they have committed a trespass against me. 28 For when I had brought them into the land, for the which I lifted up mine hand to give it to them, then they saw every high hill, and all the thick trees, and they offered there their sacrifices, and there they presented the provocation of their offering: there also they made their sweet savour, and poured out there their drink offerings. 29 Then I said unto them, What is the high place whereunto ye go? And the name thereof is called Bamah unto this day.

He prolonged the period of their wandering in the wilderness to forty years that they might forget the idols of Egypt which they had carried with them in their hearts, and brought them into a new land, and behold, they adopted the pagan worship of this country and set up their worship on the high places like the people of the region. Instead of being the holy people of God, glorifying God in the midst of the nations, they went after the uncleanness of the nations.

entries.section: 6. Their rebellion in the days of Ezekiel:

paragraphs.text: 30 "Wherefore say unto the house of Israel, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Are ye polluted after the manner of your fathers? and commit ye whoredom after their abominations? 31 For when ye offer your gifts, when ye make your sons to pass through the fire, ye pollute yourselves with all your idols, even unto this day: and shall I be enquired of by you, O house of Israel? As I live, saith the Lord GOD, I will not be enquired of by you. 32 And that which cometh into your mind shall not be at all, that ye say, We will be as the heathen, as the families of the countries, to serve wood and stone.

The process of rebellion is not a historical process but a present reality: it began with the appearance of the people as a nation, pursued them in the wilderness to the new generation, burned all the more when they entered the Promised Land, and is still working in them even at the time when Ezekiel was speaking with the elders. The Lord rebukes them: "Are ye polluted after the manner of your fathers? and commit ye whoredom after their abominations? For when ye offer your gifts, when ye make your sons to pass through the fire, ye pollute yourselves with all your idols, even unto this day" [30-31]. Therefore the answer was, "As I live, saith the Lord GOD, I will not be enquired of by you." He does not accept their question nor answer their requests until their hearts change. He disciplines them with a mighty hand and a stretched out arm, pours out His wrath on them, scatters them and pleads with them openly [33-35].

entries.section: 7. Their rebellion in the land of captivity:

paragraphs.text: 33 As I live, saith the Lord GOD, surely with a mighty hand, and with a stretched out arm, and with fury poured out, will I rule over you: 34 And I will bring you out from the people, and will gather you out of the countries wherein ye are scattered, with a mighty hand, and with a stretched out arm, and with fury poured out. 35 And I will bring you into the wilderness of the people, and there will I plead with you face to face. 36 Like as I pleaded with your fathers in the wilderness of the land of Egypt, so will I plead with you, saith the Lord GOD. 37 And I will cause you to pass under the rod, and I will bring you into the bond of the covenant: 38 And I will purge out from among you the rebels, and them that transgress against me: I will bring them forth out of the country where they sojourn, and they shall not enter into the land of Israel: and ye shall know that I am the LORD. 39 "As for you, O house of Israel, thus saith the Lord GOD; Go ye, serve ye every one his idols, and hereafter also, if ye will not hearken unto me: but pollute ye my holy name no more with your gifts, and with your idols.

entries.section: 7. Their rebellion in the land of captivity:

paragraphs.text: In all this He does not take vengeance but disciplines in order to bring them into a new covenant. "And I will cause you to pass under the rod, and I will bring you into the bond of the covenant: and I will purge out from among you the rebels, and them that transgress against me" [37-38]. He brings them into the wilderness, not the wilderness of Sinai as He did with their fathers, but into a state of dryness and drought within the captivity and their scattering among the nations, for the sake of their repentance through the rod (Lev 27:32).

40 For in mine holy mountain, in the mountain of the height of Israel, saith the Lord GOD, there shall all the house of Israel, all of them in the land, serve me: there will I accept them, and there will I require your offerings, and the firstfruits of your oblations, with all your holy things. 41 I will accept you with your sweet savour, when I bring you out from the people, and gather you out of the countries wherein ye have been scattered; and I will be sanctified in you before the heathen. 42 And ye shall know that I am the LORD, when I shall bring you into the land of Israel, into the country for the which I lifted up mine hand to give it to your fathers. 43 And there shall ye remember your ways, and all your doings, wherein ye have been defiled; and ye shall lothe yourselves in your own sight for all your evils that ye have committed. 44 And ye shall know that I am the LORD, when I have wrought with you for my name's sake, not according to your wicked ways, nor according to your corrupt doings, O ye house of Israel, saith the Lord GOD."

After presenting a picture of Israel's turning aside to idolatry, as an ancient, violent and destructive turning aside in its results, and in spite of the dark and evil past, in the same chapter He dawns upon them with a future full of hope, of their return from captivity and their reform, as a symbol of man's return from the captivity of sin and the reform of his corrupt nature. He brings us into "mine holy mountain," into His sanctuaries, the high mountain, that is, into the Church of Christ, where we worship God in Christ Jesus, so that God smells our offerings as a sweet savour [41] and accepts us. It is a salvation not by our own merits but through free grace, for He says: "not according to your wicked ways, nor according to your corrupt doings, O ye house of Israel, saith the Lord GOD" [44].

45 Moreover the word of the LORD came unto me, saying, 46 "Son of man, set thy face toward the south, and drop thy word toward the south, and prophesy against the forest of the south field; 47 And say to the forest of the south, Hear the word of the LORD; Thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I will kindle a fire in thee, and it shall devour every green tree in thee, and every dry tree: the flaming flame shall not be quenched, and all faces from the south to the north shall be burned therein. 48 And all flesh shall see that I the LORD have kindled it: it shall not be quenched." 49 "Then said I, Ah Lord GOD! they say of me, Doth he not speak parables?"

Although He dawned upon them with hope of their return and reform, He affirms the necessity of discipline first by the fiery destroying sword of Nebuchadnezzar. He begins with a supernatural fire in the southern region, the fire of bitter discipline, until it burns all the thorns of sin.
He begins with the south (Teman), the southern desert, as a sign of the discipline of the southern kingdom (Judah and Jerusalem).

The prophet turned his face toward the south [46-47], that is, toward the land of Israel, to see as from afar the forests of Lebanon... proclaiming: "Thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I will kindle a fire in thee, and it shall devour every green tree in thee, and every dry tree: the flaming flame shall not be quenched, and all faces from the south to the north shall be burned therein" [47]. Thus God pours out the fire of His judgment on them that all may realize His holiness and His justice.

The prophet ends the chapter by saying: "Ah Lord GOD! they say of me, Doth he not speak parables?" [49]. This is the state of the soul that is slack in its search for its Savior, for it finds His speech obscure parables. As St. Ambrose says in his comment on the words of the Song: ["By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, but I found him not" (Song 3:1). (She seeks Him by night because He speaks in parables, for He made darkness His dwelling, and "night unto night sheweth knowledge" (Ps 19:3)... but she does not find Him in this way...].
Take my rebellion away from me!
* You are all love, my God, but I am a rebellious man!
Who can save me from my ungrateful nature but You, O my Savior?!
* The elders asked You in the land of captivity, and You did not answer them, because You want their repentance and their returning to You.
I see in the speech of Your prophet with them my own ungrateful nature!
In Egypt they rebelled against You; they came out with a mighty hand and a high arm, but they carried the worship of the Egyptians in their hearts!
In the wilderness You were wonderful in Your care for them, but they did not cease to murmur.
In the Promised Land You were a fortress for them, but they disobeyed Your commandments and took part in the worship of idols!
You disciplined them by captivity... and there, instead of repentance, they were filled with abominations!
What, then, will You do with them?!
* Circumstances did not create murmuring, but I, by the corruption of my heart, make an excuse of every circumstance to declare my rebellion!
Save me, O Lord, from my continual ingratitude!
Establish me in You, that I may bear partnership in the divine nature.
By partaking of Your Body and Blood, which are given for me, I bear the nature of self-giving love!

1 And the word of the LORD came unto me, saying, 2 "Son of man, set thy face toward Jerusalem, and drop thy word toward the holy places, and prophesy against the land of Israel, 3 And say to the land of Israel, Thus saith the LORD; Behold, I am against thee, and will draw forth my sword out of his sheath, and will cut off from thee the righteous and the wicked. 4 Seeing then that I will cut off from thee the righteous and the wicked, therefore shall my sword go forth out of his sheath against all flesh from the south to the north: 5 That all flesh may know that I the LORD have drawn forth my sword out of his sheath: it shall not return any more. 6 Sigh therefore, thou son of man, with the breaking of thy loins; and with bitterness sigh before their eyes. 7 And it shall be, when they say unto thee, Wherefore sighest thou? that thou shalt answer, For the tidings; because it cometh: and every heart shall melt, and all hands shall be feeble, and every spirit shall faint, and all knees shall be weak as water: behold, it cometh, and shall be brought to pass, saith the Lord GOD."
He asked him to direct his gaze toward Jerusalem [1] and to prophesy openly against the holy land, the holy city and the holy Temple.

He who had previously stood interceding for them and pleading on their behalf in more than one place (Ezek 9:8) is now called to proclaim the judgments of God which come upon Israel, who declared her rejection of the commandment and her deliberate stubbornness. He speaks the words of the Lord, saying: "Behold, I am against thee, and will draw forth my sword out of his sheath, and will cut off from thee the righteous and the wicked" [3]. Since these matters are no longer in the eyes of the Lord, He sends His sword upon her and stands against her, and cuts off from her the righteous and the wicked. This does not mean here that He kills both without distinction between them, but He removes the righteous from her to transfer him to the land of the Chaldeans like the good figs (Jer 24), and removes the wicked by killing him in Judah, so the land loses both, through captivity and the sword. The Lord made clear His attitude toward the good figs in the Book of Jeremiah as follows: "Like these good figs, so will I acknowledge them that are carried away captive of Judah, whom I have sent out of this place into the land of the Chaldeans for their good. For I will set mine eyes upon them for good, and I will bring them again to this land: and I will build them, and not pull them down; and I will plant them, and not pluck them up. And I will give them an heart to know me, that I am the LORD: and they shall be my people, and I will be their God: for they shall return unto me with their whole heart" (Jer 24:5-7). Thus He cuts off the good figs and the bad from Jerusalem, but separates the one from the other.

He asked him to sigh bitterly in public so that they would ask him the reason for his sighing, and he would answer openly, "For the tidings; because it cometh: and every heart shall melt, and all hands shall be feeble, and every spirit shall faint, and all knees shall be weak as water: behold, it cometh, and shall be brought to pass" [7]. God is not giving a parable but true tidings and a coming reality at which all tremble!

8 Again the word of the LORD came unto me, saying, 9 "Son of man, prophesy, and say, Thus saith the LORD; Say, A sword, a sword is sharpened, and also furbished: 10 It is sharpened to make a sore slaughter; it is furbished that it may glitter: should we then make mirth? it contemneth the rod of my son, as every tree. 11 And he hath given it to be furbished, that it may be handled: this sword is sharpened, and it is furbished, to give it into the hand of the slayer. 12 Cry and howl, son of man: for it shall be upon my people, it shall be upon all the princes of Israel: terrors by reason of the sword shall be upon my people: smite therefore upon thy thigh. 13 Because it is a trial, and what if the sword contemn even the rod? it shall be no more, saith the Lord GOD. 14 Thou therefore, son of man, prophesy, and smite thine hands together, and let the sword be doubled the third time, the sword of the slain: it is the sword of the great men that are slain, which entereth into their privy chambers. 15 I have set the point of the sword against all their gates, that their heart may faint, and their ruins be multiplied: ah! it is made bright, it is wrapped up for the slaughter. 16 Go thee one way or other, either on the right hand, or on the left, whithersoever thy face is set. 17 I will also smite mine hands together, and I will cause my fury to rest: I the LORD have said it."

This fearsome sword is in truth not the sword of Nebuchadnezzar but the sword of God Himself, who uses this king for discipline. It does its part well, for it is furbished and sharp, slaying the princes of Judah and the people, a great deadly sword, which is waved once, then a second time, then a third. It comes the first time after the verbal warning, the second time after the prophet smites upon his thigh [12], and the third time after he smites hand against hand [14], as though the going forth of the sword were not an end in itself, but goes forth when the leaders and the people reject God's warnings.

It is observed that it is a sharp sword that kills the wicked, but for the children of God it is "the rod of discipline" which slays in them the green tree (pagan worship) and not their souls, for He says of it: "it contemneth the rod of my son, as every tree" [10], and not every soul. It comes to destroy evil and sin, not sinners. It is a sword of trial [13] or a rod of testing: if anyone despises it he exposes himself to destruction, but if anyone turns back from his evil he is saved.

It is also observed that it is directed against the people as against all the princes of Israel who rejected his prophecy... He shows no partiality to an official at the expense of the individuals of the people, but all are equal before Him.
Finally, it stands at every gate, turning, striking right and left, so that none escapes it [15-16].

entries.section: 3. The two ways of the king of Babylon:

paragraphs.text: 18 The word of the LORD came unto me again, saying, 19 "Also, thou son of man, appoint thee two ways, that the sword of the king of Babylon may come: both twain shall come forth out of one land: and choose thou a place, choose it at the head of the way to the city. 20 Appoint a way, that the sword may come to Rabbath of the Ammonites, and to Judah in Jerusalem the defenced. 21 For the king of Babylon stood at the parting of the way, at the head of the two ways, to use divination: he made his arrows bright, he consulted with images, he looked in the liver. 22 At his right hand was the divination for Jerusalem, to appoint captains, to open the mouth in the slaughter, to lift up the voice with shouting, to appoint battering rams against the gates, to cast a mount, and to build a fort. 23 And it shall be unto them as a false divination in their sight, to them that have sworn oaths: but he will call to remembrance the iniquity, that they may be taken. 24 Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; Because ye have made your iniquity to be remembered, in that your transgressions are discovered, so that in all your doings your sins do appear; because, I say, that ye are come to remembrance, ye shall be taken with the hand.

It appears that the king of Babylon came to a meeting of two roads, one leading to Jerusalem and the other to Rabbah, the capital of the Ammonites, and here he began to consider which of them to attack first: Jerusalem or Rabbah. He used every pagan means: the sharpening of arrows to aim them down the two roads and cast lots, the inquiry of the teraphim, and the looking at the liver of the sacrifice that he offers to his god... and the answer came that he should begin with Jerusalem. In appearance the answer came through his evil pagan ways, but in reality it was God who secretly planned the discipline. The divination is false, but God, the Controller of all, turned the evil of the king and his divination to the discipline of the people.

It is observed that the Lord says: "Appoint a way, that the sword may come to... Judah in Jerusalem," since it appears that the majority of the people of Judah had crowded into the capital Jerusalem, thinking that even if all the cities of Judah fell, God would defend Jerusalem as "the city of the great King." But God affirms that she will receive the first strong blow, not only before all the cities of Judah but even before the cities of the Ammonites. Jerusalem, which knew much about God, deserved to be struck more, because she does not sin out of ignorance or lack of knowledge but in rebellion and disobedience.

25 "And thou, profane wicked prince of Israel, whose day is come, when iniquity shall have an end, 26 Thus saith the Lord GOD; Remove the diadem, and take off the crown: this shall not be the same: exalt him that is low, and abase him that is high. 27 I will overturn, overturn, overturn, it: and it shall be no more, until he come whose right it is; and I will give it him.

God directs His speech directly against King Zedekiah, who destroys his people by his evil, saying: "And thou, profane wicked prince of Israel" [25]. The day has come to remove the turban and take the king's crown from him [26]. He thought himself great and destroyed his people; therefore the situation is reversed, and the king loses his crown forever: "I will overturn, overturn, overturn it" [27]. And He brings this arrogant king down to the depths, "until he come whose right it is; and I will give it him" [27]. The Lord Christ comes in His humility and reigns forever.
If the people of Zedekiah perished by the counsel of their king, the Lord of glory will reign and raise up His people and save them to reign with Him forever.

28 "And thou, son of man, prophesy and say, Thus saith the Lord GOD concerning the Ammonites, and concerning their reproach; even say thou, The sword, the sword is drawn: for the slaughter it is furbished, to consume because of the glittering: 29 Whiles they see vanity unto thee, whiles they divine a lie unto thee, to bring thee upon the necks of them that are slain, of the wicked, whose day is come, when their iniquity shall have an end. 30 Shall I cause it to return into his sheath?
