1 The word of the LORD came again unto me, saying, 2 “Now, thou son of man, take up a lamentation for Tyrus; 3 And say unto Tyrus, O thou that art situate at the entry of the sea, which art a merchant of the people for many isles, Thus saith the Lord GOD; O Tyrus, thou hast said, I am of perfect beauty. 4 Thy borders are in the midst of the seas, thy builders have perfected thy beauty. 5 They have made all thy ship boards of fir trees of Senir: they have taken cedars from Lebanon to make masts for thee. 6 Of the oaks of Bashan have they made thine oars; the company of the Ashurites have made thy benches of ivory, brought out of the isles of Chittim. 7 Fine linen with broidered work from Egypt was that which thou spreadest forth to be thy sail; blue and purple from the isles of Elishah was that which covered thee. 8 The inhabitants of Zidon and Arvad were thy mariners: thy wise men, O Tyrus, that were in thee, were thy pilots. 9 The ancients of Gebal and the wise men thereof were in thee thy calkers: all the ships of the sea with their mariners were in thee to occupy thy merchandise. 10 They of Persia and of Lud and of Phut were in thine army, thy men of war: they hanged the shield and helmet in thee; they set forth thy comeliness. 11 The men of Arvad with thine army were upon thy walls round about, and the Gammadims were in thy towers: they hanged their shields upon thy walls round about; they have made thy beauty perfect.

If Jerusalem refers to the soul that has received the grace of God (in the Old Testament it refers to the Church enjoying the Mosaic Law and the prophets, and in the New Testament it refers to the Church that has enjoyed eternal salvation through divine grace in Christ Jesus), then Tyre here represents natural man: his position, his resources and the gifts God gave him, and then his fall and collapse through sin. So what is said here of Tyre is said of the whole of human nature. He likened it to a Phoenician ship in an excellent location, dealing with many peoples, strongly built, exceedingly precious, magnificent in its workmanship, with an excellent crew, lacking nothing. This is man, “the work of the hands of God, the Lover of mankind.”

God established her “at the entry of the sea,” for Tyre lies in the east of the Mediterranean Sea as a beautiful island with two harbors, and its location enables it to draw merchants from all the lands of the East; “a merchant of the people for many isles” [3], “thy borders are in the midst of the seas” [4]. God established man at the entries of the seas, “above every earthly creature,” being in the image of God, so that he has dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over the cattle, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth (Gen 1:26). He entrusted this trade to him that he might be a master, not a slave, of earthly and temporal things; He set his borders in all the seas, that is, he is the possessor of authority over everything. He did not want to create us to live in material or psychological deprivation, but wanted for us satisfaction in everything.

As St. Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, says: [In his treatise on the creation, God did not create man until He had created the world as a royal palace, for it is not fitting to proclaim the king until his palace is made ready.]

God established man beautiful in everything, the perfection of His creation on earth; therefore after He created him it was said: “And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good” (Gen 1:31)... And the lamentation says: “Thy builders have perfected thy beauty” [4]; the secret of our beauty is God, who built our life and gave us the inner resources and the body as a free gift from Him. But man, in pride receiving it, instead of thanking God and glorifying Him, ascribes all perfection to himself, for the lamentation says: “O Tyrus, thou hast said, I am of perfect beauty” [3].
And the secret of her beauty is:
Her boards are of fir trees of Senir, her masts of the cedars of Lebanon, her oars of the oaks of Bashan, her benches of ivory inlaid in box, from the isles of Chittim.
Her sail is fine linen with broidered work from Egypt, her covering is blue and purple from the isles of Elishah.

Her mariners are from the people of Zidon and Arvad, her pilots are wise men of Tyre itself, her calkers are the ancients of Gebal and its wise men, her men of war (her guards) are from Persia, Lud and Phut...

Thus the lamentation presented many details of the building materials of the ship and the nationality of its crew and its guards. It must be observed that among the Gentiles the ship often refers to the journey of life which man lives in the world in order to enter the harbor, just as Noah’s ark symbolized the Church or humanity enjoying divine salvation; therefore churches are often built in the shape of a ship. As Father Hippolytus says: [The sea is the world; the Church went down into it to the very depth, yet she did not perish, because her captain, Christ, is skilled. Since she bears the Cross of the Lord, she bears within her the victory over death...
The sailors are the two Testaments (the Old and the New).
And the mountains surrounding her are the love of Christ which binds the Church.
The net that is with her is the font of the new birth which renews the believers.
The Holy Spirit dwells in her as a skilled sailor, by whom the believers are sealed...
She has anchors of iron that hold her, which are the commandments of Christ Himself, strong as iron!
In her are seamen on the right and on the left, servants like the holy angels who steer the Church and guard her.
The ladder by which we go up to the deck of the ship is the remembrance of the sufferings of Christ, by which the hearts of the believers are raised to heaven.
The towers upon the ship are the fellowship of the prophets, martyrs and apostles who enter into their rest...]

And as the ship refers to humanity renewed through the Cross of Christ, it also refers to human nature before the fall; therefore what is stated in the lamentation in the way of details refers to God’s gifts to us through our humanity: a good body, a rational soul, emotions, feelings, inclinations, drives and blessed energies, because they are the work of the hands of the good God, the Lover of mankind.

We can say that the boards or beams of the ship are the members of the body, its mast is the mind, the oar is the tongue, the benches are the rest of the senses, the sail is the heart, the covering is outward conduct, the mariners are the inner energies of the soul, its pilot is the spirit of discernment and distinction, the calkers are the gifts, and the guards are the inner drives.

A. All the boards are of fir trees of Senir, that is, all the members of the body, which are like the beams of the ship, come from the mountain of light (Senir), and not, as the Gnostics thought, from the kingdom of darkness. Therefore the Fathers often dealt with this matter, and St. John Chrysostom says: [These (the followers of Mani) call the body treacherous, of an evil origin... Would this not oblige them to pluck out their eyes, because desire enters the soul by way of them?! But the truth is that it is not the eye nor any other member that is to be blamed, but our corrupt will alone is the object of blame.] He also says: [Eyes were given to us that we might look with them at creation and so glorify the Lord, but if we misuse them they become servants of fornication...] And St. Augustine says: [The spirit is good, and the body is good. And man, who is composed of the two, is certainly good, whether this goodness of his be little or much.]

B. The mast, that is, the mind, is taken from the cedars of Lebanon, which is known for its uprightness; for God created for man an upright mind that leads him all the way without deviation, since “the truly rational man has only one concern, which is to obey Almighty God with all his heart and to please Him, and he teaches himself only one thing, which is how to do, as far as he can, what agrees with God, thanking Him for His compassionate providence that works in everything that happens to him in his life.”

C. The oar that steers the ship is the tongue, for our teacher James says: “Behold also the ships, which though they be so great, and are driven of fierce winds, yet are they turned about with a very small helm, whithersoever the governor listeth. Even so the tongue is a little member, and boasteth great things” (Jas 3:4-5). And St. John Chrysostom says: [We were given a tongue to teach and praise the Creator with it, but if we do not take heed to ourselves it becomes a cause of blasphemy.]

D. The benches are the senses, which ought to be of inlaid ivory, that is, full of purity and cleanness. St. John Saba says: [Everyone who now wishes to keep his soul and his conscience from evil deeds, let him guard these senses and deliver them into the hand of the faithful God, the Helper of the weak.]

E. The sail is the heart, which ought to be of embroidered linen, clean and pure; for when the heart is sanctified man becomes a dwelling for God, and therefore the psalmist cries: “Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me” (Ps 51).

F. The covering of the ship, which is conduct, is of blue, that is, bearing the heavenly nature, and of purple, that is, bearing the mark of kings. For conduct expresses what the heart bears within; if the heart is lifted up to heaven, where our treasure is, our conduct also is directed toward heavenly things, and where it is with God, the true King, the conduct is worthy of the children of this King. Therefore the Apostle Paul says: “[He] hath raised us up together, and made us sit together in heavenly places.”
“Seek those things which are above, where Christ sitteth on the right hand of God” (Col 3:1).
And St. John Climacus says: [Great is he who overcomes the fire arising from earthly pleasures by meditation on the delights of heaven!]

G. The mariners, that is, the inner energies of the soul, he brings from Zidon and Arvad. If “Zidon” means “place of hunting,” then the living man is the one who uses all his inner energies for building, living as a skilled hunter who knows how to acquire what is for edification. If they are not used for edification, these same energies become for demolition, and if they are not like spiritual soldiers on behalf of the Kingdom of God they become like wicked soldiers on behalf of the kingdom of darkness.

H. Her pilot, who is the spirit of distinction or discernment, is from Tyre, that is, like the rock he is not shaken. This is the secret of the strength of the spiritual man: he walks with discernment, knowing how to separate good from evil, truth from falsehood, light from darkness. So he accepts what is for his edification and rejects what is for demolition with strength, without moving.

I. The calkers, that is, the gifts, are from the ancients of Gebal and its wise men. For God has given each man special gifts which he kindles with power and wisdom, so that they are in him like wise elders, working together with the gifts of others for the edification of humanity as one family.

J. As for her guards, who are the inner drives of the soul, they are from Persia, Lud and Phut, men of war, trained and of varied experience, working to protect her. Among these drives are anger, fear, motherhood, fatherhood, love, etc... All these are holy drives if they work within the spiritual framework of edification. For through anger a man rises up against sin and blames himself, through fear he reveres God and does not wound His feelings, and through motherhood, fatherhood and love he gathers in his heart a pure love toward humanity in the spirit of wisdom that is not rash. These are the men of war within the soul, who fight either for us or against us. He who is angry at others and not at himself, and who fears men and not God, and who loves for the sake of fleshly desire, turns the men of war against himself.
This is a swift and brief picture of the ship “of perfect beauty” which God gave us, that is, human nature before its deviation and fall!

12 Tarshish was thy merchant by reason of the multitude of all kind of riches; with silver, iron, tin, and lead, they traded in thy fairs. 13 Javan, Tubal, and Meshech, they were thy merchants: they traded the persons of men and vessels of brass in thy market. 14 They of the house of Togarmah traded in thy fairs with horses and horsemen and mules. 15 The men of Dedan were thy merchants; many isles were the merchandise of thine hand: they brought thee for a present horns of ivory and ebony. 16 Syria was thy merchant by reason of the multitude of the wares of thy making: they occupied in thy fairs with emeralds, purple, and broidered work, and fine linen, and coral, and agate. 17 Judah, and the land of Israel, they were thy merchants: they traded in thy market wheat of Minnith, and Pannag, and honey, and oil, and balm. 18 Damascus was thy merchant in the multitude of the wares of thy making, for the multitude of all riches; in the wine of Helbon, and white wool. 19 Dan also and Javan going to and fro occupied in thy fairs: bright iron, cassia, and calamus, were in thy market. 20 Dedan was thy merchant in precious clothes for chariots. 21 Arabia, and all the princes of Kedar, they occupied with thee in lambs, and rams, and goats: in these were they thy merchants. 22 The merchants of Sheba and Raamah, they were thy merchants: they occupied in thy fairs with chief of all spices, and with all precious stones, and gold. 23 Haran, and Canneh, and Eden, the merchants of Sheba, Asshur, and Chilmad, were thy merchants. 24 These were thy merchants in all sorts of things, in blue clothes, and broidered work, and in chests of rich apparel, bound with cords, and made of cedar, among thy merchandise.

After presenting the precious building materials of the ship, its excellent crew and its guards, mighty in experience, he began to speak of its precious cargo, for it was filled with valuable goods which it brought from many lands. It resembles the wise soul that knows how to benefit spiritually from every man, despises no one, and does not depend on its own experience alone. Man is like the bee that knows how to draw from every flower what is sweet and beautiful!

In speaking of the goods in which the ship traded, the order came according to the locations of the lands, so he began with the coasts of the Mediterranean Sea, then the eastern lands in three parallel lines from south to north. The following are the lands mentioned and the goods in which they trade.
Tarshish: silver, iron, tin and lead.
Javan, Tubal and Meshech: slaves and vessels of brass.
The house of Togarmah: horses and mules.
Dedan, Rhodes or Rodam: ivory and ebony.
Aram: emeralds, purple, broidered work, fine linen, coral and agate.
Judah and Israel: wheat of Minnith and Pannag (a place name, or perhaps a kind of sweet; perhaps he meant early figs, as in some editions), honey, oil and balm.
Damascus: the wine of Helbon and white wool.
Dan and Javan: yarn, wrought iron, cassia and calamus.
Dedan: saddle cloths for chariots.
Arabia and Kedar: lambs, rams and goats.
Sheba and Raamah: spices, precious stones and gold.
Haran, Canneh and Eden: rich blue garments and broidered work, and carpets of rich colors bound with cords made of cedar.
This is the list of the lands which trade with Tyre and the goods in which they trade, and the following is a brief outline of some of these lands:

Tarshish: this name is probably derived from the word “rashash,” found in the Akkadian language connected with shining metals and the products of mines; therefore this name became famous in the sense of “the refining of metals.”

The people of Tarshish came from Javan (Gen 10:4), and it is thought to be Tartessus, situated in the south of Spain near Gibraltar, and perhaps it is Carthage, the city situated in the northwest of Africa. It was very rich in metals such as silver beaten into plates (Jer 10:9), and iron, tin and lead. If Sheba and Dedan represent trade in the East, then Tarshish represents trade in the West; therefore it is said in the prophet Ezekiel: “Sheba, and Dedan, and the merchants of Tarshish, with all the young lions thereof, shall say unto thee, Art thou come to take a spoil? hast thou gathered thy company to take a prey? to carry away silver and gold, to take away cattle and goods, to take a great spoil?” (Ezek 38:13).

And when it is said “ships of Tarshish,” it does not necessarily mean that they are ships of the king of Tarshish or that they trade with Tarshish, but because of its commercial fame the name was applied to the huge ocean-crossing ships that sailed especially to bring precious metals.
And let us not forget that when the Lord asked Jonah to preach in Nineveh in the East, he fled to the West in a ship sailing to Tarshish (Jon 1:3).

Javan: Javan came with Tubal and the far-off isles in (Isa 66:19), where the Gentiles come to it and declare the glory of God, and the sons of the Javanites are mentioned as merchants buying the captives of Judah and Israel to remove them far from their border in (Joel 3:6), and here in (Ezek 27:13) with Tubal and Meshech as merchants of captives, slaves and vessels of brass. These three expressions refer to the Javanite, that is, Greek, colonies on the coast of Asia Minor. It is to be noted that the term Javan, Jonia, is very close to the expression of the Assyrians and Egyptians for “Greece.”
Moreover the “Javan” mentioned in (Ezek 27:19) means another Javan, most probably a tribe in Arabia or a Greek colony in Arabia.
In (Dan 8:21; 10:20; 11:2) Javan is translated “Greece,” and it most often refers here to the Macedonian Greek empire.

Tubal and Meshech: two peoples or regions in Asia Minor, linked together (Isa 66:19), and belonging to Japheth (Gen 10:2; Job 1:5), who appeared in the Assyrian records under the names Tabali and Mushki as fierce opponents of Assyria in the twelfth century B.C.
The house of Togarmah: it lies in the south of Armenia, inhabited by the descendants of Togarmah, the third son of Gomer (Gen 10:1; 1 Chr 1:6).

Dedan [15]: a people in the north of Arabia, who came from Cush the son of Ham (Gen 10:7), and it is stated in (Gen 25:3) that he was of the offspring of Abraham by Keturah after the death of Sarah. It is not difficult to understand the connection here if we remember the kinship between Arabia and Cush.

They were men of trade, from the lands of the Arabs (Isa 21:3), dwelling south of the Edomites (Jer 25:23; 49:8). The name still remains in Didan, southwest of Tema. As for modern Dedan, it is “al-Ula,” an oasis in the Wadi al-Qura in the north of the Hejaz.

Aram: taken from the Akkadian and meaning “the high land”; Aram was one of the sons of Shem (Gen 10:22-23). Aram extends from Mount Lebanon in the west to beyond the Euphrates in the east, and from the Taurus mountains in the north to Damascus in the south. This region was called Syria in the Septuagint. Abraham was called “a wandering Aramean” because he went out from Haran [one of the cities of Aram (Gen 11:3) to Canaan (Deut 26:5)]. Several Aramean states appeared, such as Aram of the two rivers (Gen 24:10), in which lie the cities of Nisibis and Edessa, and Aram of Damascus, and Aram-zobah or Zobah west of the Euphrates (which at times extended to the borders of Hamath), and Aram-maacah near Mount Hermon, in the portion of Manasseh (Josh 12:5; 13:11), and Geshur as an Aramean state near Maacah, east of the Jordan also in the portion of Manasseh (Deut 3:14), to which Absalom fled after killing his brother Amnon (2 Sam 13:37; 15:8), and Aram of Beth-rehob, most probably near the entrance of Hamath (Num 13:21; Josh 19:28).

Damascus: the capital of Syria, known from ancient times as an important commercial center. It stands at the eastern foot of the Anti-Lebanon, where in this range of mountains the two rivers Abana and Pharpar spring (2 Kgs 5:12), now called Barada and al-Awaj.

Dan: a Hebrew name meaning “judge,” a city in the north of the borders of Palestine; it was called Laish (Judg 18:29) or Leshem (Josh 19:47), but it is not, as some think, at Tell al-Qadi. The confusion arose because of the similarity of names, since “Dan” means “judge.”

Kedar: a Semitic name meaning “mighty or black,” and he is the second son of Ishmael (Gen 25:13). His descendants for the most part lived by pasturing in black tents, so Kedar became a symbol of the color black (Song 1:5). Some of them were civilized (Isa 42:11). They were owners of cattle and skilled in war, especially in shooting with the bow, and therefore they resisted Nebuchadnezzar greatly, but he made an example of them.

Sheba: Sheba and his brother Dan are mentioned as sons of Raamah, of the sons of Cush (Gen 10:7), and the two names are also mentioned as sons of Jokshan the son of Abraham by Keturah his wife (Gen 25:7).

Sheba is considered one of four important tribes or ancient peoples who inhabited southern Arabia: the Qatabanians, the Mineans, the Chattramothites (in Hebrew Hazarmaveth), and Sheba, which was the most important of them in the days of Strabo. They were famous as merchants of spices, gold and precious stones, and were very rich. They traded in slaves (Joel 3:8) and were regarded as guardians of the desert (Job 1:15; 6:19).

The Assyrian inscriptions have perhaps furnished us with the oldest testimony to the existence of Sheba, for King Tiglathpileser III (745-727 B.C.) recorded the receiving of tribute from Itamara, king of Sheba...

It appears that this people, who settled in the southwest of the peninsula (Gen 10:28), had some of their families migrate to Ethiopia (Cush) and were called Cushite (Gen 25:3), and some later extended to the northwest of the peninsula until they reached Syria.
The story of the Queen of Sheba gave them special fame, and revealed the position of women among this people socially, politically and religiously.
Raamah or Raama: Raamah the son of Cush, father of Sheba and Dedan (Gen 10:7)...

It is difficult to determine the location of Raamah, whose inhabitants are thought to be of the descendants of Raamah or Raama; some thought it to be Ptolemy’s Rhegma, west of the Persian Gulf, and others see it as Rammaitae in southern Arabia, northwest of Hadramaut and east of ancient Sheba, and this last opinion is the more probable.

Haran (Charran): the name is perhaps of Akkadian origin, meaning “road” or “caravan.” The city lies northwest of al-Massisa (Mesopotamia), on the River Balikh, a tributary of the Euphrates, about 280 miles northeast of Damascus, and 60 miles east of Carchemish (Gen 11:31-32). It is considered the meeting point of one of the main roads between Babylon and the coast of the Mediterranean, and represents an important commercial center; it was the chief center for the worship of the god Sim, the moon god.

Terah and Abraham sojourned in it for a time, and Nahor settled in it, and therefore it was called by his name (Gen 42:10; 27:43). The Assyrians seized it (2 Kgs 19:12). It is at present a small village that still keeps the name Haran.
Canneh: some scholars thought it to be “Calneh” (Amos 6:2), but it is more probably an unknown Akkadian city “Kannu,” most probably in the region of al-Massisa (Mesopotamia) near Haran.

Eden: a Hebrew name meaning “delight,” and it is different from the Garden of Eden. A province of Mesopotamia, mentioned in the Assyrian inscriptions as Bit Adini, south of Haran, at the middle of the River Euphrates.

25 “The ships of Tarshish did sing of thee in thy market: and thou wast replenished, and made very glorious in the midst of the seas. 26 Thy rowers have brought thee into great waters: the east wind hath broken thee in the midst of the seas. 27 Thy riches, and thy fairs, thy merchandise, thy mariners, and thy pilots, thy calkers, and the occupiers of thy merchandise, and all thy men of war, that are in thee, and in all thy company which is in the midst of thee, shall fall into the midst of the seas in the day of thy ruin. 28 The suburbs shall shake at the sound of the cry of thy pilots. 29 And all that handle the oar, the mariners, and all the pilots of the sea, shall come down from their ships, they shall stand upon the land; 30 And shall cause their voice to be heard against thee, and shall cry bitterly, and shall cast up dust upon their heads, they shall wallow themselves in the ashes: 31 And they shall make themselves utterly bald for thee, and gird them with sackcloth, and they shall weep for thee with bitterness of heart and bitter wailing. 32 And in their wailing they shall take up a lamentation for thee, and lament over thee, saying, What city is like Tyrus, like the destroyed in the midst of the sea? 33 When thy wares went forth out of the seas, thou filledst many people; thou didst enrich the kings of the earth with the multitude of thy riches and of thy merchandise. 34 In the time when thou shalt be broken by the seas in the depths of the waters thy merchandise and all thy company in the midst of thee shall fall. 35 All the inhabitants of the isles shall be astonished at thee, and their kings shall be sore afraid, they shall be troubled in their countenance. 36 The merchants among the people shall hiss at thee; thou shalt be a terror, and never shalt be any more.”

Tyre had become like a huge ship, perfect in its construction, strong in its guards, experienced and wise in its crew, loved by all the peoples who deal with her and seek her favor; but since she coveted and wanted to plunder her sister “Judah” on the day of her captivity, an east wind broke her and brought her down to the depths together with her wealth, her goods, her crew, her customers and her guards... There was no one to rescue and no one to help; many stood in grief and bitterness, they shaved their heads and made themselves bald like one mourning for the dead, and made a lamentation over her who used to satisfy them with good things [33]; they were in bitterness and their kings shuddered, while some stood hissing at her in mockery because she coveted and lost even her existence forever!
Steer the ship of my life!

* “Tyre,” the great city, is a ship made by Your hands; You are its maker, and You are the giver to it of every wealth, but she trusted in her riches, and resisted Your work, and so was utterly shattered!!
* I am Your ship, O my Creator!
Steer the ship of my life, for I am the work of Your hands!
* What are these boards of fir but the members of my body?!
They are Your beautiful creation; You gave me the body with the soul that they may glorify You!
Sanctify my eyes and all my senses that they may be satisfied with You!
Sanctify my emotions and my feelings, O desire of my heart!
My body is in Your hands; it is Your precious gift to me!
* What is this mast of the cedars of Lebanon which You have set up in me but the wonderful mind?!
You created it upright that it may be occupied with You throughout the journey of my short life!
My mind contemplates Your will, and so desires obedience to Your commandment, seeing in it the sweetness of fellowship with You, O Source of life!
* What is this little oar that moves all my life but the tongue?!
Sanctify it, that it may not blaspheme You, nor curse anyone, nor move in vain without purpose!
Steer it, that it may bless You and praise You and thank You continually, and bless people and overflow with sweetness to everyone!
* What are these benches of inlaid ivory but the pure senses You gave me?!

May You satisfy them with Your Holy Spirit, that they may see You, the heavenly Bridegroom of the soul, and be set aflame with love for You and for all Your creation! They are not a theater for demons, nor a pleasure-ground for fleshly desires!
My senses and my emotions and all my feelings are for You, O Beloved!
* What is this sail of embroidered linen but my little heart to which You gave purity?!
By Your Holy Spirit it grows wide to hold Him whom heaven and earth cannot contain!
Its keys are in Your hands, O Son of David, that You may enter and sup in it, and gather in it Your friends, heavenly and earthly, and establish from it Your joyful Kingdom and Your holy temple!
* What are these coverings of the ship of my life but the conduct which I practice by the work of Your grace?!
It is of blue, bearing the color of heaven, and of purple, the garment of kings.

You are wonderful, O heavenly King of kings, for You want me in my conduct to bear Your marks, to walk on earth with a heavenly heart, and to live in the narrowness of the world as a king possessing authority!
* Who are the mariners of Zidon but the inner energies of the soul?!
Grant them to be skilled hunters, working always for the edification of my soul and the edification of my brethren, knowing neither demolition nor destruction!
You gave me wonderful energies like spiritual soldiers; steer them to work on behalf of Your Kingdom, that they may not be wicked soldiers on behalf of the kingdom of darkness!
* Who is this pilot from Tyre but the spirit of discernment and distinction?!
He is the gift of Your Holy Spirit; by him I recognize the good and distinguish it from evil, by him I do not deviate from Your royal way to the right or to the left!
Self-righteousness does not deceive me, nor do desires draw me away!
By him I come to know You, O Truth!
* Who are the calkers but the gifts which You entrusted to me?!
Kindle, O Lord, Your gifts in me, that I may work with power and wisdom!
May I work in harmony and accord with the gifts of my brethren, without pride and without smallness of soul.
I thank You for giving me the gifts that suit me!
* Who are these guards from Persia, Lud and Phut but the drives which You created in me!
By the drive of love I meet You and love Your creation!
By the drive of anger I rise against my sin and complain to You of myself!
By the drive of fear I fear You in love!
Sanctify all the drives so that they deviate no more!
* Wretched is Tyre, the beautiful, rich ship, which trusted in herself and disobeyed her Creator, so she was shattered and sank in the sea of this world!
* Steer, O wonderful Captain, the ship of my life; let Your Cross be the mast of my life, and Your commandments the sailors!
Grant me ropes to support my ship.
I am in the midst of the currents of the sea of this world, but I am carried by Your Holy Spirit to the heavenly harbor!

entries.section: 1. Prophecy against the prince of Tyre:

paragraphs.text: 1 The word of the LORD came again unto me, saying, 2 "Son of man, say unto the prince of Tyrus, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Because thine heart is lifted up, and thou hast said, I am a God, I sit in the seat of God, in the midst of the seas; yet thou art a man, and not God, though thou set thine heart as the heart of God: 3 Behold, thou art wiser than Daniel; there is no secret that they can hide from thee: 4 With thy wisdom and with thine understanding thou hast gotten thee riches, and hast gotten gold and silver into thy treasures: 5 By thy great wisdom and by thy traffick hast thou increased thy riches, and thine heart is lifted up because of thy riches: 6 Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; Because thou hast set thine heart as the heart of God; 7 Behold, therefore I will bring strangers upon thee, the terrible of the nations: and they shall draw their swords against the beauty of thy wisdom, and they shall defile thy brightness. 8 They shall bring thee down to the pit, and thou shalt die the deaths of them that are slain in the midst of the seas. 9 Wilt thou yet say before him that slayeth thee, I am God? but thou shalt be a man, and no God, in the hand of him that slayeth thee. 10 Thou shalt die the deaths of the uncircumcised by the hand of strangers: for I have spoken it, saith the Lord GOD." 11 Moreover the word of the LORD came unto me, saying, 12 "Son of man, take up a lamentation upon the king of Tyrus, and say unto him, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Thou sealest up the sum, full of wisdom, and perfect in beauty. 13 Thou hast been in Eden the garden of God; every precious stone was thy covering, the sardius, topaz, and the diamond, the beryl, the onyx, and the jasper, the sapphire, the emerald, and the carbuncle, and gold: the workmanship of thy settings and of thy engravings was prepared in thee in the day that thou wast created. 14 Thou art the anointed cherub that covereth; and I have set thee so: thou wast upon the holy mountain of God; thou hast walked up and down in the midst of the stones of fire. 15 Thou wast perfect in thy ways from the day that thou wast created, till iniquity was found in thee. 16 By the multitude of thy merchandise they have filled the midst of thee with violence, and thou hast sinned: therefore I will cast thee out of the mountain of God: and I will destroy thee, O covering cherub, from the midst of the stones of fire. 17 Thine heart was lifted up because of thy beauty, thou hast corrupted thy wisdom by reason of thy brightness: I will cast thee to the ground, I will lay thee before kings, that they may behold thee. 18 Thou hast defiled thy sanctuaries by the multitude of thine iniquities, by the iniquity of thy traffick; therefore will I bring forth a fire from the midst of thee, it shall devour thee, and I will bring thee to ashes upon the earth in the sight of all them that behold thee. 19 All they that know thee among the people shall be astonished at thee: thou shalt be a terror, and never shalt thou be any more."

St. Jerome sees that the word "Tyre" means "distress." Therefore what is said about the prince or king of Tyre is meant of Satan, since he drives people into distresses and trials. Many of the Fathers saw that what is said in this chapter describes the fall of Satan from his angelic rank. This description corresponds to what is said about Lucifer in (Isa 14:12).

It is noticed in this chapter that the prince or king of Tyre is described as a good creature of God, indeed a perfect one, because Satan was not created evil; he is a good creature of God who fell through pride, by his own free will.
He was described thus:
"Thou sealest up the sum, full of wisdom, and perfect in beauty.
Thou hast been in Eden the garden of God.
Every precious stone was thy covering, the sardius... the workmanship of thy settings was prepared in thee in the day that thou wast created.
Thou art the anointed cherub that covereth; and I have set thee so: thou wast upon the holy mountain of God.
Thou hast walked up and down in the midst of the stones of fire.

entries.section: 1. Prophecy against the prince of Tyre:

paragraphs.text: Thou wast perfect in thy ways from the day that thou wast created, till iniquity was found in thee" [12-15].

Satan was one of the greatest and mightiest of the heavenly orders, the order of the Cherubim who bear the divine throne, aflame with fire like a divine chariot of fire! He was the seal of perfection, because he bore the throne; full of wisdom, for we know that the cherub is full of eyes; perfect in beauty, for he reflects the splendor of God upon himself. He was adorned with every precious stone, for God lacked him nothing; he covered with his wings upon the holy mountain of God, and wherever he was found he proclaimed the presence of God, who sanctifies all things. He walked among the stones of fire, a sign of the fiery divine presence. He was created without blemish, perfect in all his ways.

It is clear that the discourse here does not apply to man, the most perfect of God's creatures on earth, nor to any heavenly order, but to the greatest and loftiest of the orders... Tertullian says: [If we return to the prophecy of Ezekiel, we find that this angel was good by his creation but corrupted himself by his own choice. For in the person of the king of Tyre it was said of Satan: "Thou sealest up the sum... etc." And it is clear that this description [11-16] concerns the rebellion of the angel and not the prince of Tyre, for among human beings there is none who was born in the paradise of God (even Adam himself was only brought into it), and there is no one who is a cherub placed upon the holy mountain of God, that is, in the heights of heaven, except the one of whom the Lord testified that from there he fell (Lk 10:18)].

Origen of Alexandria speaks of Satan and his angels as a good creation that sinned by its own will, saying: [Those who say that Satan is not the creation of God are mistaken. For insofar as he is Satan, he is not the creation of God, but the being himself (as a creature) is the creation of God. It is like saying that a murderer is not the creation of God, but as a man he is the creation of God].

St. Cyril of Jerusalem says: [(Satan) did not sin by compulsion, as though there were in him a natural inclination to sin; otherwise the cause of sin would return to his Creator as well. Rather, he is a good creature, and by his free will he became the devil, receiving the name through his work. He was an archangel, but he was called "the devil" because of his deceptions. He was a good servant of God, and he became truly Satan. For "Satan" means "the adversary." This teaching is not of my own; it is the teaching of the inspired prophet Ezekiel, who raised a lamentation over him, saying: "Thou wast the seal of the likeness of God, the crown of splendor, born in paradise," and then he says again: "Thou walkedst perfect in thy ways from the day that thou wast created, till iniquity was found in thee." He rightly said, "till iniquity was found in thee," for iniquity did not come to him from outside, but he brought it upon himself. And immediately he points to the cause, saying: "Thine heart was lifted up because of thy beauty. By reason of the multitude of thy sins thou wast wounded and cast to the ground." This saying agrees with the word of the Lord in the Gospel: "I beheld Satan as lightning fall from heaven" (Lk 10:18)].

In raising a lamentation over Satan, He proclaims God's gifts to him and the capacities that were granted to him on the day He created him. For to the degree that much was given him, much is required of him, and to the degree that he enjoyed a towering height, his fall became great. The most important of the divine gifts to him are:

a. The gift of wisdom: "Behold, thou art wiser than Daniel; there is no secret that they can hide from thee" [3]. He gave him wisdom, so he was wiser than the prophet Daniel, to whom were revealed the secrets of the king, his personal dreams and their interpretations, to support him in his exile. It is as though God, in His dealings with Satan before his fall, revealed many secrets to him, so that He said: "There is no secret that they can hide from thee." He dealt with him as a trusted friend and a man of confidence, and hid no secret from him, saying to him: "Thou sealest up the sum, full of wisdom, and perfect in beauty" [12]. He made him the most perfect and most beautiful of His heavenly creatures, not in appearance but in wisdom; yet when he fell into pride, he fell from this height into the abyss!

Man too is the most perfect of God's creatures on earth. God adorned him not with the beauty of the body but with what is greater: the beauty of wisdom, since He created him "in His image and likeness" and wanted him to be a master who rules over the earthly creation with the spirit of divine wisdom. As pride brought the angel down to become a Satan, so pride brought man down to a corrupt, sensual nature and made him, in many matters, behave as lower than the animals, even the beasts of prey.

entries.section: 1. Prophecy against the prince of Tyre:

paragraphs.text: b. His dwelling in the garden of God: "Thou hast been in Eden the garden of God" [13]. The word Eden means "delight," as though He set him in the divine joy, enjoying the divine presence, and even sharing with the rest of the Cherubim in bearing the divine throne; and he came to an inward torment that has no end.

Man too was set by God in the garden of Eden to work and to rejoice, and by his pride he lost his true paradise and deprived himself of God, the source of joy. Therefore, for the repair of our nature it was necessary that we be planted anew in God, so that we become like those who are in the eternal paradise... For this reason St. Cyril of Jerusalem addresses those approaching Baptism thus: [Soon paradise will be opened to each one of you], for they enter into union with God in Christ Jesus, the true paradise.

c. The gift of work: The Lord Christ says, "My Father worketh hitherto, and I work" (Jn 5:17). It is the characteristic of God, who works without ceasing, and He gave it to the rational creation so that it might work continually. But Satan worked not for the glory of his Creator but for the account of his own glory, so his work became not for his edification but for his destruction. "With thy wisdom and with thine understanding thou hast gotten thee riches, and hast gotten gold and silver into thy treasures. By thy great wisdom and by thy traffick hast thou increased thy riches" [4-5]. In this God rejoices, for He desires to see the treasuries of His creation always filled with every precious wealth and riches, but what grieved Him was this: "thine heart is lifted up because of thy riches" [5]. Riches are a blessing and a grace, but the lifting up of the heart corrupts the heart of the rich man, so that he thinks himself a god: "Because thou hast set thine heart as the heart of God; behold, therefore I will bring strangers upon thee, the terrible of the nations: and they shall draw their swords against the beauty of thy wisdom, and they shall defile thy brightness. They shall bring thee down to the pit, and thou shalt die the deaths of them that are slain in the midst of the seas" [6-8]. What befalls him is not because of his wisdom, nor his beauty, nor his riches, but because of the pride of his heart; he thought himself a god, so he was deprived of his wisdom, his beauty, his riches, and life itself.

The Fathers spoke much about work and its importance, and about riches and their blessings... declaring that it is pride that corrupts work and riches. St. Clement of Alexandria wrote a book on this subject, entitled "Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?", in which he says: "We do not cast the rich man to the ground, he who benefits our brethren... A man does not squander his riches, but rather it is fitting for him to break down his inward passions that conflict with the good use of riches. For when a man becomes virtuous and good, he can use these riches in a good way. Let us therefore understand the leaving and selling of our kingdoms (Mk 10:13-17) to mean a leaving and selling of the passions of our souls."

d. He gave every precious stone [13]: The Septuagint gives the same twelve stones that were placed on the breastplate of the high priest, and with which the wall of the heavenly Jerusalem was adorned (Rev 21:19-20). They point to the divine virtues and the gifts with which God adorns the soul, so that it may enter His sanctuaries radiant and shining. For this reason the Lord comforts His struggling Church, saying to her: "O thou afflicted, tossed with tempest, and not comforted, behold, I will lay thy stones with fair colours, and lay thy foundations with sapphires. And I will make thy windows of agates, and thy gates of carbuncles, and all thy borders of pleasant stones... This is the heritage of the servants of the LORD, and their righteousness is of me, saith the LORD" (Isa 54:11-17). God adorns His rational creation with gifts and virtues... but when it falls into pride, it becomes a cause of judgment against it!

entries.section: 1. Prophecy against the prince of Tyre:

paragraphs.text: e. The fiery nature: "Thou art the anointed cherub that covereth; and I have set thee so: thou wast upon the holy mountain of God" [14]. He set him with a fiery nature, a blazing cherub, and made him dwell in the sanctuaries, so he became without excuse. God has given us the capacities of the new nature and planted us in Him, "the holy mountain," so we have become without excuse before Him.

entries.section: 1. Prophecy against the prince of Tyre:

paragraphs.text: f. "Thou hast walked up and down in the midst of the stones of fire" [16], for he was like a cherub walking among the Cherubim and Seraphim who blaze with fire. He ought to have remained like them, a holy fire, and not to fall from among them. So the Cherubim condemn Satan, because he was with them and fell! And the Apostles also will judge the twelve tribes of Israel, because they were Jews and accepted the faith, whereas the Jews rejected faith in Christ, the mystery of the sanctification and salvation of mankind!

Pride makes the creature a god in his own eyes: "Thine heart is lifted up, and thou hast said, I am a God" [2]. Therefore it brings him down to die the most hideous death: "Thou shalt die the deaths of the uncircumcised by the hand of strangers: for I have spoken it, saith the Lord GOD" [10]. The Phoenicians practiced circumcision, and considered that one who dies uncircumcised is despised and in great shame! Thus pride does not only kill him, but also puts him in great shame!

As for the place of the slaying, according to the Septuagint, "I will cut thee off (cast thee) as one slain from the mountain of God" [16]. St. Jerome clarifies for us this mountain of God on which the king of Tyre was slain, saying: [The mountain of God is rich in its blessings (Ps 86:16); this is the mountain mentioned by Ezekiel, on which the king of Tyre was punished].

[(The mountain) points to the presence of the Savior who became flesh, for in Him the divine nature dwelt. Truly, there is no other way in which the Holy Spirit found His dwelling immediately and continually except in the Savior, and as John says: "Upon whom thou shalt see the Spirit descending, and remaining on him, the same is he" (Jn 1:33), "the LORD will dwell in it for ever" (Ps 68:16), in the body which He took from the blessed Mary]. Through this holy mountain Satan was wounded, since he found no place in it; through the Lord Christ Satan was driven out from mankind.

20 Again the word of the LORD came unto me, saying, 21 "Son of man, set thy face against Zidon, and prophesy against it, 22 And say, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I am against thee, O Zidon; and I will be glorified in the midst of thee: and they shall know that I am the LORD, when I shall have executed judgments in her, and shall be sanctified in her. 23 For I will send into her pestilence, and blood into her streets; and the wounded shall be judged in the midst of her by the sword upon her on every side; and they shall know that I am the LORD. 24 And there shall be no more a pricking brier unto the house of Israel, nor any grieving thorn of all that are round about them, that despised them; and they shall know that I am the Lord GOD. 25 Thus saith the Lord GOD; When I shall have gathered the house of Israel from the people among whom they are scattered, and shall be sanctified in them in the sight of the heathen, then shall they dwell in their land that I have given to my servant Jacob. 26 And they shall dwell safely therein, and shall build houses, and plant vineyards; yea, they shall dwell with confidence, when I have executed judgments upon all those that despise them round about them; and they shall know that I am the LORD their God."

We have already spoken of Zidon as the "land of hunting." She shared with Tyre in mocking Judah over its captivity, and became a pricking brier and a grieving thorn. Since she embittered the life of the children of God, He sends pestilence upon her to be a painful thorn to her.

Finally He makes clear that He does all this in order to gather His scattered people and sanctify His name in them, to satisfy them with good things and grant them peace! This is God's continual longing, to see mankind return to rest in Him, and be satisfied and filled with peace as a holy bride to Him.
A lesson from Satan!
* Satan has become a lesson to me!
You created him among the Cherubim, perfect and full of wisdom and beauty!
He knows many of Your divine secrets!
But through pride he collapsed from heaven to the abyss!
You made me the most wonderful of Your creatures on earth, You granted me mind, wisdom, and beauty!
Grant me the spirit of humility, that I may cling to You, and enjoy the splendor of Your beauty upon me!
* You set him in heaven, rejoicing and exulting in Your presence; by his stubbornness he collapsed into eternal torment!
You set me in the garden of Eden to work and to praise!
When will You lift me up to Your paradise, to enjoy eternal glory?!
* God gave him riches, and his heart was lifted up by his riches!
You have not left me in want of the works of Your honor!
When shall I possess You, my treasure and my wealth!
You are my love! You are my praise!
You are my joy and the exultation of my heart!
You are my satisfaction and my wealth!
With You I want nothing!
* You adorned him with every precious stone; by his disobedience he became ugly, deprived of everything beautiful and precious!
You adorned me with gifts like precious stones; kindle in me Your gifts as a precious inheritance!
* You created him a fiery cherub, You made him dwell in the sanctuaries, and by his own will he collapsed to dwell in an eternal fire that is never quenched!
You renewed me by Your fiery Holy Spirit, to carry me to the throne of Your glory, to a light that none can approach!
When shall I become like the cherub, and like a servant of light!
I await Your coming, O true Light!

1 In the tenth year, in the tenth month, in the twelfth day of the month, the word of the LORD came unto me, saying, 2 "Son of man, set thy face against Pharaoh king of Egypt, and prophesy against him, and against all Egypt: 3 Speak, and say, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I am against thee, Pharaoh king of Egypt, the great crocodile that lieth in the midst of his rivers, which hath said, My river is mine own, and I have made it for myself. 4 But I will put hooks in thy jaws, and I will cause the fish of thy rivers to stick unto thy scales, and I will bring thee up out of the midst of thy rivers, and all the fish of thy rivers shall stick unto thy scales. 5 And I will leave thee thrown into the wilderness, thee and all the fish of thy rivers: thou shalt fall upon the open fields; thou shalt not be brought together, nor gathered: I have given thee for meat to the beasts of the field and to the fowls of the heaven. 6 And all the inhabitants of Egypt shall know that I am the LORD, because they have been a staff of reed to the house of Israel. 7 When they took hold of thee by thy hand, thou didst break, and rend all their shoulder: and when they leaned upon thee, thou brakest, and madest all their loins to be at a stand."

The prophet Ezekiel dates this prophecy to the tenth year of the captivity, when Pharaoh advanced with his armies toward Jerusalem to deliver it from the siege. The men of Judah did not listen to the warnings of Jeremiah or Ezekiel, but leaned upon Pharaoh against Babylon, and rose in revolt against Babylon, and the Pharaoh of Egypt went out to rescue them from Babylon... which led afterward to the destruction of the city and the killing of many.

God offered the fitting comparison. Since Tyre was an island rich in its trade and proud of its merchants, He likened it to a ship, precious in the materials of its building and its cargo, and perfect in its crew and its guards. But Pharaoh of Egypt relied, with his men, on the Nile of Egypt, which made Egypt fertile; therefore He likened him to the great crocodile that lies in the midst of his rivers [3], for the river Nile was famous for its crocodiles.

God called Pharaoh "the great crocodile" perhaps because the Egyptians worshiped crocodiles and so became crocodiles, and their king was called "the great crocodile." He who worships stones becomes a stone, and he who worships vanity becomes vanity, and he who worships the true God becomes "true" and enjoys partnership in the divine nature.

The sin of Tyre was its exploitation of the fall of Judah and its greedy seizing of this opportunity, but the sin of Pharaoh was pride, for with his strong army he thought he was able to do everything, "which hath said, My river is mine own, and I have made it for myself" [3]. It is said that by this was meant Pharaoh Khafra, who boasted of two things: that he himself made with his own hands the power and security he enjoyed, and that this was for his own sake. He set up the "ego" as a god, as the maker of the river, the secret of Egypt's fertility and greatness, and said it made this for its own sake. The historian Herodotus relates of this king that he reigned in great prosperity for twenty-five years, and his heart was lifted up by his success, saying that God Himself could not remove him from his kingdom. The prophet Jeremiah spoke of this pride thus: "Who is this that cometh up as a flood, whose waters are moved as the rivers? Egypt riseth up like a flood, and his waters are moved like the rivers; and he saith, I will go up, and will cover the earth; I will destroy the city and the inhabitants thereof" (Jer 46:7-8).
What does God do with this proud crocodile who thinks he is the creator of the river for his own account?!

He says: "I will put hooks in thy jaws, and I will cause the fish of thy rivers to stick unto thy scales, and I will bring thee up out of the midst of thy rivers, and all the fish of thy rivers shall stick unto thy scales.
And I will leave thee thrown into the wilderness, thee and all the fish of thy rivers.
Thou shalt fall upon the open fields; thou shalt not be brought together, nor gathered.
I have given thee for meat to the beasts of the field and to the fowls of the heaven" [4-5].

Since in the pride of his heart he thought that the power and prosperity he had were the work of his own hands, God deprives him of these blessings and drives him out from the midst of his rivers, to die as a fish dies outside the water. And since he thought that everything was created to serve himself, with everything working for his service and his account, he is cast into the wilderness; he dies with none to ask after him and none to bury him, becoming prey for the beasts of the field and food for the fowls of the heaven! And since he gathered around him many who took refuge in him or fought with him, they become like the fish sticking to his scales; whether nations or commanders, chariots or army, they receive the same fate. Thus pride robs him of his goods and his honor and even his life, and humbles even those who cling to him and rely on him. It is said that this Pharaoh went out to fight the people of Cyrene, who had driven out his friend Aricius, king of Libya, in order to restore him to his kingdom; but the Egyptians rebelled against him in his absence, so neither he nor his commanders returned to his kingdom, and he was cast into the wilderness with them.

This is the work of pride in the life of one who belongs to the greatest heavenly order (the devil), who by his pride lost heaven and fell to the abyss; in place of divine friendship he entered into enmity with God, and in place of heavenly glory he entered into perpetual humiliation. He was shattered and shattered with him many of his angels and also of human beings! By the same disease our first parents fell from paradise and were deprived of continual existence in the divine presence, and bequeathed to their offspring all toil and misery! We were driven out from the river of life, and cast into the wilderness of this life, to die spiritually and become the prey of all the beasts of the field (the demon of injustice and cruelty) and the fowls of the heaven (the demon of pride).

He returns to liken Pharaoh of Egypt to a staff of reed to the house of Israel [6]; he is like a staff, but of reed (cane), which breaks when a man leans upon it, and the shoulder of the one who leans on it is torn and weakened. Instead of supporting him, it shatters his strength, as the prophet Isaiah says: "For Egypt helps in vain and to no purpose; therefore have I called her Rahab that sitteth still" (Isa 30:7). Pharaoh of Egypt encouraged King Zedekiah to revolt against Babylon, to betray the covenant and break the oath, so Hezekiah was lost, Jerusalem and all the cities of Judah were shattered, and Pharaoh was defeated.

It should be noted here that the discipline of Pharaoh and the fish sticking to his scales was by leaving them to die in the wilderness, to be eaten by the beasts of the field and the fowls of the heaven. This is the most hideous death, which the Egyptians hated, for they were anxious for the body and built tombs to preserve it until the spirit should return to clothe itself again with its body.

8 "Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I will bring a sword upon thee, and cut off man and beast out of thee. 9 And the land of Egypt shall be desolate and waste; and they shall know that I am the LORD: because he hath said, The river is mine, and I have made it. 10 Behold, therefore I am against thee, and against thy rivers, and I will make the land of Egypt utterly waste and desolate, from Migdol to Syene, even unto the border of Cush. 11 No foot of man shall pass through it, nor foot of beast shall pass through it, neither shall it be inhabited forty years. 12 And I will make the land of Egypt desolate in the midst of the countries that are desolate, and her cities among the cities that are laid waste shall be desolate forty years: and I will scatter the Egyptians among the nations, and will disperse them through the countries."

In the pride of his heart Pharaoh thought that he was the maker of the great river and the defender of the nations around him, but the Lord brings a sword upon him and cuts off man and beast. Through pride man loses his humanity, "his intellectual life," and also his animal nature, "his earthly life"; he loses what belongs to mind and body together. The extent of this loss is a complete loss, stretching from the north, "Migdol," to the south, "Syene," on the border of Cush.

"Migdol" is a Semitic name meaning "tower"; it was most probably a fortified city on the northeastern border of Egypt toward Palestine, now Tell el-Her, twelve miles west of Pelusium. It lies on the road by which the Jews passed during their exodus from Egypt.

Syene, in Egyptian Sewen, is on the eastern bank of the river on the southern border of Egypt. Opposite it on the other side is "Elephantine Island." It was a source of granite for the Egyptian statues, and also a strong center of defense on the southern border.
As for Cush, it most often means "Ethiopia" or "Abyssinia," and here it means the land of Nubia.

So the discipline of Pharaoh of Egypt is a comprehensive discipline, in which his land becomes a ruin where neither man nor beast dwells, extending from the far south; but at the same time it is temporary and for a fixed period (forty years), unlike the other nations, for whom the decree was that the discipline be everlasting. He scatters and disperses the Egyptians for a time. Perhaps this is a reference to the confidence which Egypt holds in the heart of God after accepting faith in the Lord Christ, for He says through the prophet Isaiah: "Behold, the LORD rideth upon a swift cloud, and shall come into Egypt... And the LORD shall be known to Egypt, and the Egyptians shall know the LORD in that day, and shall do sacrifice and oblation; yea, they shall vow a vow unto the LORD, and perform it" (Isa 19).
She spends the days of her idolatry like one wandering in the wilderness, so that she may return to faith in God her Savior and worship Him.

entries.section: 3. The return and restoration of Egypt:

paragraphs.text: 13 "Yet thus saith the Lord GOD; At the end of forty years will I gather the Egyptians from the people whither they were scattered: 14 And I will bring again the captivity of Egypt, and will cause them to return into the land of Pathros, into the land of their birth; and they shall be there a base kingdom. 15 It shall be the basest of the kingdoms; neither shall it exalt itself any more above the nations: for I will diminish them, that they shall no more rule over the nations. 16 And it shall be no more the confidence of the house of Israel, which bringeth their iniquity to remembrance, when they shall look after them: but they shall know that I am the Lord GOD."

entries.section: 3. The return and restoration of Egypt:

paragraphs.text: The Lord gave Pharaoh of Egypt a lesson, he who stirred up the king of Judah and made him not listen to the voice of the prophets; instead of supporting him, he and his people were scattered for forty years, and then He restored the kingdom of Egypt to Pathros, the land of Pathros [14], an Egyptian word meaning "the land of the south." By Pathros is meant Upper Egypt, as opposed to "Lower and Middle Egypt"; Lower Egypt, or the Delta, was more desirable than Upper Egypt. It should be noted that after Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem captive, some Jews settled in Pathros (Jer 44:1-2, 15).

It is as though by the return of the kingdom to "Pathros" He means its weakness and its inability to make war and to support others, so that it does not return again to its pride, and does not deceive the people of God by being a support for them against Babylon.

entries.section: 4. His being delivered to the king of Babylon:

paragraphs.text: 17 And it came to pass in the seven and twentieth year, in the first month, in the first day of the month, the word of the LORD came unto me, saying, 18 "Son of man, Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon caused his army to serve a great service against Tyrus: every head was made bald, and every shoulder was peeled: yet had he no wages, nor his army, for Tyrus, for the service that he had served against it: 19 Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I will give the land of Egypt unto Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon; and he shall take her multitude, and take her spoil, and take her prey; and it shall be the wages for his army. 20 I have given him the land of Egypt for his labour wherewith he served against it, because they wrought for me, saith the Lord GOD. 21 In that day will I cause the horn of the house of Israel to bud forth, and I will give thee the opening of the mouth in the midst of them; and they shall know that I am the LORD."

Finally, instead of defending Judah, Pharaoh of Egypt falls into the grasp of the king of Babylon, who takes his wealth and seizes him as spoil and plunders him. The Lord delivers him to the king of Babylon as a recompense for what he did to Tyre. Tyre had seized Jerusalem and plundered it, so God stirred up Babylon against it, and when it had destroyed Tyre He rewarded it with the wealth of Pharaoh. Nebuchadnezzar attacked Egypt in the thirty-seventh year of his reign (568-567 B.C.) and took much from it, but it did not become part of his kingdom.

entries.section: 4. His being delivered to the king of Babylon:

paragraphs.text: But the main subject is not the reward of the king of Babylon, who destroyed Tyre that had gloated over Jerusalem; rather, what occupies the mind of God is to raise up a horn (that is, a power) for the salvation of His people [21] and to open the mouth of His prophet in the midst of the people to proclaim this salvation in a spirit of hope and joy, for He says: "I will give thee the opening of the mouth in the midst of them; and they shall know that I am the LORD" [21].
My river is mine own, and I have made it for myself!
* Pharaoh of Egypt prides himself on the river Nile, and counts it his river, which his hands made for himself!
How strange is man, who ascribes to himself what belongs to his God, and instead of giving thanks and praise to God, the Creator of the world for his sake, thinks himself a god!
* You disciplined Egypt for a time, and You came to her, O Savior, as upon a light cloud!
You shattered her idols and set up Your altar in her midst!
* Hasten, O Savior, to my soul!
Let the idols of my heart tremble before Your presence!
And let Your divine altar be set up within me!
* Take away from me ingratitude and teach me thanksgiving!
The river Nile is the work of Your hands!
Your gifts are more than can be counted!
What shall I render unto You, O Lord, for the multitude of Your kindnesses?!

1 The word of the LORD came again unto me, saying, 2 "Son of man, prophesy and say, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Howl ye, Woe worth the day! 3 For the day is near, even the day of the LORD is near, a cloudy day; it shall be the time of the heathen. 4 And the sword shall come upon Egypt, and great pain shall be in Cush, when the slain shall fall in Egypt, and they shall take away her multitude, and her foundations shall be broken down. 5 Cush, and Put, and Lud, and all the mingled people, and Chub, and the men of the land that is in league, shall fall with them by the sword. 6 Thus saith the LORD; They also that uphold Egypt shall fall; and the pride of her power shall come down: from Migdol to Syene shall they fall in it by the sword, saith the Lord GOD. 7 And she shall be desolate in the midst of the countries that are desolate, and her cities shall be in the midst of the cities that are wasted. 8 And they shall know that I am the LORD, when I have set a fire in Egypt, and when all her helpers shall be destroyed. 9 In that day shall messengers go forth from me in ships to make the careless Cush afraid, and great pain shall come upon them, as in the day of Egypt: for, lo, it cometh."

When the Lord asked the prophet Ezekiel to prophesy against Pharaoh of Egypt, He did not direct the call to howl to Pharaoh nor to all the people of Egypt, but directed it as a general call to the whole pagan world, since Pharaoh of Egypt represented it at that time, saying, "Howl ye, Woe worth the day!" [2]. And He called the day of Pharaoh "the day of the LORD," because it is a discipline from the Lord upon all the nations! Therefore it was said: "I made the nations to shake at the sound of his fall, when I cast him down to hell with them that descend into the pit" (Ezek 31:16); "And they shall tremble at every moment, every man for his own life, in the day of thy fall" (Ezek 32:10). Thus the news of his fall resounds in the whole world, and all creation trembles at it.

It must be noted that Pharaoh here points to "Satan," as the instigator of rebellion against the prophetic words, who thinks himself a possessor of authority, able to support many. We spoke of Pharaoh as a symbol of Satan in our study of the Book of Exodus, in his resistance to the prophet Moses and Aaron. As Origen says: [In my opinion, some names of peoples or kings that we read of in the Holy Bible undoubtedly belong to the evil angels or the opposing powers, such as Pharaoh king of Egypt, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and Assyria].

If Pharaoh, as a symbol of Satan, thinks himself a possessor of authority to whom the other nations resort and in whom they take refuge, God proclaims his psychological defeat and his shattering by fear. He made his day "a cloudy day" [2]. The cloud, as we saw before, is a sign of the divine glory; it covers the holy mountain or the holy tent or the temple, declaring man's entrance into invisible mysteries that cannot be grasped. But for Satan or Pharaoh the cloud represents a state of darkness, in which he cannot act and does not know what to do. If he thought himself a leader, he walks in the darkness and stumbles, and those who cling to him and shelter under his wings stumble with him. Therefore He says: "In that day shall messengers go forth from me in ships to make the careless Cush afraid, and great pain shall come upon them, as in the day of Egypt: for, lo, it cometh" [9]. The nearest nation to him is "Cush," by which perhaps Nubia is meant, and also some regions in Asia. In any case, terror filled the heart of Pharaoh, and even the heart of the nearest kingdom to him that sheltered under his shadow; so what will be the fate of the other, distant nations?! The one who terrified them is the Lord Himself: "messengers go forth from me in ships to make the careless Cush afraid," because she left the Lord and resorted to Pharaoh.
With the fall of Pharaoh and his terror, "Cush (Nubia or Ethiopia), and Put, and Lud, and all the mingled people, and Chub, and the men of the land that is in league, shall fall with them" [5].
We have already spoken of Cush and also of Put and Lud (Ezek 27:10); as for his saying "all the mingled people," some translate it "the mixed people" and others "Arabia"...

As for Chub, some see it as Lub (Libya), most probably a people who dwelt in northeastern Africa, and the Septuagint has: "the Libyans." "The men of the land that is in league" means the countries that entered into a covenant with Pharaoh for their protection, especially against the attack of the king of Babylon.

The pride of the devil must be brought down completely throughout his whole kingdom, from the far north (Migdol) to the far south (Syene) [6], and he collapses with all his helpers and those joined to him: "And they shall know that I am the LORD, when I have set a fire in Egypt, and when all her helpers shall be destroyed" [8].

10 "Thus saith the Lord GOD; I will also make the wealth of Egypt to cease by the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon. 11 He and his people with him, the terrible of the nations, shall be brought to destroy the land: and they shall draw their swords against Egypt, and fill the land with the slain. 12 And I will make the rivers dry, and sell the land into the hand of the wicked: and I will make the land waste, and all that is therein, by the hand of strangers: I the LORD have spoken it. 13 Thus saith the Lord GOD; I will also destroy the idols, and I will cause their images to cease out of Noph; and there shall be no more a prince of the land of Egypt: and I will put a fear in the land of Egypt. 14 And I will make Pathros desolate, and will set fire in Zoan, and will execute judgments in No. 15 And I will pour my fury upon Sin, the strength of Egypt; and I will cut off the multitude of No. 16 And I will set fire in Egypt: Sin shall have great pain, and No shall be rent asunder, and Noph shall have distresses daily. 17 The young men of Aven and of Pibeseth shall fall by the sword: and these cities shall go into captivity. 18 At Tehaphnehes also the day shall be darkened, when I shall break there the yokes of Egypt: and the pomp of her strength shall cease in her: as for her, a cloud shall cover her, and her daughters shall go into captivity. 19 Thus will I execute judgments in Egypt: and they shall know that I am the LORD."

In place of pride and arrogance, fear and trembling come upon Pharaoh and all the surrounding nations that sheltered in him. And in place of his riches and wealth, as he said, "My river is mine own, and I have made it for myself" (Ezek 29:3, 9), the rivers become dry [12]. And in place of his kingship and authority, He delivers his land into the hand of the wicked strangers [12]. In place of security and rest, the Lord sets a fire, and his kingdom loses its hope, for it loses its youth in the war, and its daughters in captivity! He thought himself a god, and behold, his idols and his worship are shattered [13].

The kingdom of the devil must come to an end; his awe and his deceptive fear vanish, all his capacities collapse, and he is cast into the eternal fire with all who followed him and took refuge in him.
All the centers of power that worked for his service under his authority will be shattered, which are symbolized by the fortified Egyptian cities mentioned here, the most important of which are:

a. Noph: "Thus saith the Lord GOD; I will also destroy the idols, and I will cause their images to cease out of Noph; and there shall be no more a prince of the land of Egypt: and I will put a fear in the land of Egypt" [13]. When He wished to speak of the destruction of all the authority of Pharaoh (a symbol of Satan) and the end of his kingdom, so that no prince of his appears any more, He chose "Noph" (in Hebrew), which in Egyptian is "Menefer" or "Minfri," and in Greek "Memphis" Μέμφις, and is counted the most famous city in Egypt. Menes built it when he united Lower and Upper Egypt, and it became the capital of ancient Egypt; only Thebes rivaled it in size and importance, until the Greeks built the city of Alexandria as a capital.

Memphis is about ten miles south of Cairo, beside Mit Rahina. The palaces of the kings were built inside the capital Memphis or beside it, and the pyramids were built near it, twelve miles south of the center of the ruins of Memphis, and in them the kings were buried.

After the building of Alexandria, Memphis took second place, and it was crowded with inhabitants until the Arabs entered Egypt, when it quickly fell into ruin. The growth of Fustat and Cairo went hand in hand with the ruin of Memphis, since the stones and building materials were carried off from Memphis.
The bull Apis was worshiped in Memphis as sacred to the god Ptah, the chief god of the city, "the god of fire."
b. Pathros [14]: We said that it is "the land of the south," meaning Upper Egypt; as He destroys the idols from Memphis in Lower Egypt, so He lays waste Upper Egypt.

c. Zoan [14]: On the eastern bank of the Delta, built seven years after Hebron (Num 13:22). The fields of Zoan are mentioned in (Ps 78:12, 43) as the place where the wonders connected with the exodus of the children of Israel from Egypt were wrought, and it is mentioned in (Isa 19:11, 13; 30:4) perhaps as the capital of Egypt. It was known by the name "Avaris" as the capital of the Hyksos; it was neglected after their expulsion, but attention was restored to it in the Ramesside period, in the days of the reign of Seti I and Ramesses II, and it bore the name "Raamses" (Ex 1:11); its Greek name is "Tanis," and it is now called "San el-Hagar."
d. No: He says that God executes His judgments on No and cuts off its multitude [15].

No, No-Amon, Amon-No: an Egyptian name meaning the city of Amon. He was the greatest of the gods of Egypt, especially from the seventeenth dynasty. (The word Amon in Egyptian means the hidden or concealed one, and in Hebrew it means amen or the maker.)

No-Amon, which is the city of Thebes, lies in Upper Egypt, 400 miles south of Memphis, on both banks of the Nile. Ahmose gave it great importance by expelling the Hyksos, liberating Egypt, reunifying it, and laying the foundation stone of the Egyptian empire that the 18th and 19th dynasties built. His successors cared for the city, and it grew in splendor and magnificence. It had a hundred gates, and its priest, the priest of Amon, was counted the second man in the state. Even when Memphis later became the capital of Egypt, Thebes kept its importance because of the worship of the god Amon and the wealth it contained in temples, buildings, and obelisks. In the seventh century B.C., Esarhaddon the Syrian conqueror reached it in 671 B.C., and his son Ashurbanipal conquered and occupied it in 664 B.C. (Nah 3:8), but did not destroy it completely. When it led the revolt of Upper Egypt against the Romans, the Roman armies destroyed it and it became a collection of ruins. That region still bears witness, at Luxor, Karnak, Qurna, Medinet Habu, the tombs of the kings, Deir el-Bahari, and so on, to the greatness of those monuments, which draw the eyes of the whole world as a museum of the greatest human civilization that history has seen.

e. Sin: "And I will pour my fury upon Sin, the strength of Egypt" [15]; "Sin shall have great pain" [16]. It is the only city placed at the disposal of the Assyrian; it was undoubtedly in the place of Pelusium, to keep the gates of Egypt open before the Assyrian king.
It was called the strength of Egypt because many battles were fought at it. Its site is now Tell el-Farama, 20 miles northeast of Qantara.
f. Aven: "The young men of Aven and of Pibeseth shall fall by the sword: and these cities shall go into captivity" [17].

The city of On (Aven), in Egyptian "Iunu" and in Greek "Heliopolis." The seat of the sun god Ra. It is now Tell Hassan, or Ain Shams, seven miles northeast of Cairo; there was found the house of the father-in-law of Joseph (Gen 41:45, 50).

Its temple was of great importance, the kings loved it, and its priests were the most learned of priests; therefore a tradition exists that Plato and many of the Greek philosophers studied at Heliopolis.
It is as though God wished to declare that the young men of this city of learning fall by the sword and its existence comes to an end, for learning without faith does not build up the soul.
g. Pibeseth or Phibeseth:
An Egyptian name meaning "the house of the goddess Bast" (Pi-Bastis); its Greek name is "Bubastis." It is now called Tell Basta, beside Zagazig, east of the Delta.

h. Tehaphnehes: "And the fire shall grow dark in Tehaphnehes, when I shall break there the yokes of Egypt: and the pomp of her strength shall cease in her" [18]. It is the city to which some Jews resorted when they fled to Egypt after the killing of Gedaliah (Jer 43:7). In Greek it is called "Daphne," now "Tell Defenneh," 10 miles west of Qantara; in the Septuagint it is "Taphnis," and its meaning is "the fortress or citadel of Penahse." Penahse was most probably a commander with authority from Thebes, who lived in the 11th century B.C. and led a revolt in the north, so several cities arose bearing his name.

Herodotus mentions that Daphnae was the fortress of Egypt on the Asian side, and that the Greeks guarded it. In its ruins were found many Greek pottery vessels and also iron weapons and arrowheads of bronze and iron bearing a Greek character, besides many remains that bear witness that it was a huge trade route.

20 And it came to pass in the eleventh year, in the first month, in the seventh day of the month, that the word of the LORD came unto me, saying, 21 "Son of man, I have broken the arm of Pharaoh king of Egypt; and, lo, it shall not be bound up to be healed, to put a roller to bind it, to make it strong to hold the sword. 22 Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I am against Pharaoh king of Egypt, and will break his arms, the strong, and that which was broken; and I will cause the sword to fall out of his hand. 23 And I will scatter the Egyptians among the nations, and will disperse them through the countries. 24 And I will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon, and put my sword in his hand: but I will break Pharaoh's arms, and he shall groan before him with the groanings of a deadly wounded man. 25 But I will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon, and the arms of Pharaoh shall fall down; and they shall know that I am the LORD, when I shall put my sword into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall stretch it out upon the land of Egypt. 26 And I will scatter the Egyptians among the nations, and disperse them among the countries; and they shall know that I am the LORD."

Having spoken of the ruin that befell his fortified cities, he begins to speak of his arm, how a deadly wound struck it that cannot be healed, so that he can no longer bear a weapon, neither to defend himself nor those who sheltered in him. At the same time God strengthens the arms of the king of Babylon and puts the sword in his hand to discipline Pharaoh of Egypt, so that his hands fall and his people are scattered!
This is a picture of the satanic work that resists the divine plan, which ends in complete failure, however successful it may appear at the beginning.
Fire in the city of fire!
* The Egyptians worshiped the god Ptah in Memphis, the city of the god of fire!
