And Pharaoh thought that he was the fiery man, the possessor of authority, to whom the nations resort and he protects them.
Behold, the Lord makes the day of Pharaoh a day of cloud, a day of darkness and fear, so his spirit is shattered, and terror falls on all Egypt!
God kindles the fire of His discipline and breaks all the powers of Pharaoh!
* Instead of protecting others, he becomes a terror!
He loses his wealth and his arms are shattered!
* Teach me, O Lord, the spirit of humility!
You are a refuge for me and for my brethren!
I and they need Your protection and Your care, O wise Shepherd of souls!

1 And it came to pass in the eleventh year, in the third month, in the first day of the month, that the word of the LORD came unto me, saying, 2 "Son of man, speak unto Pharaoh king of Egypt, and to his multitude; Whom art thou like in thy greatness? 3 Behold, the highest of the cedars in Lebanon, with fair branches, and with a shadowing shroud, and of an high stature; and his top was among the thick boughs. 4 The waters made him great, the deep set him up on high with her rivers running round about his plants, and sent out her little rivers unto all the trees of the field. 5 Therefore his height was exalted above all the trees of the field, and his boughs were multiplied, and his branches became long because of the multitude of waters, when he shot forth. 6 All the fowls of heaven made their nests in his boughs, and under his branches did all the beasts of the field bring forth their young, and under his shadow dwelt all great nations. 7 Thus was he fair in his greatness, in the length of his branches: for his root was by great waters. 8 The cedars in the garden of God could not exceed him: the cypress trees were not like his boughs, and the plane trees were not like his branches; nor any tree in the garden of God was like unto him in his beauty. 9 I have made him fair by the multitude of his branches: so that all the trees of Eden, that were in the garden of God, envied him."
God commands Ezekiel to ask Pharaoh of Egypt:
"Whom art thou like in thy greatness?
Behold, (Assyria) the highest of the cedars in Lebanon, with fair branches, and with a shadowing shroud, and of an high stature; and his top was among the thick boughs..." [2-3].

Whether He rebukes Pharaoh of Egypt because he exalts himself in his own eyes on account of the gifts and endowments God gave him, or presents to him Assyria, which bore the same trait of "pride," as an example for him, the picture presented applies to man, whom God has flooded with every possibility of success, but instead of glorifying God he fell into pride and so collapsed. This is a lamentation over every soul, and it approaches the lamentation over the prince of Tyre as a symbol of the devil, whom God made above every earthly and heavenly creature, a cherub in His garden bearing the throne. He hid from him none of the secrets, but when he became proud he fell.

Some see that God asks Pharaoh to think about Assyria, the great kingdom that fell. In 609 B.C. Pharaoh Necho went to Carchemish to help the Assyrian empire, which was suffering Babylonian attacks. But the efforts failed, and Assyria was torn out of history, like a cedar tree in Lebanon that has been uprooted.

entries.section: And now, what has God given us?

paragraphs.text: The Lord summed up His gifts to us in three matters:

entries.section: And now, what has God given us?

paragraphs.text: a. "Behold, (Assyria) the highest of the cedars in Lebanon" [3].
Assyria was the greatest state at that time, appearing like the lofty cedar tree; its king was greater than all the kings of the surrounding states, who were subject to him.

God created us as the most perfect earthly creature, setting us on the sixth day after He had brought all things into being for our rest. He gave us a rational soul in His image and likeness, and granted us dominion over every earthly creature. He wished not to humble him but to exalt him, not to deprive him but to satisfy him, not to make him a pliant instrument in His hand but a being with a free will... He raised him to the utmost limits.
"Thus was he fair in his greatness, in the length of his branches...

entries.section: And now, what has God given us?

paragraphs.text: The cedars in the garden of God could not exceed him: the cypress trees were not like his boughs, and the plane trees were not like his branches; nor any tree in the garden of God was like unto him in his beauty. I have made him fair by the multitude of his branches: so that all the trees of Eden, that were in the garden of God, envied him" [7-9]. He is God's planting, the work of His hands; He planted him in His garden and set him fair, fairer than all the trees of His garden, so that Satan envied him for the splendor which the Lord poured upon him, and urged him to pride and to exalt himself against God!

b. "With fair branches" [3]. Satan envied him because of the multitude of his branches [9], for "all the fowls of heaven made their nests in his boughs, and under his branches did all the beasts of the field bring forth their young, and under his shadow dwelt all great nations" [6].
He likens the nations subject to Assyria to birds that shelter among the branches of the tree, or like the beasts of the earth that bring forth their young under its branches.

What are these many fair branches that God gave, to shelter the fowls of heaven and for the beasts of the field to bring forth their young under its shadow, if not the nature of love that God placed in him, so that man might extend with his heart toward all mankind, and even toward every earthly creature? In him the saints find rest, and in him the suffering find rest, and to him all resort to find in him a spacious heart able to embrace many. God created man a being beloved and loving, the object of the love of God and His angels, and his heart too is made wide to love.

Truly Assyria widened by its might and authority to embrace many nations under its banner, and also Pharaoh of Egypt under its authority; but the children of God widen with true inward love so that, if possible, they love even those who oppose them and the wicked, so that all may find their rest in them.

c. His planting by the overflowing streams of water: "The waters made him great, the deep set him up on high with her rivers running round about his plants, and sent out her little rivers unto all the trees of the field" [4]. If Pharaoh drinks from the overflowing waters of the Nile, which gave him riches and wealth and upheld him in his greatness, until he was satisfied and overflowed upon the rest of the nations, sending streams of water to all the trees of the field, then in this he resembles Assyria also, which relied on the Tigris and the Euphrates... But behold, Assyria has fallen!

As for us believers, we must experience that this is the work of God's grace in us. For we are planted by the waters of holy Baptism, and are watered inwardly by the Holy Spirit, who gives us uprightness so that our stature enters into the cloud, and our branches stretch out in every direction, and this is reflected even upon others, so that they receive the work of the Spirit in them. They are kindled by His fire when they see us kindled by His holy fire, and they enjoy the work of holy Baptism when they touch its effectiveness in us.

If the height of the cedar tree until its top reaches the cloud [3] points to the life of perfection and sanctification that God gave to man, for by them he enters into the mysteries of the Kingdom and beholds the hidden divine glories, and if the multitude of branches points to the power of love by which the heart is widened for all, then both of them, "holiness and love," are the gift of the Holy Spirit who works in us through the waters of holy Baptism, for He says: "Therefore his height was exalted above all the trees of the field, and his boughs were multiplied, and his branches became long because of the multitude of waters, when he shot forth" [5]. In the waters of Baptism we sprout as a new branch in the true Vine, and by the divine Spirit we grow continually in uprightness upward and in the multitude of branches outward.

Therefore Abba St. Isaac the Syrian says: [If good is done to you, openly or secretly, be sure that Baptism and faith are the two mediators of this good, for by them you were called to good works in Christ Jesus].

And Father Methodius says: [Those who are enlightened receive the features of Christ... For He necessarily imprints on each of them the form of the Word and His image and His features, so that Christ is reckoned as born in each of them, by the action of the Holy Spirit... and those who are baptized become other christs].
As St. James of Sarug says in one of his homilies on Baptism: [Baptism writes your name above in heaven, in the church of the firstborn, and you become a son of the Father who sits on high!]
Thus the true believer combines spiritual beauty and height and loftiness, and power and love... until he surpasses all the other trees, and they even envy him.

entries.section: 2. The fall of the cedar tree:

paragraphs.text: 10 "Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; Because thou hast lifted up thyself in height, and he hath shot up his top among the thick boughs, and his heart is lifted up in his height; 11 I have therefore delivered him into the hand of the mighty one of the heathen; he shall surely deal with him: I have driven him out for his wickedness. 12 And strangers, the terrible of the nations, have cut him off, and have left him: upon the mountains and in all the valleys his branches are fallen, and his boughs are broken by all the rivers of the land; and all the people of the earth are gone down from his shadow, and have left him. 13 Upon his ruin shall all the fowls of the heaven remain, and all the beasts of the field shall be upon his branches: 14 To the end that none of all the trees by the waters exalt themselves for their height, neither shoot up their top among the thick boughs, neither their oaks stand up in their height, all that drink water: for they are all delivered unto death, to the nether parts of the earth, in the midst of the children of men, with them that go down to the pit. 15 Thus saith the Lord GOD; In the day when he went down to the grave I caused a mourning: I covered the deep for him, and I restrained the floods thereof, and the great waters were stayed: and I caused Lebanon to mourn for him, and all the trees of the field fainted for him. 16 I made the nations to shake at the sound of his fall, when I cast him down to hell with them that descend into the pit: and all the trees of Eden, the choice and best of Lebanon, all that drink water, shall be comforted in the nether parts of the earth. 17 They also went down into hell with him unto them that be slain with the sword; and they that were his arm, that dwelt under his shadow in the midst of the heathen. 18 To whom art thou thus like in glory and in greatness among the trees of Eden? yet shalt thou be brought down with the trees of Eden unto the nether parts of the earth: thou shalt lie in the midst of the uncircumcised with them that be slain by the sword. This is Pharaoh and all his multitude, saith the Lord GOD."

The Book of the prophet Ezekiel focuses on the sin of pride as the secret of the fall. Here he says: "Because thou hast lifted up thyself in height, and he hath shot up his top among the thick boughs, and his heart is lifted up in his height; I have therefore delivered him into the hand of the mighty one of the heathen; he shall surely deal with him: I have driven him out for his wickedness" [10-11]. God desired to see him with his stature lifted up and his top reaching within the cloud (the thick boughs), but when his heart was lifted up in his loftiness, he fell from the height of his stature and his top came down from the cloud. Many have been lifted up in their spiritual stature and entered into the hidden mysteries of God while keeping a humble heart, as happened with St. Mary. The Virgin praised God, saying: "He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree." Therefore the Fathers warned us against pride and vainglory or arrogance, as they urged us to humility.
St. John Climacus says: [Humility is the heavenly ladder that can lift the soul from the pit of iniquities to heaven].

[If the pride of some of the angels turned them into demons (Isa 14:14; 1 Tim 3:6), then without doubt humility can make angels of demons (fallen souls); therefore let those who have fallen take courage].

entries.section: The fruit of pride and its work in us is:

paragraphs.text: a. Pride humbled Assyria and subjected it to Babylon, and it does the same to Pharaoh of Egypt:

entries.section: The fruit of pride and its work in us is:

paragraphs.text: "Strangers, the terrible of the nations, have cut him off" [12]. Truly the grace of God forsakes the proud man, and he becomes prey to the demons; by this these terrible strangers cut him off. But the humble man is upheld by the grace of God, and the beasts of the field submit to him, and he reigns over the earth. Therefore it was said: "Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth" (Mt 5:5).

b. The matter does not stop at the demons' raging against him, but he loses the inward traits that were given him: "Upon the mountains and in all the valleys his branches are fallen, and his boughs are broken by all the rivers of the land; and all the people of the earth are gone down from his shadow, and have left him" [12]. This is a bitter picture of the soul, for its destruction is not the result of an outward war but the result of an inward death; its branches fall after they dry up and lose all vitality wherever it is found, whether on the high mountains or in the low valleys, in the wilderness or by the rivers. His corruption springs from within him whatever the circumstances, so he becomes without branches, barren and dry, in whose shade no one takes shelter, and in whom no man finds rest, and he is left alone.

St. John Chrysostom wrote many discourses on this matter, declaring that no one can harm a man unless the man harms himself. Through pride a man shatters his life, attributing his failure to the circumstances around him or to the people who deal with him. The fault is in the tree, which bore its own dryness, not in the mountains or valleys or rivers or peoples that left it.

entries.section: The fruit of pride and its work in us is:

paragraphs.text: c. Instead of the fowls of heaven flying to him to rest in the shade of his branches, and the beasts of the field fleeing to him to bring forth their young under his shadow, it was said: "Upon his ruin (the fallen tree) shall all the fowls of the heaven remain, and all the beasts of the field shall be upon his branches" [13]. The tree became a ruin with no use in it, so the birds settle on it in contempt of it, and the animals come to it as to a place of desolation. The soul becomes a bearer of the fowls of heaven, that is, the spirit of arrogance and haughtiness, and bears the beasts of the field, or the spirit of violence, ferocity, and bestiality.

entries.section: The fruit of pride and its work in us is:

paragraphs.text: d. It falls into the abyss and becomes a warning to the other trees: "To the end that none of all the trees by the waters exalt themselves for their height... for they are all delivered unto death, to the nether parts of the earth, in the midst of the children of men, with them that go down to the pit" [14].

entries.section: The fruit of pride and its work in us is:

paragraphs.text: e. Man loses his joy and brings himself and those around him into sorrow: "In the day when he went down to the grave I caused a mourning: I covered the deep for him, and I restrained the floods thereof, and the great waters were stayed: and I caused Lebanon to mourn for him, and all the trees of the field fainted for him. I made the nations to shake at the sound of his fall, when I cast him down to hell" [15-16].

The soul loses the secret of its joy, for it is deprived of the rivers of holy grace, and the living waters dry up for it, so other souls grieve for it, and also tremble in fear for themselves, they who share with it in its sins.

entries.section: The fruit of pride and its work in us is:

paragraphs.text: f. He ended his discourse on the end of the proud by saying: "Thou shalt lie in the midst of the uncircumcised with them that be slain by the sword" [18]. His end is not only a hideous death, that is, being slain by the sword, but even in his lying down he is among the uncircumcised, that is, the defiled, as though he lost his life here on earth in its most hideous form, which is being slain by the sword, and loses his other life by being counted with the defiled.
Thus all greatness is lost, and all glory vanishes, and the soul is deprived of the fruit of the divine grace that was offered to it freely! This is the work of pride!
Take pride away from me!
* Pharaoh of Egypt did not learn from the king of Assyria, the lofty cedar tree, which became cast on the ground.
Instead of sheltering the fowls of heaven and shading the beasts of the field, it became dry and worthless!
* Take pride away from me, O Teacher of humility!
Teach me to be planted by the waters of Your grace in Your paradise, and to bear the fruit of the true Spirit!
* I confess to You my sin and my weakness, and I thank You for the riches of Your grace in my life!
All good in me is from You, O Maker of good things.

1 And it came to pass in the twelfth year, in the twelfth month, in the first day of the month, that the word of the LORD came unto me, saying, 2 "Son of man, take up a lamentation for Pharaoh king of Egypt, and say unto him, Thou art like a young lion of the nations, and thou art as a crocodile in the seas: and thou camest forth with thy rivers, and troubledst the waters with thy feet, and fouledst their rivers. 3 Thus saith the Lord GOD; I will therefore spread out my net over thee with a company of many people; and they shall bring thee up in my net. 4 Then will I leave thee upon the land, I will cast thee forth upon the open field, and will cause all the fowls of the heaven to remain upon thee, and I will fill the beasts of the whole earth with thee. 5 And I will lay thy flesh upon the mountains, and fill the valleys with thy carcasses. 6 I will also water with thy blood the land wherein thou swimmest, even to the mountains; and the horizons shall be full of thee. 7 And when I shall put thee out, I will cover the heaven, and make the stars thereof dark; I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon shall not give her light. 8 All the bright lights of heaven will I make dark over thee, and set darkness upon thy land, saith the Lord GOD. 9 I will also vex the hearts of many people, when I shall bring thy destruction among the nations, into the countries which thou hast not known. 10 Yea, I will make many people amazed at thee, and their kings shall be horribly afraid for thee, when I shall brandish my sword before them; and they shall tremble at every moment, every man for his own life, in the day of thy fall."

The last lamentation begins with Pharaoh, then his multitude, then the nations that imitated him or relied upon him. This lamentation came about two months after the news of the capture of Jerusalem reached the prophet Ezekiel and the men of the captivity.

The lamentation began thus: He said to him, "Thou art like a young lion (a lion) of the nations, and thou art as a crocodile in the seas" [2]. He imagined himself a lion protecting the nations from the king of Babylon, and did not realize that he was merely a crocodile confined to his river, unable to go out of the land of Egypt to rescue Jerusalem or any other city from the hands of Babylon. He thought himself able to deliver, and so he stirred up the king of Judah; and when Jerusalem was besieged he could not save her. He became like one who troubles the waters with his feet, so that he neither rests nor leaves others at rest. This is "the great crocodile that lieth in the midst of his rivers" (Ezek 29:3).

In chapter 29 the great crocodile boasted of himself, saying: "My river is mine own, and I have made it for myself" (Ezek 29:3, 9). This arrogant spirit did not destroy the crocodile alone, but destroyed the fish that clung to his scales as well. He flowed forth with the rivers of his pride over the rivers of others and fouled them with his feet [2]. Therefore his judgment became harsh and bitter, bringing death upon others also. For the Lord spread His net to catch this crocodile together with the fish, the many (peoples) who imitated him or clung to his scales (Ezek 32:3; 29:4).

entries.section: The chastisements of the Lord are:

paragraphs.text: a. He repeats the same punishment mentioned in chapter 29. He brings him out of his river, the object of his boasting and arrogance, and casts him upon dry land to die with the fish that cling to him, and to become prey for the fowls of heaven and the beasts of the field.

entries.section: The chastisements of the Lord are:

paragraphs.text: b. Since this great crocodile prides himself on his Nile and the flood that it brings, which gives fertility to the land and enriches him with good things, therefore, instead of the flood of water, God floods the land with the blood of the crocodile until it reaches the mountains and the valleys are filled with it [6]. Pride turns the water into blood, and the blood of the proud man is poured out, bearing the smell of death which all loathe: the high mountains as well as the low valleys. Instead of words of boasting that draw many to take refuge in him, the smell of death rises, and all turn away from him.

entries.section: The chastisements of the Lord are:

paragraphs.text: c. When his blood goes out of him, this great crocodile becomes a stinking carcass cast upon the mountains and in the valleys. Having thought himself a support for others, he becomes a burden of stench which everyone wants to be rid of. He makes him and those around him "captives" in lands they do not know [9].

d. His judgment does not stop at his own destruction, the destruction of the peoples that clung to him, the turning of the river waters into deadly blood, and his becoming a burden from whose stinking carcass the mountains and valleys want to be rid. Rather, the effect of his pride reaches to the sun and the moon and the other stars, for it is said: "And when I shall put thee out, I will cover the heaven, and make the stars thereof dark; I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon shall not give her light. All the bright lights of heaven will I make dark over thee, and set darkness upon thy land, saith the Lord GOD" [7-8].

This is a bitter picture of the signs of the end as the Lord Christ Himself proclaimed them (Mt 24:29), and of the signs of the false christ (Rev 8:12). It is as though the judgment of the proud man is a pledge of the great judgment, and a shadow of the age of the Antichrist!

What are these heavens whose light is covered, if not man's loss of every heavenly thought and his failure to taste eternal life? What are these stars that are darkened, if not the inner spiritual powers and the senses of the body? Instead of being the secret of inner enlightenment by the Holy Spirit, they become the secret of the soul's darkness and ruin. He covers the sun with a cloud, for the soul no longer sees its Christ, the Sun of Righteousness, shining within it; and the moon does not give her light, for the life of the Church, with its worship and its preaching, has no effect upon it. As for the land over which darkness is set, it is the body of man, which, instead of being a holy temple enlightened by the Lord, becomes a place of darkness.

In short, pride destroys man utterly. It deprives him of Christ, the Sun of Righteousness, and of the Church, the shining moon; it shatters his inner powers, corrupts his heart and his body, and darkens all his thoughts! Heaven and earth become dark for him, the sun and the moon as though they did not exist, and the stars fall within him.

entries.section: The chastisements of the Lord are:

paragraphs.text: e. In the face of this total ruin of soul and body, of mind and heart, a state of terror and trembling spreads among the many peoples with their kings, for it is said: "Yea, I will make many people amazed at thee, and their kings shall be horribly afraid for thee, when I shall brandish my sword before them; and they shall tremble at every moment, every man for his own life, in the day of thy fall" [10]. The destruction of the proud terrifies the hearts of sinners, for they feel that their own judgment has drawn near.

11 "For thus saith the Lord GOD; The sword of the king of Babylon shall come upon thee. 12 By the swords of the mighty will I cause thy multitude to fall, the terrible of the nations, all of them: and they shall spoil the pomp of Egypt, and all the multitude thereof shall be destroyed. 13 I will destroy also all the beasts thereof from beside the great waters; neither shall the foot of man trouble them any more, nor the hoofs of beasts trouble them. 14 Then will I make their waters deep, and cause their rivers to run like oil, saith the Lord GOD. 15 When I shall make the land of Egypt desolate, and the country shall be destitute of that whereof it was full, when I shall smite all them that dwell therein, then shall they know that I am the LORD. 16 This is the lamentation wherewith they shall lament her: the daughters of the nations shall lament her: they shall lament for her, even for Egypt, and for all her multitude, saith the Lord GOD."

The chastisement does not stop at Pharaoh, but reaches his multitude, who fall by the swords of the mighty men of the king of Babylon. The pride of Pharaoh, of his multitude and of his animals is shaken.

If Pharaoh represents the proud soul, then his multitude represents the powers of the soul, which work either for its building up or for its pulling down, while his animals signify the body with its senses and powers. Destruction embraces man with all his capacities, those of the soul and those of the body together.
As for the great waters that are dried up, they are God's gifts and free graces, which God withdraws from the arrogant soul.

entries.section: 3. Lamentation over Pharaoh with the nations:

paragraphs.text: 17 It came to pass also in the twelfth year, in the fifteenth day of the month, that the word of the LORD came unto me, saying, 18 "Son of man, wail for the multitude of Egypt, and cast them down, even her, and the daughters of the famous nations, unto the nether parts of the earth, with them that go down into the pit. 19 Whom dost thou pass in beauty? go down, and be thou laid with the uncircumcised. 20 They shall fall in the midst of them that are slain by the sword: she is delivered to the sword: draw her and all her multitudes. 21 The strong among the mighty shall speak to him out of the midst of hell with them that help him: they are gone down, they lie uncircumcised, slain by the sword. 22 Asshur is there and all her company: his graves are about him: all of them slain, fallen by the sword: 23 Whose graves are set in the sides of the pit, and her company is round about her grave: all of them slain, fallen by the sword, which caused terror in the land of the living. 24 There is Elam and all her multitude round about her grave, all of them slain, fallen by the sword, which are gone down uncircumcised into the nether parts of the earth, which caused their terror in the land of the living; yet have they borne their shame with them that go down to the pit. 25 They have set her a bed in the midst of the slain with all her multitude: her graves are round about him: all of them uncircumcised, slain by the sword: though their terror was caused in the land of the living, yet have they borne their shame with them that go down to the pit: he is put in the midst of them that be slain. 26 There is Meshech, Tubal, and all her multitude: her graves are round about him: all of them uncircumcised, slain by the sword, though they caused their terror in the land of the living. 27 And they shall not lie with the mighty that are fallen of the uncircumcised, which are gone down to hell with their weapons of war: and they have laid their swords under their heads, but their iniquities shall be upon their bones, though they were the terror of the mighty in the land of the living. 28 Yea, thou shalt be broken in the midst of the uncircumcised, and shalt lie with them that are slain with the sword. 29 There is Edom, her kings, and all her princes, which with their might are laid by them that were slain by the sword: they shall lie with the uncircumcised, and with them that go down to the pit. 30 There be the princes of the north, all of them, and all the Zidonians, which are gone down with the slain; with their terror they are ashamed of their might; and they lie uncircumcised with them that be slain by the sword, and bear their shame with them that go down to the pit. 31 Pharaoh shall see them, and shall be comforted over all his multitude, even Pharaoh and all his army slain by the sword, saith the Lord GOD. 32 For I have caused my terror in the land of the living: and he shall be laid in the midst of the uncircumcised with them that are slain with the sword, even Pharaoh and all his multitude, saith the Lord GOD."

entries.section: 3. Lamentation over Pharaoh with the nations:

paragraphs.text: At the end of the prophecy against Pharaoh and his multitude, he joined with him in the lamentation "the daughters of the famous nations" [18], declaring that they should wail over them together with Pharaoh's multitude, because all of them have gone down to the nether parts of the earth with them that go down into the pit. Perhaps by those daughters he meant the nations that were bound to Pharaoh and his army and his authority, as women are bound to their men and seek their protection...

It is the end of the multitude of the nations to go down into the lower pit, into hell, as slain men cast down with the uncircumcised. This expression is repeated many times in this section [19, 25, 27, 29, 30, 31]. They were like mighty men who had terror and dread in the land of the living, and they went down with their uncleanness (the uncircumcised) as slain men cast down in hell.

entries.section: 3. Lamentation over Pharaoh with the nations:

paragraphs.text: Living examples were set before Pharaoh and his multitude of great nations that were like mighty men in the land of the living and ended up cast down like the uncircumcised, slain by the sword, going down to hell, such as Asshur [22], Elam [24], Meshech and Tubal [26], Edom [29] and all the Zidonians [30].

We have already spoken about these lands or kingdoms, except Elam, which is named after Elam son of Shem (Gen 10:22). In the days of Abraham, Chedorlaomer king of Elam was the leader of the kings of the East who invaded the Jordan region (Gen 14:1-11). The borders of this kingdom lay beyond the river Tigris, east of the kingdom of Babylon, south of Assyria and Media, north of the Persian Gulf, and west of Persia. Its capital was Shushan (Susa), and for that reason the Elamites were called Shushanchites. In the eighth century B.C. the kings of Assyria defeated Elam and took its men as mercenary soldiers in their army, and they took part in the attack on Jerusalem (Isa 22:6). The Medes (the Persians) annexed it to their empire and made it one of their provinces, and in consideration of its standing they made Shushan their capital (Dan 8:2). The Elamites were among the peoples who were carried to Samaria to dwell there after the captivity of Judah, and when the Jews returned from the captivity, the remnant of these immigrants were among those who opposed the idea of rebuilding the Temple (Ezra 4:9). Around 200 B.C. the Elamites regained their strength, and some of their kings gained power over cities in Babylon. Today Elam is part of Iran, called the province of Khuzestan.
Make me a lion's whelp, not a crocodile!
* Pharaoh put on the skin of a lion's whelp to protect the nations, and behold, he is a crocodile who devours the nations like the fish around him!

* With an arrogant spirit he claimed that he had made the Nile of Egypt with his own hands, and he did not know that by his pride he had fouled the waters of the Nile with his feet; he neither rested nor let the nations around him rest!
* Because of him the heavens covered their lights, and the earth was in darkness!
His soul (the heaven) was corrupted, and also his body (the earth)!
* Make me, O Lord, a lion's whelp, a son to You, O Lion that came out of the midst of Judah!
Grant me humility, that I may not trouble the water of grace in my heart!
Shine with Your light within me, O Sun of Righteousness, that my soul may shine like a new heaven!
And let my body be sanctified like a new earth!

1 Again the word of the LORD came unto me, saying, 2 "Son of man, speak to the children of thy people, and say unto them, When I bring the sword upon a land, if the people of the land take a man of their coasts, and set him for their watchman: 3 If when he seeth the sword come upon the land, he blow the trumpet, and warn the people; 4 Then whosoever heareth the sound of the trumpet, and taketh not warning; if the sword come, and take him away, his blood shall be upon his own head. 5 He heard the sound of the trumpet, and took not warning; his blood shall be upon him. But he that taketh warning shall deliver his soul. 6 But if the watchman see the sword come, and blow not the trumpet, and the people be not warned; if the sword come, and take any person from among them, he is taken away in his iniquity; but his blood will I require at the watchman's hand. 7 So thou, O son of man, I have set thee a watchman unto the house of Israel; therefore thou shalt hear the word at my mouth, and warn them from me. 8 When I say unto the wicked, O wicked man, thou shalt surely die; if thou dost not speak to warn the wicked from his way, that wicked man shall die in his iniquity; but his blood will I require at thine hand. 9 Nevertheless, if thou warn the wicked of his way to turn from it; if he do not turn from his way, he shall die in his iniquity; but thou hast delivered thy soul."

Before we speak of his responsibility, we would like to clarify that the Lord's address to him was thus: "Speak to the children of thy people" [2]. He did not say to him "the children of My people"; and likewise He says "as my people" [31], that is, as though they were My people. For since they had not yet enjoyed reconciliation with God, God does not call them "My people." This is what we saw in our study of the Book of Exodus: when God is in a state of reconciliation with His people, He says, "My people, My sabbaths, My feasts, My incense, My offerings..." attributing to Himself personally the people and all their worship, their feasts and their offerings. But in a state of grief on their account He says to the prophet "thy people," as He says to them "your feasts, your sabbaths, your offerings," and so on...

God had begun this group of prophecies and commandments with an indirect rebuke, saying to them: I can no longer call you My people... You are the people of Ezekiel, as though you were My people. Accept My commandment and enter into repentance, and I shall make you a people for Myself and I shall be a God to you; or as He said by the mouth of the prophet Ezekiel: "My dwelling place also shall be over them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people" (Ezek 37:27).

He then spoke of his responsibility as a watchman, bound to be frank for the salvation of their souls and the salvation of his own soul; for if he stops proclaiming the message out of courtesy to them, every soul that perishes will be required of him... "But if the watchman see the sword come, and blow not the trumpet, and the people be not warned; if the sword come, and take any person from among them, he is taken away in his iniquity; but his blood will I require at the watchman's hand" [6]. These words still terrify every bishop, priest or deacon... for if they neglect to warn the people, whatever their circumstances or positions, their own souls will be required in place of the souls that perish... We have already given examples of this.
The following are some comments of the Fathers on the responsibility of the watchmen and their obligation to warn sinners and not to be silent:

*According to what is written in Ezekiel, the watchmen must not keep silent about vice while the sword hangs over them, for this silence profits neither them nor the sinners; rather, they ought to watch and warn. In this those who give the warning are profited, though the two are not profited together, the speaker and the hearer.

St. Gregory of Nazianzus *The first thing I do is to present to my people a report that I draw from above, that I may fulfil my work as a watchman (Isa 21:6; 62:6; Hab 2:1). If I do not stop the coming of the sword, I save my own soul and the souls of those who hear me, by proclaiming the disobedience of my people, counting what belongs to them as belonging to me. In this I obtain some rest and tenderness.
St. Gregory of Nazianzus *The watchmen and overseers were set in the Church over the people in order to rebuke sin without mercy.

St. Augustine *What kind of blood does God require at the hand of the watchman, if not that which is poured out from the sinner? For thus the heart of the fool perishes, for it is said: "Hearken unto me, ye that have lost your hearts," since they poured out the blood and lost the strength of the living soul.

Origen *If you were entrusted with guarding a spring of pure water for the flock, and saw the flock drinking mud, would you not work to remove the mud from the water? But now you are not tending a spring of water but of blood and spirit. If you see one in whom there is sin, which is more dangerous than dust and mud, and he comes to it, will you not grieve? Will you not prevent him? What excuse have you? For God has given you this honor for this purpose, that you may distinguish these things. This is your office; here is your peace, and here is your crown, not merely that you wear a shining white garment!
St. John Chrysostom

entries.section: 2. We do not despair, for God is merciful:

paragraphs.text: 10 "Therefore, O thou son of man, speak unto the house of Israel; Thus ye speak, saying, If our transgressions and our sins be upon us, and we pine away in them, how should we then live? 11 Say unto them, As I live, saith the Lord GOD, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live: turn ye, turn ye from your evil ways; for why will ye die, O house of Israel?"

If the prophet was bound to be perfectly frank in proclaiming the divine commandment and the prophecies, without flattery or courtesy, for the salvation of their souls and of his own soul as well, this does not mean that he should be harsh with them. If he had spoken violently before, it was because the danger of the captivity was coming; but now that the captivity has actually taken place and all have come under the bitterness of the bitter cup, there is no need for despair; rather, the proclamation of God's mercies and His love for mankind begins, even in the midst of His harsh chastisements.
"Thus ye speak, saying,
If our transgressions and our sins be upon us, and we pine away in them, how should we then live?
Say unto them,
As I live, saith the Lord GOD, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live:
turn ye, turn ye from your evil ways; for why will ye die, O house of Israel?" [10-11].

Formerly they drank iniquity like water, making light of sin and its power in their lives; and when they began to fall under chastisement in earnest, they were assailed by despair, saying that they were pining away, that is, perishing, so how could they live after that...? But the Lord, who rebuked them bitterly before the chastisement, now soothes them with love, lest they be crushed by the cutting off of hope.
The Fathers comment on these divine words that give hope as follows:
*Through these divine words the sinner returns to hope, but there is also another snare which he fears, namely that through this very hope he sins all the more (making light of sin).
St. Augustine *Let him love, because God desires mercy rather than sacrifice (Hos 6:6), and let him fear, because He hates sin!
Let him love, for God desires the repentance of the sinner and not his death, and let him fear, for He hates the sinners who do not repent!
Tertullian *It is the mission of the Savior to call sinners, not the righteous, for, as He Himself said: "They that be whole need not a physician" (Mt 9:12-13).
He desires the repentance of the sinner and not his death (Ezek 33:11), and He carries on His shoulders the poor lost sheep. And thus when the prodigal son returned, his father received him with joy.
St. Jerome

entries.section: 3. God does not reckon with us for our past:

paragraphs.text: 12 "Therefore, thou son of man, say unto the children of thy people, The righteousness of the righteous shall not deliver him in the day of his transgression: as for the wickedness of the wicked, he shall not fall thereby in the day that he turneth from his wickedness; neither shall the righteous be able to live for his righteousness in the day that he sinneth. 13 When I shall say to the righteous, that he shall surely live; if he trust to his own righteousness, and commit iniquity, all his righteousnesses shall not be remembered; but for his iniquity that he hath committed, he shall die for it. 14 Again, when I say unto the wicked, Thou shalt surely die; if he turn from his sin, and do that which is lawful and right; 15 If the wicked restore the pledge, give again that he had robbed, walk in the statutes of life, without committing iniquity; he shall surely live, he shall not die. 16 None of his sins that he hath committed shall be mentioned unto him: he hath done that which is lawful and right; he shall surely live. 17 Yet the children of thy people say, The way of the Lord is not equal: but as for them, their way is not equal. 18 When the righteous turneth from his righteousness, and committeth iniquity, he shall even die thereby. 19 But if the wicked turn from his wickedness, and do that which is lawful and right, he shall live thereby. 20 Yet ye say, The way of the Lord is not equal. O ye house of Israel, I will judge you every one after his ways."

When the Lord opens to us the door of hope, He wants us to enter it with all strength and without fear, and so He offers us every assurance. He does not reckon with us for our past, nor even for our present, if we now offer sincere repentance. He does not desire our destruction, but seeks our salvation by every way, offering us every possibility of returning to Him. At the same time, since God fears for His children who stand lest they fall, He warns them not to rely on their past, lest they become careless and fall...

St. Jerome says: [In the life of Christians we look not at the beginnings but at the ends. Paul began in a bad way, but his end was good. The beginning of Judas was worthy of praise, but his end was blameworthy because of his betrayal...

The life of the Christian is the true ladder of Jacob, upon which the angels ascend and descend, while the Lord stands upon it, stretching out His hands to those who slip, supporting them, and looking upon those who ascend the painful steps].

We saw in our interpretation of chapter eighteen how Origen used it to answer those who speak of a difference of human natures, showing that the wicked can repent and the righteous can fall... For some thought that man has a good or an evil nature that cannot be changed. Among his words: [The soul of the righteous man is subject to change, as Ezekiel testifies, saying that the righteous man can forsake the commandments of God, and his former righteousness is not reckoned to him].
If the righteous man turns back from his righteous life in the Lord he dies, while if the wicked man repents of his wickedness he finds the life in Christ taking him up.
"When the righteous turneth from his righteousness, and committeth iniquity, he shall even die thereby.

entries.section: 3. God does not reckon with us for our past:

paragraphs.text: But if the wicked turn from his wickedness, and do that which is lawful and right, he shall live thereby" [18-19].

entries.section: 3. God does not reckon with us for our past:

paragraphs.text: Let us therefore beware of sin lest we die; and if we have died by it, let us receive the Lord our righteousness and live by Him. St. Ambrose says: [Everyone who gives himself up to evil pleasures is dead, for "she that liveth in pleasure is dead while she liveth" (1 Tim 5:6), and those who are without faith go down to hell while they are still alive, even if they seem to be alive with us, for they are in hell. Everyone who takes usury or commits theft is not living, as you read in Ezekiel. But if that man keeps the commandments of the Lord to do them, he lives, and he lives by them [19]... Let us then hasten to that life, for whoever touches Life lives. And the woman truly touched it, she who touched the hem of His garment and was healed, and was freed from death, and it was said to her: "Thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace" (Lk 8:48; Mt 9:22). If he that touches a dead body is unclean, then he who touched the Living One is truly saved. Let us then seek this Living One, but take care not to seek Him among the dead, lest it be said to us as to the women: "Why seek ye the living among the dead? He is not here, but is risen" (Lk 24:5-6).

21 And it came to pass in the twelfth year of our captivity, in the tenth month, in the fifth day of the month, that one that had escaped out of Jerusalem came unto me, saying, "The city is smitten." 22 Now the hand of the LORD was upon me in the evening, afore he that was escaped came; and had opened my mouth, until he came to me in the morning; and my mouth was opened, and I was no more dumb. 23 Then the word of the LORD came unto me, saying, 24 "Son of man, they that inhabit those wastes of the land of Israel speak, saying, Abraham was one, and he inherited the land: but we are many; the land is given us for inheritance. 25 Wherefore say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Ye eat with the blood, and lift up your eyes toward your idols, and shed blood: and shall ye possess the land? 26 Ye stand upon your sword, ye work abomination, and ye defile every one his neighbour's wife: and shall ye possess the land? 27 Say thou thus unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD; As I live, surely they that are in the wastes shall fall by the sword, and him that is in the open field will I give to the beasts to be devoured, and they that be in the forts and in the caves shall die of the pestilence. 28 For I will lay the land most desolate, and the pomp of her strength shall cease; and the mountains of Israel shall be desolate, that none shall pass through. 29 Then shall they know that I am the LORD, when I have laid the land most desolate because of all their abominations which they have committed."

A man from Jerusalem was able to escape when the city was smitten and to run to where the prophet Ezekiel and the captive people were, to tell them of the smiting of Jerusalem. This was in the twelfth year of the first captivity of Judah, in the tenth month, on the fifth day of the month; that is, the news reached them after about six months. Here his mouth was opened to speak and Ezekiel was no longer silent [22], since all heard the truth of his prophecies which he had declared to them before.

They had said to him before that if God gave all this land as an inheritance to Abraham, who was one man, would He not give them this land, they being many? [24] How far are God's measures from man's! God looks upon the heart and gives generously to the pure heart, even if it is unique in the world, and does not give on account of multitude. Man, however, looks not to purity of heart but to abundance of number. They thought that God would never forsake the city or the Temple, whatever abominations they committed, so long as they offered Him sacrifices and offerings, even if their hearts were devoted to idols and turned aside to evil. God desires pure worship, not an abundance of ordinances and formalism in worship! Abraham, the obedient believer, was worthy to inherit all this land, while among those myriads of his descendants at that time there was found none worthy of the inheritance!!! How much the Church needs true saints in whose hearts God may rest, even if their numbers are very few! Therefore the word of God came to the prophet Ezekiel that they should be purified and so inherit the land. In other words, that they should become like Abraham their father and so be worthy to inherit him!
This is repentance... It is a return to the holy, hidden life!

entries.section: 5. A return of the heart, not of form:

paragraphs.text: 30 "Also, thou son of man, the children of thy people still are talking against thee by the walls and in the doors of the houses, and speak one to another, every one to his brother, saying, Come, I pray you, and hear what is the word that cometh forth from the LORD. 31 And they come unto thee as the people cometh, and they sit before thee as my people, and they hear thy words, but they will not do them: for with their mouth they shew much love, but their heart goeth after their covetousness. 32 And, lo, thou art unto them as a very lovely song of one that hath a pleasant voice, and can play well on an instrument: for they hear thy words, but they do them not. 33 And when this cometh to pass, (lo, it will come,) then shall they know that a prophet hath been among them."

When the news arrived, crowds flocked to Ezekiel to listen to him. They had come to know that he spoke only the truth. Perhaps they also flocked to him in great numbers and with longing because, after he had been speaking to them words of rebuke and repentance before the fall of Jerusalem, he began to speak of vengeance on the wicked who rejoiced at their fall (Ezek 25-32) and to give hope of return and restoration. Perhaps, too, they came to him to listen to his wonderful literary style.

entries.section: 5. A return of the heart, not of form:

paragraphs.text: The prophet feared that they would come to him to listen merely for intellectual pleasure or passing delight, and not for sincere repentance, for the Lord said to him: "They come unto thee as the people cometh, and they sit before thee as my people, and they hear thy words, but they will not do them: for with their mouth they shew much love, but their heart goeth after their covetousness" [31]. His words became like measured poetry presented in a beautiful voice to the tunes of music, which they enjoy for a while and do not do! God does not want mere enjoyment; He wants action... sincere repentance that comes from the heart, and that is practical!
Take away from me the spirit of failure!
* How wonderful You are, O Lord, in Your plan toward us!

You permitted harsh chastisement for the people, even to the Babylonian captivity, and You threatened to destroy the holy city Jerusalem and its Temple, and You asked Your prophet, as a watchman, to speak the truth even if it wounds!
And yet, in spite of all this, when the people were taken captive, You take despair away from them!
You urge them to sincere repentance filled with hope!
* Behold, I am in Your hands, O Savior of my soul!
Who can rescue me from the feeling of failure but You!
In Your chastisement of me, hold my depths that they may not collapse!
Reveal Yourself within me, that my soul may not be shattered!
Make me repent, and support me with the spirit of hope!
*You, my Lord, care for the heart and not the form!
You seek one holy heart like the heart of Abraham, better than many who mix truth with falsehood!
Sanctify us! Count us the few holy ones for Yourself!
Take over my heart, my mind and my feelings!
Take over my body and my conduct!
I am in Your hands; I ask for the work of Your Holy Spirit in me!

1 And the word of the LORD came unto me, saying, 2 "Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel, prophesy, and say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD unto the shepherds; Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! should not the shepherds feed the flocks? 3 Ye eat the fat, and ye clothe you with the wool, ye kill them that are fed: but ye feed not the flock. 4 The diseased have ye not strengthened, neither have ye healed that which was sick, neither have ye bound up that which was broken, neither have ye brought again that which was driven away, neither have ye sought that which was lost; but with force and with cruelty have ye ruled them. 5 And they were scattered, because there is no shepherd: and they became meat to all the beasts of the field, when they were scattered. 6 My sheep wandered through all the mountains, and upon every high hill: yea, my flock was scattered upon all the face of the earth, and none did search or seek after them. 7 Therefore, ye shepherds, hear the word of the LORD; 8 As I live, saith the Lord GOD, surely because my flock became a prey, and my flock became meat to every beast of the field, because there was no shepherd, neither did my shepherds search for my flock, but the shepherds fed themselves, and fed not my flock; 9 Therefore, O ye shepherds, hear the word of the LORD; 10 Thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I am against the shepherds; and I will require my flock at their hand, and cause them to cease from feeding the flock; neither shall the shepherds feed themselves any more; for I will deliver my flock from their mouth, that they may not be meat for them."
"Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves.
Should not the shepherds feed the flocks?!
Ye eat the fat, and ye clothe you with the wool, ye kill them that are fed: but ye feed not the flock.

The diseased have ye not strengthened, neither have ye healed that which was sick, neither have ye bound up that which was broken, neither have ye brought again that which was driven away, neither have ye sought that which was lost; but with force and with cruelty have ye ruled them" [2-4]. When the heart of the shepherd turns away from the people of God to himself, he tends his own interests; he works for the sake of his own honor or possessions or bodily comfort, and so on... instead of caring for their needs and interests. He does not care for the sick, or the wounded, or the broken, or the driven away, or the lost, but cares for his selfishness. Such a one is not counted a shepherd but a hireling, who seeks the wage and not sonship; and sometimes he is counted a thief who steals the flock instead of guarding and supporting it.
*There are hirelings who work in the Church, of whom the Apostle Paul says: "For all seek their own, not the things which are Jesus Christ's" (Phil 2:21).

What does "seek their own" mean? That they do not love Christ freely. They do not seek the things that are God's but seek temporal benefits; they gape for gain and are fond of seeking honor from men. Whenever any overseer desires such things and serves God in order to obtain them, then whoever this man may be, he is counted a hireling and cannot count himself among the sons, because of such men the Lord also said: "Verily I say unto you, They have their reward" (Mt 6:5)...

There are hirelings among us also, but the Lord alone separates them; He who knows the hearts separates them, though we are sometimes able to know them, for the Lord did not speak in vain in His discourse about the wolves: "Ye shall know them by their fruits" (Mt 6:17).

St. Augustine The shepherd's love of himself deprives him of the tender fatherhood that is gentle with the weak, and turns him not only into a hireling but into a violent tyrant, who loses his fatherhood and opens the door to tyranny. This violence drives the people to be scattered, so that they become a prey to all the beasts of the field [5], for they wander "through all the mountains, and upon every high hill, and upon all the face of the earth" [6].

Man becomes a prey to every kind of demon that devours the sheep of God because of the neglect of the shepherds and their preoccupation with themselves. Then the flock walks without aim or shelter, moving from mountain to mountain, from hill to hill, and from place to place, without discernment, wisdom or knowledge. The demons play with it, handing it over from one to another until it is utterly crushed.
"Behold, I am against the shepherds; and I will require my flock at their hand" [10].
Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles, says:

[Since the Lord has appointed us to steer the ship of His Church, may we, with His help and by the guidance of the two Testaments, govern the ship of His Church so that it may not turn aside to the right or to the left through our neglect, but may remain effortlessly in the straight course of life amid the great perils of this world. And just as no ship can gain earthly profits without hardships, so the ship of the Church cannot enjoy the gains and the joy of eternal things without many hardships].

The Lord cries out, saying: "Ye shepherds... my flock became a prey" [7-8], laying the responsibility upon them, since they became the means of crushing and destroying souls instead of being a refuge and a shelter for them from the ravening wolves.

Pope Athanasius the Apostolic wrote to Bishop Dracontium laying upon him the pastoral responsibility, saying to him: [Before you received the grace of the episcopate no one knew you, but you have become the one from whom the people expect to be given food, that is, the teachings of the Holy Scriptures. When they expect that and suffer hunger while you alone are filled, our Lord Jesus Christ will come and you will stand before Him; what defense will you offer when He finds His flock hungry?].

Sometimes it does not stop at their drinking the sweet waters alone or devouring spiritual food without their people; rather, what is more bitter is that in their selfishness they sometimes keep the deep waters for themselves, drinking from them, and do not leave even the shallow waters to their people, but foul them with their feet and offer them full of mud:

"Seemeth it a small thing unto you to have eaten up the good pasture, but ye must tread down with your feet the residue of your pastures? and to have drunk of the deep waters, but ye must foul the residue with your feet? And as for my flock, they eat that which ye have trodden with your feet; and they drink that which ye have fouled with your feet" [18-19]. St. Jerome sees that it is the muddy feet of the heretics that trouble the clear waters and corrupt the faith of the flock.

11 For thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I, even I, will both search my sheep, and seek them out. 12 As a shepherd seeketh out his flock in the day that he is among his sheep that are scattered; so will I seek out my sheep, and will deliver them out of all places where they have been scattered in the cloudy and dark day. 13 And I will bring them out from the people, and gather them from the countries, and will bring them to their own land, and feed them upon the mountains of Israel by the rivers, and in all the inhabited places of the country. 14 I will feed them in a good pasture, and upon the high mountains of Israel shall their fold be: there shall they lie in a good fold, and in a fat pasture shall they feed upon the mountains of Israel. 15 I will feed my flock, and I will cause them to lie down, saith the Lord GOD. 16 I will seek that which was lost, and bring again that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken, and will strengthen that which was sick: but I will destroy the fat and the strong; I will feed them with judgment. 17 And as for you, O my flock, thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I judge between cattle and cattle, between the rams and the he goats. 18 Seemeth it a small thing unto you to have eaten up the good pasture, but ye must tread down with your feet the residue of your pastures? and to have drunk of the deep waters, but ye must foul the residue with your feet? 19 And as for my flock, they eat that which ye have trodden with your feet; and they drink that which ye have fouled with your feet. 20 "Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD unto them; Behold, I, even I, will judge between the fat cattle and between the lean cattle. 21 Because ye have thrust with side and with shoulder, and pushed all the diseased with your horns, till ye have scattered them abroad; 22 Therefore will I save my flock, and they shall no more be a prey; and I will judge between cattle and cattle."

"Behold, I, even I, will both search my sheep, and seek them out" [11]. Nothing is more precious to God than the human soul, which He brought into being in His image and likeness. If He has delivered His people into the hands of shepherds, it is only to honor humanity itself, that it may share with God, in His name and by His power, in the shepherding of souls; but God keeps this divine work for Himself, taking pride in it, saying: "Behold, I, even I, will both search my sheep, and seek them out."

In His shepherding of His flock He does not tolerate the selfishness of the shepherds whom He appointed to serve His children, and so He stands Himself against them, counting every neglect or fault in shepherding as aimed at Him personally. He reassures every soul that the shepherds have exploited or neglected, saying: "Behold, I am against the shepherds; and I will require my flock at their hand, and cause them to cease from feeding the flock; neither shall the shepherds feed themselves any more; for I will deliver my flock from their mouth, that they may not be meat for them" [10]. He stands against them and takes over the shepherding Himself! He delights to call Himself "Shepherd," repeating the words "my flock" 14 times in this chapter, affirming that they are His people, for when He says "my people" they are His; He delivers them from the evil shepherds as He delivers them from the enemy outside, and takes their life into His own hands.

If the shepherds have preyed upon the flock, the Great Shepherd takes over His flock to judge for the weak flock against the violent shepherds: "Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD unto them; Behold, I, even I, will judge between the fat cattle (the tyrannical shepherd) and between the lean cattle (the poor flock)... Therefore will I save my flock, and they shall no more be a prey; and I will judge between cattle and cattle" [20-22]. All are equal before Me, shepherds and flock; I judge them all and judge between them, between cattle and cattle!

Thus the successful servant is the one who always lifts his eyes to the coming of the Great Shepherd, who will judge all without distinction. He does not show partiality nor care for honors; on the contrary, the one to whom more is given will be judged more and be required of more! The faithful servant is also the one who is always hidden in the Good Shepherd, so that he serves only through the one Shepherd, and works only by Him according to His divine mind. In this the servant is not puffed up against those he serves, nor does he think himself better than his brethren.

entries.section: 3. The rise of a new shepherding:

paragraphs.text: 23 "And I will set up one shepherd over them, and he shall feed them, even my servant David; he shall feed them, and he shall be their shepherd. 24 And I the LORD will be their God, and my servant David a prince among them; I the LORD have spoken it. 25 And I will make with them a covenant of peace, and will cause the evil beasts to cease out of the land: and they shall dwell safely in the wilderness, and sleep in the woods. 26 And I will make them and the places round about my hill a blessing; and I will cause the shower to come down in his season; there shall be showers of blessing. 27 And the tree of the field shall yield her fruit, and the earth shall yield her increase, and they shall be safe in their land, and shall know that I am the LORD, when I have broken the bands of their yoke, and delivered them out of the hand of those that served themselves of them. 28 And they shall no more be a prey to the heathen, neither shall the beast of the land devour them; but they shall dwell safely, and none shall make them afraid. 29 And I will raise up for them a plant of renown, and they shall be no more consumed with hunger in the land, neither bear the shame of the heathen any more. 30 Thus shall they know that I the LORD their God am with them, and that they, even the house of Israel, are my people, saith the Lord GOD. 31 And ye my flock, the flock of my pasture, are men, and I am your God, saith the Lord GOD."

Having spoken of God's care for mankind, he proclaimed the summit of this shepherding through "the Lord Christ," the true spiritual King, the Son of David, saying: "And I will set up one shepherd over them, and he shall feed them, even my servant David; he shall feed them, and he shall be their shepherd" [23]. Without doubt "my servant David" does not mean the resurrection of King David from the dead to reign anew, but the appearing of the Lord Christ, the Son of God who became a servant, to reign over us through His love and humility.

On this St. John Chrysostom says: [As for Ezekiel and the other prophets, their speaking of David's coming and rising again does not mean that he is the one who died]. And Origen says: [It is not the patriarch (father) David who rises and rules the saints, but Christ]. St. Augustine also says: [Ezekiel speaks prophetically in the person of God the Father, telling beforehand about the Lord Christ in a prophetic way as "David," who took the form of a servant and became man, He who is the Son of God].
He speaks of this Good Shepherd, the Messiah the Savior, as one who:

entries.section: 3. The rise of a new shepherding:

paragraphs.text: a. Makes a covenant with mankind [25], which He writes not on tablets of stone but engraves in blood upon His holy body with divine love, so that He brings us into His bowels and we receive Him as an eternal Bridegroom.

b. Causes the evil beasts to cease out of the land, so that they dwell safely in the wilderness and sleep in the woods [25]. What are these evil beasts that He causes to cease out of the land if not the works of the old man, full of violence, which are removed from the land of our body so that we live in peace and safety?
Perhaps by the evil beasts He meant the Gentiles, who were like ravening beasts, which receive the faith and turn from their beastly nature to live with a new spirit and a new nature.

entries.section: 3. The rise of a new shepherding:

paragraphs.text: c. Sends down the shower in its season upon the hill about Him [26], which is the descent of the Lord Christ Himself from heaven, refreshing the soul and quenching the fire of its evils.

entries.section: 3. The rise of a new shepherding:

paragraphs.text: d. Gives the tree of the field, which is the Church, its fruit, and the earth yields her increase, so that safety comes upon the land [27]. He plants the tree of the New Covenant in His holy body, and it bears much fruit. He plants us in Him, so that our nature is blessed in Him and the land of our body is in constant safety.

e. Breaks the bands of their yoke and delivers them out of the hand of those that served themselves of them [27]. On the Cross He tears up the handwriting that was against us and frees us from the bondage of Satan, who had dominion over us. As the Apostle says: "Blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us, which was contrary to us, and took it out of the way, nailing it to his cross; and having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it" (Col 2:14-15). Therefore the prophet Ezekiel goes on to affirm, in the words of the Lord Himself: "And they shall no more be a prey to the heathen, neither shall the beast of the land devour them; but they shall dwell safely, and none shall make them afraid" [28]; that is, they will not become the prey of the demons, nor will the beast of the passions of the body (the earth) devour them, but they will be filled with the power of the Holy Spirit, the Giver of comfort and victory.

entries.section: 3. The rise of a new shepherding:

paragraphs.text: f. His work does not stop at breaking the yoke of the bondage of evil and driving out the beastly nature, but He offers the positive side: "I will raise up for them a plant of renown" [29]. He removes the old nature and gives the new nature, which is in His image, to work for man's being satisfied with Him personally.

entries.section: 3. The rise of a new shepherding:

paragraphs.text: g. What the Lord prides Himself upon is that He makes them "His people," and He is their God dwelling in their midst and united with them... "Thus shall they know that I the LORD their God am with them, and that they, even the house of Israel, are my people, saith the Lord GOD. And ye my flock, the flock of my pasture, are men, and I am your God, saith the Lord GOD" [30-31]. This is the conclusion of all His gifts: He comes forth as God to them, and they are His flock, His people; He takes pride in them and they take pride in Him. Therefore St. John the Beloved heard a description of heaven or eternal life thus: "Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men, and he will dwell with them, and they shall be his people, and God himself shall be with them, and be their God" (Rev 21:3).
You are my Shepherd!
*How wonderful You are, my Lord, in Your shepherding of me!
You threaten every selfish shepherd who seeks his own at the expense of Your flock!
You Yourself judge between the violent shepherds and the crushed flock!
*You came to our earth as a good Shepherd, You laid down Yourself for me and for every man!
You opened Your heavens to us as a satisfying pasture!
You surrounded us with Your Holy Spirit as a dew that softens our hearts.
You gave us the fruit of the Spirit in our depths!
*How sweet are Your words! And how mighty!
You speak and You do:
"Behold, I, even I, will both search my sheep, and seek them out...
I will feed them in a good pasture...
I will feed my flock, and I will cause them to lie down...

I will seek that which was lost, and bring again that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken, and will strengthen that which was sick: but I will destroy the fat and the strong; I will feed them with judgment."

1 Moreover the word of the LORD came unto me, saying, 2 "Son of man, set thy face against mount Seir, and prophesy against it, 3 And say unto it, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, O mount Seir, I am against thee, and I will stretch out mine hand against thee, and I will make thee most desolate. 4 I will lay thy cities waste, and thou shalt be desolate, and thou shalt know that I am the LORD. 5 Because thou hast had a perpetual hatred, and hast shed the blood of the children of Israel by the force of the sword in the time of their calamity, in the time that their iniquity had an end: 6 Therefore, as I live, saith the Lord GOD, I will prepare thee unto blood, and blood shall pursue thee: sith thou hast not hated blood, even blood shall pursue thee. 7 Thus will I make mount Seir most desolate, and cut off from it him that passeth out and him that returneth. 8 And I will fill his mountains with his slain men: in thy hills, and in thy valleys, and in all thy rivers, shall they fall that are slain with the sword. 9 I will make thee perpetual desolations, and thy cities shall not return: and ye shall know that I am the LORD. 10 Because thou hast said, These two nations and these two countries shall be mine, and we will possess it; whereas the LORD was there: 11 Therefore, as I live, saith the Lord GOD, I will even do according to thine anger, and according to thine envy which thou hast used out of thy hatred against them; and I will make myself known among them, when I have judged thee. 12 And thou shalt know that I am the LORD, and that I have heard all thy blasphemies which thou hast spoken against the mountains of Israel, saying, They are laid desolate, they are given us to consume. 13 Thus with your mouth ye have boasted against me, and have multiplied your words against me: I have heard them. 14 Thus saith the Lord GOD; When the whole earth rejoiceth, I will make thee desolate. 15 As thou didst rejoice at the inheritance of the house of Israel, because it was desolate, so will I do unto thee: thou shalt be desolate, O mount Seir, and all Idumea, even all of it: and they shall know that I am the LORD."

During the prophecies against the foreign nations that rejoiced at Israel's fall (Ezek 25-33), the prophet Ezekiel prophesied against Seir together with Moab (Ezek 25:8), and also prophesied against Edom, which includes mount Seir within it (Ezek 25:12). Why then did he return to prophesy at some length against Seir while speaking of the inner reformation? 1. We cannot separate the outward work from the inward work. Truly God wanted to prepare the way for the return and the inner reformation, at the level of the people and the shepherds, by tearing down the outward powers of evil; but in actual practice the two reformations are bound together. There is no tearing down of the outward powers of evil without repentance beginning within, and no reformation without the beginning of the tearing down of outward evil. Moreover, every inner reformation stirs up the outward enemy (the devil) and enrages him; therefore Nehemiah built with one hand and held the weapon in the other. So when a man works spiritually he must be watchful against every war that rises against him to destroy him. 2. Perhaps he took care to speak of mount Seir in particular because news reached the captives that the Edomites had gradually infiltrated Judah after the breaking of Jerusalem and occupied it, so the prophet wished to assure them that God would rescue the land from the hands of those who occupied it, especially since the dispute over the land between Israel and Edom was an ancient matter (Gen 27:40). In this he opened a new reason for the reformation, for God intervenes to reform on account of the slanders of the people of Seir, which appears clearly in the following chapter.

The foundations on which the prophecy against them rests are: 1. Hatred: Seir's hatred of the people was an ancient hatred rooted in the depths of their hearts, for He says: "Because thou hast had a perpetual hatred, and hast shed the blood of the children of Israel by the force of the sword in the time of their calamity, in the time that their iniquity had an end" [5]. The hatred did not stop at rejoicing in their calamity but turned into injustice and bloodshed that delivered them to the sword. She loved the ... Therefore blood pursues her, or as the Lord says: "Sith thou hast not hated blood, even blood shall pursue thee" [6].

With the measure that a man measures, it shall be measured to him, and into the pit that he digs for his brother he himself falls; the cross that Haman prepared for Mordecai, he himself was hanged on it. 2. Its seizing of others: "Because thou hast said, These two nations and these two countries shall be mine, and we will possess it; whereas the LORD was there..." [10]. Thus when a man wants to seize a land that is not his own, and to possess what is not his, he does not realize that the invisible God looks and beholds the injustice. She wanted to possess what was not hers, and therefore loses what is hers, for her cities become waste and she becomes desolate [4]. 3. Its arrogance, full of blasphemy: "Thus with your mouth ye have boasted against me, and have multiplied your words against me: I have heard them" [13]. When she wanted to possess what was not hers, the Lord was there, seeing their wickedness; and when she was arrogant in her heart and spoke with her lips against God, God was listening. He has been long-suffering for a long time, but He repays her for her blasphemy. 4. She rejoiced at the harm of Judah on the day of its chastisement: when Judah fell under chastisement she was not admonished but rejoiced in her gloating, and therefore she deserved the wrath of God: "As thou didst rejoice at the inheritance of the house of Israel, because it was desolate, so will I do unto thee: thou shalt be desolate, O mount Seir, and all Idumea, even all of it: and they shall know that I am the LORD" [15].

That is, what befell mount Seir is the fruit of its inward sin, bearing the same fruit as its deeds, and also for the building up of the people of God; for since these had usurped their rights, God defends His children for the sake of His holy name, "and they shall know that I am the LORD."
Let all Your enemies be scattered!
* Who is Seir (Edom), who gloats over Your Church, if not the violent enemy of the good, the shedder of blood?!
Behold, my enemy hates me!
His hatred of me is very ancient; it is a hatred of You, O Beloved of my soul!
He hates me greatly, because he hates You!
He prepared the Cross for You, and by it he himself was crushed!
* My enemy wants to seize my heart; it is neither his nor mine, but wholly Yours!
He wants to possess what is not his, to seize Your Kingdom that is within me!
Arise, O Lord, and let all Your enemies be scattered, and let all who hate Your name flee from before Your face!
* My enemy is arrogant, but his end is in hell!
As for me, bear me by Your Holy Spirit into the bosom of Your Father!

1 "Also, thou son of man, prophesy unto the mountains of Israel, and say, Ye mountains of Israel, hear the word of the LORD: 2 Thus saith the Lord GOD; Because the enemy hath said against you, Aha, even the ancient high places are ours in possession: 3 Therefore prophesy and say, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Because they have made you desolate, and swallowed you up on every side, that ye might be a possession unto the residue of the heathen, and ye are taken up in the lips of talkers, and are an infamy of the people: 4 Therefore, ye mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord GOD; Thus saith the Lord GOD to the mountains, and to the hills, to the rivers, and to the valleys, to the desolate wastes, and to the cities that are forsaken, which became a prey and derision to the residue of the heathen that are round about; 5 Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; Surely in the fire of my jealousy have I spoken against the residue of the heathen, and against all Idumea, which have appointed my land into their possession with the joy of all their heart, with despiteful minds, to cast it out for a prey. 6 Prophesy therefore concerning the land of Israel, and say unto the mountains, and to the hills, to the rivers, and to the valleys, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I have spoken in my jealousy and in my fury, because ye have borne the shame of the heathen: 7 Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; I have lifted up mine hand, Surely the heathen that are about you, they shall bear their shame. 8 But ye, O mountains of Israel, ye shall shoot forth your branches, and yield your fruit to my people of Israel;
